$$

question.:question/problem:
Find $(\mathbf{f}\times \mathbf{g})^{'}(t)$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{f}(t) & =⟨t,\hspace{0.167em}5,\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{4}⟩, \\ \mathbf{g}(t) & =⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{3},\hspace{0.167em}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the cross product rule, we can write:

$$
(\mathbf{f}\times \mathbf{g})^{'}(t)={\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)\times \mathbf{g}(t)+\mathbf{f}(t)\times {\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.167em}0,\hspace{0.167em}4{t}^{3}⟩ \\ {\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\hspace{0.167em}3{t}^{2},\hspace{0.167em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)\times \mathbf{g}(t) & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 4{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{2} & {t}^{3} & t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & t\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{2} & t\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ {t}^{2} & {t}^{3}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-4{t}^{6},\hspace{0.167em}4{t}^{5}-t,\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{3}⟩, \\ \mathbf{f}(t)\times {\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t) & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ t & 5 & {t}^{4} \\ 2t & 3{t}^{2} & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}5 & {t}^{4} \\ 3{t}^{2} & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}t & {t}^{4} \\ 2t & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}t & 5 \\ 2t & 3{t}^{2}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨5-3{t}^{6},\hspace{0.167em}2{t}^{5}-t,\hspace{0.167em}3{t}^{3}-10t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf{f}\times \mathbf{g})^{'}(t) & =⟨-4{t}^{6},\hspace{0.167em}4{t}^{5}-t,\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{3}⟩+⟨5-3{t}^{6},\hspace{0.167em}2{t}^{5}-t,\hspace{0.167em}3{t}^{3}-10t⟩ \\  & =⟨-7{t}^{6}+5,\hspace{0.167em}6{t}^{5}-2t,\hspace{0.167em}4{t}^{3}-10t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find $(\mathbf{f}\times \mathbf{g})^{'}(t)$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{f}(t) & =⟨6{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2t,\hspace{0.222em}6⟩ \\ \mathbf{g}(t) & =⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}3{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}4t-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the cross product rule, we can write:

$$
(\mathbf{f}\times \mathbf{g})^{'}(t)={\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)\times \mathbf{g}(t)+\mathbf{f}(t)\times {\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6)⟩ \\  & =⟨12t,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}6t,\hspace{0.222em}4⟩\end{aligned}

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)\times \mathbf{g}(t) & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 12t & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 3{t}^{2} & (4t-1)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3{t}^{2} & (4t-1)\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}12t & 0 \\ 3 & (4t-1)\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}12t & 2 \\ 3 & 3{t}^{2}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨8t-2,\hspace{0.222em}12t-48{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}36{t}^{3}-6⟩ \\ \mathbf{f}(t)\times {\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t) & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 6{t}^{2} & 2t & 6 \\ 0 & 6t & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2t & 6 \\ 6t & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}6{t}^{2} & 6 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}6{t}^{2} & 2t \\ 0 & 6t\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-28t,\hspace{0.222em}-24{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}36{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}

Finally,

question.:question/problem: Given $\mathbf{f}(t)=⟨1-{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}1-{t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}1-t⟩$, find $({\mathbf{f}}^{'}\times \mathbf{f})^{'}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the cross product rule, we can write:

$$({\mathbf{f}}^{'}\times \mathbf{f})^{'}(t)={\mathbf{f}}^{''}(t)\times \mathbf{f}(t)+{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)\times {\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)$$

Let's now find the first and second derivative of the function.

$$\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}-3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}-1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{f}}^{''}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2t)\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}-6t\hspace{0.167em},\hspace{0.167em}0⟩\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, we obtain:

question.:question/problem: Find $(u(t)\mathbf{f}(t))^{'}$ where $\mathbf{f}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}t \\ \operatorname{cos}t \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}$ and $u(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the scalar function multiple rule, we can write

$$
(u(t)\mathbf{f}(t))^{'}={u}^{'}(t)\mathbf{f}(t)+u(t){\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t).
$$

Let's find ${u}^{′}(t)$ and ${\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}t \\ -\operatorname{sin}t \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {u}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)=\operatorname{cos}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(u(t)\mathbf{f}(t))^{'} & ={u}^{'}(t)\mathbf{f}(t)+u(t){\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}t \\ \operatorname{cos}t \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}+\operatorname{sin}t\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}t \\ -\operatorname{sin}t \\ {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t \\ \operatorname{cos}t\operatorname{cos}t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}t\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t \\ -\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{sin}t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}2t \\ {\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}t\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}2t \\ -{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}2t \\ {\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}2t \\ \operatorname{cos}2t \\ {e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $\mathbf{f}(u)=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}u \\ {u}^{3} \\ \operatorname{ln}u\end{bmatrix}$ and $u(t)={e}^{t}$, then $(\mathbf{f}∘u)^{'}(t)=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the chain rule, we can write

$$
(\mathbf{f}∘u)^{'}(t)={\mathbf{f}}^{'}(u(t)){u}^{'}(t).
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(u) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{cos}u) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\hspace{0.167em}({u}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}u)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}u \\ 3{u}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{u}\end{bmatrix} \\ {u}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf{f}∘u)^{'}(t) & ={\mathbf{f}}^{'}(u(t)){u}^{'}(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}(u(t)) \\ 3(u(t))^{2} \\ \frac{1}{u(t)}\end{bmatrix}\cdot {u}^{'}(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}({e}^{t}) \\ 3({e}^{t})^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}({e}^{t}) \\ 3{e}^{2t} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}({e}^{t}){e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{3t} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar function multiple rule:

$$
\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}(t)\mathbf f(t)+u(t)\mathbf f^{\prime}(t).
$$

The scalar is itself a product. Differentiate both factors:

$$
u^{\prime}(t)=1\cdot\ln t+t\cdot\frac{1}{t}=\ln t+1.
$$



$$
\mathbf f^{\prime}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 t \\ e^{t} \\ - \frac{1}{t^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Substitute both terms and add corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}&=\big(\ln t+1\big)\begin{bmatrix}t^{2} \\ e^{t} \\ \frac{1}{t}\end{bmatrix}\\&\quad+\big(t \ln{\left(t \right)}\big)\begin{bmatrix}2 t \\ e^{t} \\ - \frac{1}{t^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\\&=\begin{bmatrix}t^{2} \left(3 \ln{\left(t \right)} + 1\right) \\ \left(\left(t + 1\right) \ln{\left(t \right)} + 1\right) e^{t} \\ \frac{1}{t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the third component, the two logarithmic terms cancel:

$$
\frac{\ln t+1}{t}-\frac{\ln t}{t}=\frac{1}{t}.
$$

The inner function is itself a composition. Differentiate the square root and its input $1+t^2$:

$$
u'(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+t^2}}\cdot2t=\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}.
$$

The outer vector derivative is

$$
\mathbf g'(u)=\begin{bmatrix}1/u \\ 2u \\ -1/u^2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf g\circ u)'(t)&=\mathbf g'(u(t))u'(t) \\

&=\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{t}{1+t^2} \\ 2t \\ -\dfrac{t}{(1+t^2)^{3/2}}\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $A(t)=t/(1+t^2)$, $B(t)=2t$, and $C(t)=-t/(1+t^2)^{3/2}$. These formulas hold for every real $t$, since $u(t)\geq1$.

question.:question/problem:
Find $\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}$, where

$$
u(t)=t + 2,\qquad \mathbf f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 t \\ 2 \\ t^{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar function multiple rule:

$$
\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}=u^{\prime}(t)\mathbf f(t)+u(t)\mathbf f^{\prime}(t).
$$

Differentiate the scalar and each vector component.

$$
u^{\prime}(t)=1.
$$



$$
\mathbf f^{\prime}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 3 t^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Substitute both contributions and add corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}&=\big(1\big)\begin{bmatrix}2 t \\ 2 \\ t^{3}\end{bmatrix}\\&\quad+\big(t + 2\big)\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 3 t^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $\mathbf h(t)=u(t)\mathbf f(t)$. For each component, the two terms are:

$$
\begin{aligned}h_{1}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(2 t\big)\\&\quad+\big(2 t + 4\big)\\&=4 t + 4\\h_{2}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(2\big)\\&\quad+\big(0\big)\\&=2\\h_{3}^{\prime}(t)&=\big(t^{3}\big)\\&\quad+\big(3 t^{2} \left(t + 2\right)\big)\\&=4 t^{3} + 6 t^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 Therefore,

$$
\big(u(t)\mathbf f(t)\big)^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}4 t + 4 \\ 2 \\ 4 t^{3} + 6 t^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf f(u)=\begin{bmatrix}e^{u} \\ \cos{\left(u \right)} \\ \sin{\left(u \right)}\end{bmatrix}$ and $u(t)=4 t - 3$. Find $(\mathbf f\circ u)'(t)$.

$$

Products and reciprocals of exponential factors simplify by adding or subtracting their exponents.

question.:question/problem: Given $f(t)=(- t^{3} - 1)\,i+(3 t^{2} + 3)\,j+t^{2}\,k$, evaluate $(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the dot product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime\prime}(t)\cdot f(t)+f^{\prime}(t)\cdot f^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- t^{3} - 1)=- 3 t^{2} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t^{2} + 3)=6 t \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{2})=2 t \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =- 3 t^{2}\,i+6 t\,j+2 t\,k \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t^{2})=- 6 t \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(6 t)=6 \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t)=2 \\ f^{\prime\prime}(t) & =- 6 t\,i+6\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(0)(-1)+(6)(3)+(2)(0) \\  & =18 \\ P_2 & =(0)(0)+(0)(0)+(0)(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(0) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

\begin{aligned}f(t) & =(t - 2)\,i- 2 t\,j+t\,k \\ g(t) & =(t^{2} + t)\,i+t\,j+t^{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the dot product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime}(t)\cdot g(t)+f(t)\cdot g^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t - 2)=1 \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 2 t)=-2 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1 \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =\,i-2\,j+\,k \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{2} + t)=2 t + 1 \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1 \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{3})=3 t^{2} \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =(2 t + 1)\,i+\,j+3 t^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(1)(t^{2} + t)+(-2)(t)+(1)(t^{3}) \\  & =t^{3} + t^{2} - t \\ P_2 & =(t - 2)(2 t + 1)+(- 2 t)(1)+(t)(3 t^{2}) \\  & =3 t^{3} + 2 t^{2} - 5 t - 2\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =4 t^{3} + 3 t^{2} - 6 t - 2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$ Assume $t>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the dot product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime}(t)\cdot g(t)+f(t)\cdot g^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 \ln{(t )})=- \frac{3}{t} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 2 t)=-2 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)=- \frac{2}{t^{2}} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =- \frac{3}{t}\,i-2\,j- \frac{2}{t^{2}}\,k \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t)=-3 \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 \ln{(t )})=\frac{3}{t} \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- \frac{2}{t}\right)=\frac{2}{t^{2}} \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =-3\,i+\frac{3}{t}\,j+\frac{2}{t^{2}}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\left(- \frac{3}{t}\right)(- 3 t)+(-2)(3 \ln{(t )})+\left(- \frac{2}{t^{2}}\right)\left(- \frac{2}{t}\right) \\  & =- 6 \ln{(t )} + 9 + \frac{4}{t^{3}} \\ P_2 & =(- 3 \ln{(t )})(-3)+(- 2 t)\left(\frac{3}{t}\right)+\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)\left(\frac{2}{t^{2}}\right) \\  & =9 \ln{(t )} - 6 + \frac{4}{t^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\cdot g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =3 \ln{(t )} + 3 + \frac{8}{t^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given $f(t)=⟨3 t^{3} + 3,\,2 t,\,2 t^{2} + 1⟩$, find $(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the dot product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime\prime}(t)\cdot f(t)+f^{\prime}(t)\cdot f^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t^{3} + 3)=9 t^{2} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t)=2 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t^{2} + 1)=4 t \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =⟨9 t^{2},\,2,\,4 t⟩ \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(9 t^{2})=18 t \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2)=0 \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(4 t)=4 \\ f^{\prime\prime}(t) & =⟨18 t,\,0,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(18 t)(3 t^{3} + 3)+(0)(2 t)+(4)(2 t^{2} + 1) \\  & =54 t^{4} + 8 t^{2} + 54 t + 4 \\ P_2 & =(9 t^{2})(9 t^{2})+(2)(2)+(4 t)(4 t) \\  & =81 t^{4} + 16 t^{2} + 4\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =135 t^{4} + 24 t^{2} + 54 t + 8\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given $f(t)=- 3 t^{3}\,i+(3 t^{2} - 2)\,j+2 t\,k$, find $(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the dot product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime\prime}(t)\cdot f(t)+f^{\prime}(t)\cdot f^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t^{3})=- 9 t^{2} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t^{2} - 2)=6 t \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t)=2 \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =- 9 t^{2}\,i+6 t\,j+2\,k \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 9 t^{2})=- 18 t \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(6 t)=6 \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2)=0 \\ f^{\prime\prime}(t) & =- 18 t\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(- 18 t)(- 3 t^{3})+(6)(3 t^{2} - 2)+(0)(2 t) \\  & =54 t^{4} + 18 t^{2} - 12 \\ P_2 & =(- 9 t^{2})(- 9 t^{2})+(6 t)(6 t)+(2)(2) \\  & =81 t^{4} + 36 t^{2} + 4\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f^{\prime}\cdot f)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =135 t^{4} + 54 t^{2} - 8\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given $f(t)=⟨3 t^{2} - 1,\,- 3 t - 3,\,3 t^{3} - 3⟩$, find $(f^{\prime}\times f)^{\prime}(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cross product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f^{\prime}\times f)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime\prime}(t)\times f(t)+f^{\prime}(t)\times f^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t^{2} - 1)=6 t \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t - 3)=-3 \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t^{3} - 3)=9 t^{2} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =⟨6 t,\,-3,\,9 t^{2}⟩ \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(6 t)=6 \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(-3)=0 \\ f^{\prime\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(9 t^{2})=18 t \\ f^{\prime\prime}(t) & =⟨6,\,0,\,18 t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 6 & 0 & 18 t \\ 3 t^{2} - 1 & - 3 t - 3 & 3 t^{3} - 3\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{1,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 18 t \\ - 3 t - 3 & 3 t^{3} - 3\end{vmatrix}=54 t^{2} + 54 t \\ P_{1,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}6 & 18 t \\ 3 t^{2} - 1 & 3 t^{3} - 3\end{vmatrix}=36 t^{3} - 18 t + 18 \\ P_{1,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 3 t^{2} - 1 & - 3 t - 3\end{vmatrix}=- 18 t - 18 \\ P_1 & =⟨54 t^{2} + 54 t,\,36 t^{3} - 18 t + 18,\,- 18 t - 18⟩ \\ P_2 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 6 t & -3 & 9 t^{2} \\ 6 t & -3 & 9 t^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{2,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 9 t^{2} \\ -3 & 9 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=0 \\ P_{2,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}6 t & 9 t^{2} \\ 6 t & 9 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=0 \\ P_{2,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}6 t & -3 \\ 6 t & -3\end{vmatrix}=0 \\ P_2 & =⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f^{\prime}\times f)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =⟨54 t^{2} + 54 t,\,36 t^{3} - 18 t + 18,\,- 18 t - 18⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find $(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2 t^{2} \\ t + 2\end{bmatrix} \\ g(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}t \\ t - 1 \\ - 3 t^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cross product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times g^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(-3)=0 \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t^{2})=4 t \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t + 2)=1 \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4 t \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1 \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t - 1)=1 \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t^{2})=- 6 t \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ - 6 t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 4 t & 1 \\ t & t - 1 & - 3 t^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{1,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}4 t & 1 \\ t - 1 & - 3 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=- 12 t^{3} - t + 1 \\ P_{1,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ t & - 3 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=t \\ P_{1,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 t \\ t & t - 1\end{vmatrix}=- 4 t^{2} \\ P_1 & =\begin{bmatrix}- 12 t^{3} - t + 1 \\ t \\ - 4 t^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ P_2 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -3 & 2 t^{2} & t + 2 \\ 1 & 1 & - 6 t\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{2,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 t^{2} & t + 2 \\ 1 & - 6 t\end{vmatrix}=- 12 t^{3} - t - 2 \\ P_{2,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}-3 & t + 2 \\ 1 & - 6 t\end{vmatrix}=2 - 17 t \\ P_{2,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 2 t^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=- 2 t^{2} - 3 \\ P_2 & =\begin{bmatrix}- 12 t^{3} - t - 2 \\ 2 - 17 t \\ - 2 t^{2} - 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\times g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}- 24 t^{3} - 2 t - 1 \\ 2 - 16 t \\ - 6 t^{2} - 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}$ given that $f(t)=⟨e^{- t},\,e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩$ and $v(t)=e^{t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar function multiple rule:

$$
(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}=v(t)f^{\prime}(t)+v^{\prime}(t)f(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{- t})=- e^{- t} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{3 t})=3 e^{3 t} \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{t + 3})=e^{t + 3} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =⟨- e^{- t},\,3 e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩ \\ v^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{t})=e^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(e^{t})⟨- e^{- t},\,3 e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3 e^{4 t},\,e^{t} e^{t + 3}⟩ \\ P_2 & =(e^{t})⟨e^{- t},\,e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,e^{4 t},\,e^{t} e^{t + 3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(v(t)f(t))^{\prime} & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =⟨0,\,4 e^{4 t},\,2 e^{2 t + 3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨\operatorname{sin}u,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}4v\operatorname{cos}u⟩.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}.$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(\operatorname{sin}u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v\operatorname{cos}u)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-4v\operatorname{sin}u⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(\operatorname{sin}u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v\operatorname{cos}u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}4\operatorname{cos}u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \operatorname{cos}u & 0 & -4v\operatorname{sin}u \\ 0 & 2v & 4\operatorname{cos}u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -4v\operatorname{sin}u \\ 2v & 4\operatorname{cos}u\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}u & -4v\operatorname{sin}u \\ 0 & 4\operatorname{cos}u\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{cos}u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨8{v}^{2}\operatorname{sin}u,\hspace{0.222em}-4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}u,\hspace{0.222em}2v\operatorname{cos}u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface defined by the equations

$$
\displaystyle x = u + v, y = v^{2} + \sin u, z = uv.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution: The fundamental vector product is $r_u\times r_v$, in that order. We have $r_u=\langle1,\cos u,v\rangle$ and $r_v=\langle1,2v,u\rangle$. Expanding the cross product gives $$r_u\times r_v=\langle u\cos u-2v^2,v-u,2v-\cos u\rangle.$$

question.:question/problem:
$${∬}_{D}\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A,\,D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le \pi \}$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨2u\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}3u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}u⟩$ for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le \pi .$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u\operatorname{cos}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}3\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u\operatorname{cos}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}-3u\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2\operatorname{sin}v & 3\operatorname{cos}v & 1 \\ 2u\operatorname{cos}v & -3u\operatorname{sin}v & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}v & 1 \\ -3u\operatorname{sin}v & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}v & 1 \\ 2u\operatorname{cos}v & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}v & 3\operatorname{cos}v \\ 2u\operatorname{cos}v & -3u\operatorname{sin}v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3u\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}2u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}-6u{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v-6u{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v⟩ \\  & =⟨3u\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}2u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}-6u⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨3u\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}2u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}-6u⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(3u\operatorname{sin}v)^{2}+(2u\operatorname{cos}v)^{2}+(-6u)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{u}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+4{u}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(5{u}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+4{u}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v)+4{u}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+4{u}^{2}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v)+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+4{u}^{2}+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+40{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+8)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}}\sqrt{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+8} \\  & =\sqrt{5}u\sqrt{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{{u}^{2}}=u$ since $u\ge 0$ on $D.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{\color{blue}\sqrt{5}u\sqrt{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+8}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the parametric surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=2u-v,\,y=3u+2,\,z=u+2v
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $-1\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨2u-v,\hspace{0.222em}3u+2,\hspace{0.222em}u+2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u+2),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u+2),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\hspace{0.222em}-5,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨6,\hspace{0.222em}-5,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's denote

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}-1\le v\le 1\}.
$$

Then, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{70}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}{∬}_{D}\text{ }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨-u+v,\hspace{0.222em}u-2v,\hspace{0.222em}3v⟩$ that is subject to the constraint ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 4.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-2,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9+1} \\  & =\sqrt{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that the region ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 4$ corresponds to the disk

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 4\},
$$

of radius $2.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{19}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{19}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{19}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{19}\cdot (\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$${∬}_{D}\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A,\,D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}u-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2}⟩$ for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-{v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-{v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2v,\hspace{0.222em}2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2v & 2v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2v & 2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 1 \\ 0 & -2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2v,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2v,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(2v)^{2}+(-4uv)^{2}+(-4uv)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+32{u}^{2}{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}(1+8{u}^{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}}\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}} \\  & =2v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{{v}^{2}}=v$ since $v\ge 0$ on $D.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{\color{blue}2v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that for a surface with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}.$

In part 4, we got the surface

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,\theta )=⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta ⟩,\hspace{1em}x\in [0,1],\hspace{1em}\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta ),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}4x\operatorname{cos}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}4x\operatorname{sin}\theta ⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{\theta }^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(x),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta ),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂\theta }(2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta )⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{\theta }^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta \end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}4x\operatorname{cos}\theta  & 4x\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta  & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta \end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4x\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0 & 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta \end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4x\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0 & -2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +8{x}^{3}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta ),\hspace{0.222em}-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨8{x}^{3},\hspace{0.222em}-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding norm is

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{\theta }^{'}‖ & =\sqrt{(8{x}^{3})^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +4{x}^{4}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{64{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}} \\  & =2{x}^{2}\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the parametric surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=u+v,\,y=2-3u,\,z=1+u-v
$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $-1\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u+v,\hspace{0.222em}2-3u,\hspace{0.222em}1+u-v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2-3u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(1+u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-3,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2-3u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(1+u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+4+9} \\  & =\sqrt{22}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's denote

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le 2,\hspace{0.222em}-1\le v\le 1\}.
$$

Then, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{22}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{22}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{22}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{22}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =4\sqrt{22}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the parametric surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=u,\,y={v}^{2},\,z=\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le \sqrt{3}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}2{v}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v & 2{v}^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2v & 2{v}^{2}\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2{v}^{2}\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-2{v}^{2})^{2}+(2v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{4}+4{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}({v}^{2}+1)} \\  & =2v\sqrt{{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{{v}^{2}}=v$ since $v\ge 0$ on $D.$

Next, let's denote

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}0\le v\le \sqrt{3}\}.
$$

Then, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2v\sqrt{{v}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{0}^{1}2v\sqrt{{v}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2v\sqrt{{v}^{2}+1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}u\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2v\sqrt{{v}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
w={v}^{2}+1\,⇒\,\text{d}w=2v\,\text{d}v,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}2v\sqrt{{v}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{w}\,\text{d}w \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{w}^{3}}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\sqrt{{4}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the parametric surface defined by the equations 

$$
x={u}^{2},\,y=uv,\,z=\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $1\le v\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}uv,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}u,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & v & 0 \\ 0 & u & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}v & 0 \\ u & v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-2uv,\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-2uv,\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({v}^{2})^{2}+(-2uv)^{2}+(2{u}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{v}^{4}+4{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{u}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{({v}^{2}+2{u}^{2})^{2}} \\  & ={v}^{2}+2{u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's denote

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}1\le v\le 2\}.
$$

Then, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({v}^{2}+2{u}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({v}^{2}+2{u}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[u{v}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({v}^{2}+\frac{2}{3})\text{d}v \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}+\frac{2}{3}v]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[{2}^{3}+2(2)-({1}^{3}+2(1))] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(9) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}u-v⟩$ that is subject to the constraint ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 9.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that the region ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 9$ corresponds to the disk

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 9\},
$$

of radius $3.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot (\pi \cdot {3}^{2}) \\  & =9\pi \sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=u,\,y=v,\,z={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}.$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 2u \\ 0 & 1 & -2v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2u \\ 1 & -2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2u \\ 0 & -2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=u,\,y=v,\,z=u-{e}^{v}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}.$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}u-{e}^{v}⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-{e}^{v})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-{e}^{v})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-{e}^{v}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -{e}^{v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -{e}^{v}\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -{e}^{v}\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{v},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface defined by the equations 

$$
x={u}^{2}+1,\,y={v}^{3}+1,\,z=2u+v.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}.$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2}+1,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{3}+1,\hspace{0.222em}2u+v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}+1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{3}+1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{3}+1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}3{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 3{v}^{2} & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3{v}^{2} & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 3{v}^{2}\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-6{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-2u,\hspace{0.222em}6u{v}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$${∬}_{D}\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A,\,D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le \pi \}$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v⟩$ for $0\le u\le 4$ and $0\le v\le \pi .$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}-{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & {e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v & {e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v \\ 0 & {e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v & -{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v & {e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v \\ {e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v & -{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & {e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v \\ 0 & -{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & {e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v \\ 0 & {e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{2u}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v),\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{2u},\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨-{e}^{2u},\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-{e}^{2u})^{2}+({e}^{u}\operatorname{sin}v)^{2}+({e}^{u}\operatorname{cos}v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{4u}+{e}^{2u}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+{e}^{2u}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{4u}+{e}^{2u}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v)} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{4u}+{e}^{2u}} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2u}({e}^{2u}+1)} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2u}}\sqrt{{e}^{2u}+1} \\  & ={e}^{u}\sqrt{{e}^{2u}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{\color{blue}{e}^{u}\sqrt{{e}^{2u}+1}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$${∬}_{D}\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A,\,D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le \pi \}$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2u\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}u\operatorname{cos}v⟩$ for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le \pi .$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u\operatorname{cos}v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}2\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{cos}v⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u\operatorname{cos}v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}-u\operatorname{sin}v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 2\operatorname{sin}v & \operatorname{cos}v \\ 0 & 2u\operatorname{cos}v & -u\operatorname{sin}v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}v & \operatorname{cos}v \\ 2u\operatorname{cos}v & -u\operatorname{sin}v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & \operatorname{cos}v \\ 0 & -u\operatorname{sin}v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 2\operatorname{sin}v \\ 0 & 2u\operatorname{cos}v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v-2u{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v,\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}4{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}v⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}4{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}4{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(2u)^{2}+(2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}v)^{2}+(4{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{u}^{2}+4{u}^{4}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+16{u}^{4}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v} \\  & =\sqrt{4{u}^{2}+4{u}^{4}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}v+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v)+12{u}^{4}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v} \\  & =\sqrt{4{u}^{2}+4{u}^{4}+12{u}^{4}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v} \\  & =\sqrt{4{u}^{2}(1+{u}^{2}+3{u}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v)} \\  & =\sqrt{4{u}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}+3{u}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v} \\  & =2u\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}+3{u}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{{u}^{2}}=u$ since $u\ge 0$ on $D.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{\color{blue}2u\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}+3{u}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}v}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}1-2u+5v⟩$ that is subject to the constraint ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(1-2u+5v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-2⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(1-2u+5v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 5\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}-5,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}-5,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{(2)}^{2}+{(-5)}^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+25+1} \\  & =\sqrt{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that the region ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 2$ corresponds to the disk

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 2\}
$$

of radius $\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{30}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{30}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{30}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{30}\cdot (\pi \cdot (\sqrt{2})^{2}) \\  & =2\pi \sqrt{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}u+2v,\hspace{0.222em}2u-v⟩$ that is subject to the constraint ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-5,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨-5,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-5)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+1+9} \\  & =\sqrt{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that the region ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 1$ corresponds to the disk

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 1\},
$$

of radius $1.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{35}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{35}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{35}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{35}\cdot (\pi \cdot {1}^{2}) \\  & =\pi \sqrt{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}u\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}v\operatorname{cos}u⟩.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}.$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v\operatorname{cos}u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{sin}v,\hspace{0.222em}-v\operatorname{sin}u⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u\operatorname{sin}v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v\operatorname{cos}u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{cos}u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & \operatorname{sin}v & -v\operatorname{sin}u \\ 0 & u\operatorname{cos}v & \operatorname{cos}u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{sin}v & -v\operatorname{sin}u \\ u\operatorname{cos}v & \operatorname{cos}u\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -v\operatorname{sin}u \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}u\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & \operatorname{sin}v \\ 0 & u\operatorname{cos}v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}u\operatorname{sin}v+uv\operatorname{sin}u\operatorname{cos}v,\hspace{0.222em}-\operatorname{cos}u,\hspace{0.222em}u\operatorname{cos}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -1 & 5\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 1 & 5\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩,\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(3{u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}6u,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(3{u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 6u & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}6u & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 6u \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-6u,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-6u⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨-6u,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-6u⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-6u)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(-6u)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{u}^{2}+4+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{72{u}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4(18{u}^{2}+1)} \\  & =2\sqrt{18{u}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{\color{blue}2\sqrt{18{u}^{2}+1}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-2{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨-2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-2{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-2{v}^{2})^{2}+(-2{u}^{2})^{2}+(4uv)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}+16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({u}^{4}+{v}^{4}+4{u}^{2}{v}^{2})} \\  & =2\sqrt{{u}^{4}+{v}^{4}+4{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{\color{blue}2\sqrt{{u}^{4}+{v}^{4}+4{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the parametric surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=2u-v,\,y=3u+2,\,z=u+2v
$$

for $0\le u\le 5$ and $-1\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u-v,\,3u+2,\,u+2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,3,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\,-5,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨6,\,-5,\,3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's denote

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 5,\,-1\le v\le 1}.
$$

Then, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{70}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}{∬}_{D}\text{ }\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot 5\cdot 2 \\  & =10 \sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the parametric surface $r(u,v)=⟨-u+v,\,u-2v,\,3v⟩$ that is subject to the constraint ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 20.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,3,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨3,\,3,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9+1} \\  & =\sqrt{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that the region ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 20$ corresponds to the disk

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 20},
$$

of radius $2 \sqrt{5}.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{19}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{19}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{19}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{19}\cdot (\pi \cdot (2 \sqrt{5})^{2}) \\  & =20 \sqrt{19} \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\iint_D\boxed{}\,\mathrm{d}A,\quad D=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 2\}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $r(u,v)=\langle u + v,\,3 - v,\,3 u + 5 v + 1\rangle$ for $0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 2.$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint_S\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u &=\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\rangle \\  &=\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(u + v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(3 - v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(3 u + 5 v + 1\right)\rangle \\  &=\langle 1,\,0,\,3\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v &=\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\rangle \\  &=\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(u + v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(3 - v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(3 u + 5 v + 1\right)\rangle \\  &=\langle 1,\,-1,\,5\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v &=\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  &=\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -1 & 5\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 5\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\rangle \\  &=\langle 3,\,-2,\,-1\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\| &=\left\|\langle 3,\,-2,\,-1\rangle\right\| \\  &=\sqrt{\left(3\right)^2+\left(-2\right)^2+\left(-1\right)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{9+4+1} \\  &=\sqrt{14} \\  &=\sqrt{14}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\mathrm{d}S &=\iint_D\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm{d}A \\  &=\iint_D \sqrt{14}\,\mathrm{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $r(u,v)=\langle 2 u^{2},\,u - v^{2},\,v^{2}\rangle$ for $0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2.$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint_S\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u &=\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\rangle \\  &=\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(2 u^{2}\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(u - v^{2}\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(v^{2}\right)\rangle \\  &=\langle 4 u,\,1,\,0\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v &=\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\rangle \\  &=\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(2 u^{2}\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(u - v^{2}\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(v^{2}\right)\rangle \\  &=\langle 0,\,- 2 v,\,2 v\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v &=\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 4 u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 2 v & 2 v\end{vmatrix} \\  &=\langle \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ - 2 v & 2 v\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}4 u & 0 \\ 0 & 2 v\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}4 u & 1 \\ 0 & - 2 v\end{vmatrix}\rangle \\  &=\langle 2 v,\,- 8 u v,\,- 8 u v\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\| &=\left\|\langle 2 v,\,- 8 u v,\,- 8 u v\rangle\right\| \\  &=\sqrt{\left(2 v\right)^2+\left(- 8 u v\right)^2+\left(- 8 u v\right)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{4 v^{2}+64 u^{2} v^{2}+64 u^{2} v^{2}} \\  &=\sqrt{128 u^{2} v^{2} + 4 v^{2}} \\  &=\sqrt{4 v^{2} \left(32 u^{2} + 1\right)} \\  &=\sqrt{4 v^{2}}\sqrt{32 u^{2} + 1} \\  &=2 v \sqrt{32 u^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{v^2}=v$ since $v\ge 0$ on $D.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\mathrm{d}S &=\iint_D\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm{d}A \\  &=\iint_D 2 v \sqrt{32 u^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}A\end{aligned}
$$
