question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface defined by the equations

$$
x=u+v,\qquad y=u^2+v,\qquad z=uv.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization $\mathbf r(u,v)$, the fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Differentiate with respect to one parameter while holding the other fixed.

In vector form, $\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u+v,\,u^2+v,\,uv\rangle$. The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,\,2u,\,v\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,1,\,u\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 2u & v \\ 1 & 1 & u\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Each component subtracts two nonzero products. In particular, the middle cofactor has a minus sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_1&=(2u)u-v\cdot1=2u^2-v,\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_2&=-(1\cdot u-v\cdot1)=v-u,\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_3&=1\cdot1-(2u)1=1-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\langle 2u^2-v,\,v-u,\,1-2u\rangle.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u+v,\,uv,\,u\sin(uv)\rangle.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization $\mathbf r(u,v)$, the fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Differentiate with respect to one parameter while holding the other fixed.

The third coordinate requires the product rule when differentiating with respect to $u$, and the chain rule for $\sin(uv)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\bigl(u\sin(uv)\bigr)&=\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv),\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\bigl(u\sin(uv)\bigr)&=u^2\cos(uv).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,\,v,\,\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv)\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,u,\,u^2\cos(uv)\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & v & \sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv) \\ 1 & u & u^2\cos(uv)\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Expand and simplify one component at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_1&=u^2v\cos(uv)-u\bigl(\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv)\bigr)\\&=-u\sin(uv),\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_2&=-\bigl(u^2\cos(uv)-\sin(uv)-uv\cos(uv)\bigr)\\&=\sin(uv)+u(v-u)\cos(uv),\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_3&=1\cdot u-v\cdot1=u-v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\langle -u\sin(uv),\,\sin(uv)+u(v-u)\cos(uv),\,u-v\rangle.
$$

The first component retains the product-rule term after the two $u^2v\cos(uv)$ terms cancel.

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface defined by the equations

$$
x=u,\qquad y=v,\qquad z=uv.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization $\mathbf r(u,v)$, the fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Differentiate with respect to one parameter while holding the other fixed.

In vector form, the surface is $\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u,\,v,\,uv\rangle$. The tangent vectors to its grid curves are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,\,0,\,v\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 0,\,1,\,u\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Their ordered cross product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{vmatrix}\\&=\langle 0\cdot u-v\cdot1,\,-(1\cdot u-v\cdot0),\,1\cdot1-0\cdot0\rangle\\&=\langle -v,\,-u,\,1\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the part of the parametric surface

$$

that is subject to the constraint $u^2+v^2\le3$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface parametrized by $\mathbf r(u,v)$ over $D$,

$$
A(S)=\iint_D\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\mathrm dA.
$$

First compute the tangent vectors:

$$
\mathbf r_u=\langle1,1,1\rangle,\qquad \mathbf r_v=\langle-1,1,2\rangle.
$$

Their fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}

The parameter region $D=[-1,1]\times[0,2]$ is a rectangle. Its side lengths are $1-(-1)=2$ and $2-0=2$, so its area is $4$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The surface-area integrand is the magnitude of the fundamental vector product:

$$
A(S)=\iint_D \left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm dA.
$$

First, differentiate each coordinate with respect to each parameter:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 2u,\sin v,2\cos v\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 0,u\cos v,-2u\sin v\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Compute the cross product of these tangent vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2u&\sin v&2\cos v\\0&u\cos v&-2u\sin v\end{vmatrix}\\&=\langle -2u\sin^2v-2u\cos^2v,4u^2\sin v,2u^2\cos v\rangle\\&=\langle -2u,4u^2\sin v,2u^2\cos v\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Take its magnitude, using the sum of the squares of its components:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|&=\sqrt{4u^2+16u^4\sin^2v+4u^4\cos^2v}\\&=\sqrt{4u^2\left(1+4u^2\sin^2v+u^2\cos^2v\right)}\\&=\sqrt{4u^2\left(1+u^2+3u^2\sin^2v\right)}\\&=2u\sqrt{1+u^2+3u^2\sin^2v}.\end{aligned}
$$

We used $\sin^2v+\cos^2v=1$ in both simplifications. Also, $\sqrt{u^2}=|u|=u$ because $u\ge0$ on $D.$ The edge $u=0$ collapses to a point; it has zero area and does not introduce repeated coverage of the surface interior.

Therefore, the required integral is

$$
A(S)=\iint_D 2u\sqrt{1+u^2+3u^2\sin^2v}\,\mathrm dA.
$$

The missing expression is $2u\sqrt{1+u^2+3u^2\sin^2v}$; the integral does not need to be evaluated.

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}- u v\\- u\\v\end{pmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- u v)&=- v\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- u)&=-1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- u v)&=- u\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- v\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}- u\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- v & -1 & 0\\- u & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(-1)(1)\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- v)(1)\\&\quad +(0)(- u)\\&=v.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- v)(0)\\&\quad -(-1)(- u)\\&=- u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\v\\- u\end{pmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u)&=1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(2 u - e^{v})&=2\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(2 u - e^{v})&=- e^{v}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\- e^{v}\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1 & 2 & 0\\0 & - e^{v} & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(2)(1)\\&\quad -(0)(- e^{v})\\&=2.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(1)(1)\\&\quad +(0)(0)\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(1)(- e^{v})\\&\quad -(2)(0)\\&=- e^{v}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\- e^{v}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2xy+{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\left(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\left(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2yz,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+2z\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2z)r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=xy+{y}^{2}z+x{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+2xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂y}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\left(\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\left(\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +0\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y)={y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂g}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =0\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that $$
\displaystyle w(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2},
$$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=2r+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=2,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2r}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(r,\theta )={r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{∂g}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r}=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂g}{∂\theta }=-3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $u(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xyz,$ find $\frac{∂u}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $u(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =\frac{∂u}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂u}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂u}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂u}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z}=2{x}^{2}z+xy\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}(2z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $v(x,y,z)=2y-xz,$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $v(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂v}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂v}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂v}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂v}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂v}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂v}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x}=-z,\,\frac{∂v}{∂y}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-z, \\ \frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta } & =-(-z)r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2)r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4{x}^{2}{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂z}=8{x}^{2}z\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂z} & =8{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}{z}^{2}+xz,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2{y}^{2}z+x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $u(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂u}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂y}=\frac{∂u}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂u}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ,\,\frac{∂u}{∂\theta }=4r\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(4r\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $u(r,\theta )=r(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂u}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂x}=\frac{∂u}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂u}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂r}=2+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂u}{∂\theta }=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)={x}^{3}{z}^{4}+{y}^{3}{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

question.:question/problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )={r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2y-xy,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(x-1)\operatorname{ln}(2x+1),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}.

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{2x+1}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(x-1)\cdot \frac{2}{2x+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2x+1)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2(x-1)}{2x+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & =\frac{2(0-1)}{2(0)+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2(0)+1) \\  & =(-2)+\operatorname{ln}(1) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-2.$

question.:question/problem:
If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is defined by the equation $y=f(x)\cdot h(x),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi .$

Slope $\,=${{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}+h\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =-2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & =-2{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =-2{e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2{e}^{\pi }.$

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=cos⁡xlog⁡x,$ find ${f}^{′}(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(cos⁡x)}^{′}log⁡x+cos⁡x{(log⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =(-sin⁡x)(log⁡x)+(cos⁡x)\left(\frac{1}{xln⁡10}\right) \\  & =\frac{cos⁡x}{xln⁡10}-sin⁡xlog⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)={e}^{x}$ and $v(x)=2+sin⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}({e}^{x}sec⁡(x))^{′} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =({e}^{x})^{′}\cdot (2+sin⁡(x))+{e}^{x}\cdot (2+sin⁡(x))^{′} \\  & =({e}^{x})(2+sin⁡(x))+({e}^{x})(cos⁡(x)) \\  & =(2+sin⁡(x)){e}^{x}+{e}^{x}cos⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=2{x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=cos⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{x}^{2}cos⁡(x))^{′} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(2{x}^{2})^{′}\cdot cos⁡(x)+2{x}^{2}\cdot (cos⁡(x))^{′} \\  & =(4x)(cos⁡(x))+(2{x}^{2})(-sin⁡(x)) \\  & =4xcos⁡(x)-2{x}^{2}sin⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $v(x)=tan⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{x}tan⁡(x))^{′} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(\sqrt{x})^{′}\cdot tan⁡(x)+\sqrt{x}\cdot (tan⁡(x))^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}(tan⁡(x))+(\sqrt{x})({sec}^{2}⁡(x)) \\  & =\frac{tan⁡(x)}{2\sqrt{x}}+\sqrt{x}{sec}^{2}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)={4}^{x}$ and $v(x)=tan⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\frac{\pi }{2}} & =-(\frac{\pi }{2}+2)sin⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+cos⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =-(\frac{\pi }{2}+2)(1)+0 \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Differentiate ${x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}+f\frac{\text{d}(x)}{\text{d}x} \\  & =x\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1 \\  & =(2-3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(3+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$

question.:question/problem:
The pastry shop's total cost and revenue per month (in dollars) from selling cakes can be modeled by the equations $y=1\,600+5n$ and $y=64+17n,$ respectively, where $n$ is the number of cakes sold.

question.:question/problem:
Mary wonders where and when they'd meet if Sam left home $3.8$ minutes earlier and walked with a speed of $50$ meters per minute. She finds that the distance $d$ from home they'd meet can be modeled using the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}d+60t &=960 \\ d-50t &=190.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $t$ is the time (in minutes) since Mary left the community park.

Mary and Sam would meet at a distance of $\,$
{{field-2}}$\,$meters from home.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve the given system of linear equations, we will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the second equation looks like the easiest.

Using the second equation, we can isolate $d$ adding to both sides of the equation $50t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d-50t &=190 \\ d &=190+50t\end{aligned}
$$

So, we replace $d$ with $190+50t$ in the first equation and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d+60t=960 \\ (190+50t)+60t & =960 \\ 190+110t & =960 \\ 110t & =960-190 \\ 110t & =770 \\ t & =\frac{770}{110} \\ t & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, they would have met after $t=7$ minutes.

If we substitute $t=7$ into $d=190+50t$, we can find the value of $d:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =190+50t \\  & =190+50(7) \\  & =540\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, they meet at a distance of $540$ meters from home.

question.:question/problem:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6x - 8y - 31 &=0 \\ 2x - 4y - 6 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6x - 8y - 31 &=0 && (1) \\ 2x - 4y - 6 &=0 && (2)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2x - 4y - 6 &= 0 \\ 2x - 4y &= 6 \\ 2x &= 6 + 4y \\ x &= \dfrac{6 + 4y}{2} \\ x &= 3 + 2y \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=3+2y$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 6x - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 6(3 + 2y) - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 18 + 12y - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ -13 + 4y &= 0 \\ 4y &= 13 \\ y &= \dfrac{13}{4} \end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute

$$
y=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 6x - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 8\left(\dfrac{13}{4}\right) - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 26 - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 57 &= 0 \\ 6x &= 57 \\ x &= \dfrac{19}{2} \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=\dfrac{19}{2}$ and

$$
y=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

, which can be written as

$$
\left(\dfrac{19}{2},\dfrac{13}{4}\right)
$$

question.:question/problem: The inequality $-10\le x\le 3$ can be expressed in interval notation as
question.:question/worked-solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "or equal to" symbols. So, the endpoints $-10$ and $3$ *are* included. 

$$
-10\,\,\le \,\,x\,\,\le \,\,3
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
[-10,3]
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in [-10,3].
$$

question.:question/problem:
Suppose $$
\displaystyle \int_{C_{1}}f(x, y)ds = 2
$$ for some function $f(x, y)$, where $C_{1}$ is parametrized by ${\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}⟩$ for $0 \le t \le 1$.

Which of the following must be true?

1. $$
\displaystyle \int_{-C_{1}}f(x, y)ds =-2
$$
2. $$
\displaystyle \int_{-C_{1}}f(x, y)ds = 2
$$
3. $$
\displaystyle \int_{C_{2}}f(x, y)ds = 4,
$$ where $C_{2}$ is parametrized by ${\mathbf{r}}_{2}(u)=⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}4{u}^{2}⟩$ for $0 \le u \le \frac{1}{2}$.
question.:question/worked-solution: A scalar line integral with respect to arc length is unchanged by reversing orientation, so statement II is true and statement I is false. Also $r_2(u)=r_1(2u)$ for $0\le u\le\tfrac12$, which traverses the same curve once. Its scalar line integral is $2$, rather than $4$. Thus only II must be true.

question.:question/problem:
![](images/55/558dbbc424725ca0d9bad628968489cc2e32d67136102290666ff055a634bc16.png)

Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is a path that traverses a semicircle of radius $2$ once in the counterclockwise direction, as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The path $C$ is made up of two parts, as shown below:

![](images/82/82fedadbb33b1747832bac25d9cda8e0b6b18b0fab411a870e90bc09ce47226e.png)

Now, we make use of the following facts:

- If $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ is a piecewise-smooth curve, we have

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s.
$$

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ is a semi-circle of radius $r=2.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\,\text{d}s=\pi r=2\pi .
$$

The path ${C}_{2}$ is a line segment of length $4.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\,\text{d}s=4.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=2\pi +4=2(\pi +2).
$$

question.:question/worked-solution: The integral of $1$ with respect to arc length is the length of $C$. The diagram shows a quarter-circle arc of radius $2$ and its straight chord. The arc length is $2(\pi/2)=\pi$, and the chord length is $\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt2$. Hence $$\int_C ds=\pi+2\sqrt2.$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curves $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$, defined parametrically as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\hspace{1em}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{cos}t⟩, & 0\le t\le 2\pi  \\ {C}_{2}:\hspace{1em}{\mathbf{r}}_{2}(\theta ) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}2\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{cos}2\theta ⟩, & 0\le \theta \le \pi \end{aligned}
$$

Now suppose $$
\displaystyle \int_{C_{1}}f(x, y)ds = k
$$ for some function $f(x, y)$ and real number $k$. Which of the following must be true?

1. $$
\displaystyle \int_{-C_{1}}f(x, y)ds = k
$$
2. $$
\displaystyle \int_{C_{2}}f(x, y)ds = k
$$
3. $$
\displaystyle \int_{C_{2}}f(x, y)ds = \frac{1}{2}k
$$
question.:question/worked-solution: Scalar line integrals are independent of orientation, so I holds. Set $t=2\theta$; as $\theta$ runs from $0$ to $\pi$, $t$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$. Both parametrizations therefore traverse the same circle once, giving the same integral $k$. Thus II holds. III does not hold for arbitrary $k$, so the statements that must be true are I and II.

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=5.
$$

$$

$$

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

The paths ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are line segments of length $8.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs have lengths $8$ and $6.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\,\text{d}s=\sqrt{{8}^{2}+{6}^{2}}=10.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=8+10+8=26.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_1:\quad \mathbf r_1(t)&=\langle t,t^2\rangle, &0\le t\le 2,\\
C_2:\quad \mathbf r_2(u)&=\langle 2u,4u^2\rangle, &0\le u\le 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose $f$ is continuous along the curves and

$$
\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3.
$$

The notation $-C_1$ means $C_1$ with its orientation reversed. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $C_1$, eliminating $t$ gives $y=x^2$ with $0\le x\le 2$. For $C_2$, $x=2u$ gives $y=4u^2=x^2$, again with $0\le x\le 2$. Both trace this entire parabolic arc once, in the same direction; equivalently, $\mathbf r_2(u)=\mathbf r_1(2u)$.

Independence of parametrization gives

$$
\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3.
$$

Changing parameter speed does not multiply this value by $2$, so the proposed value $-6$ is incorrect. Independence of orientation also gives

$$
\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3,
$$

so the proposed value $3$ is incorrect. Select only the statement with $\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3$. A scalar line integral may be negative when $f$ takes negative values; the nonnegative arc-length element does not force the integral to be positive.

$$

What is the value of $\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
A scalar line integral with respect to arc length is independent of orientation. Reversing the arrows does not change the arc-length element $\mathrm{d}s$ or the values of $f$ along the curve. Therefore,

$$
\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=6.
$$

The answer is $6$. Reversing orientation does not negate the integral, cancel it, or count the curve twice.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C_1$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_1(t)=\langle\sqrt{1+9t^2},3t\rangle
$$

for $0\le t\le \frac13$. The curve $C_2$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_2(u)=\langle\sqrt{1+(1-2u)^2},1-2u\rangle
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac12$.

Suppose $f$ is continuous along the curves and

$$
\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=k.
$$

The notation $-C_2$ means $C_2$ with its orientation reversed. Which statements must be true for every such $f$? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $C_1$, $y=3t$, so $x=\sqrt{1+y^2}$ and $y$ increases from $0$ to $1$. For $C_2$, $y=1-2u$, so $x=\sqrt{1+y^2}$ and $y$ decreases from $1$ to $0$. Thus both trace exactly once the same branch and interval,

$$
x=\sqrt{1+y^2},\qquad 0\le y\le 1,
$$

with opposite orientations. In particular,

$$
\mathbf r_2(u)=\mathbf r_1\!\left(\frac{1-2u}{3}\right).
$$

A scalar line integral with respect to arc length is independent of both parametrization and orientation. Hence

$$
\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=k.
$$

Reversing $C_2$ once more also preserves the value:

$$
\int_{-C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=k.
$$

The parameter change has derivative $-2/3$, but this is not a factor multiplying the line integral: the speed factor in $\mathrm{d}s$ and the parameter interval change together. The proposed value $2k/3$ is therefore not guaranteed. It agrees with $k$ when $k=0$, but fails, for example, when $f=1$ and $k$ is the positive length of this arc.

Select the statements with values $k$ on $C_2$ and on $-C_2$.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C_1$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_1(t)=\langle 2(t)^4-(t)^2,(t)\rangle
$$

for $0\le t\le 2$. The curve $C_2$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_2(u)=\langle 2(1-3u)^4-(1-3u)^2,(1-3u)\rangle
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac{1}{3}$. Suppose $f$ is continuous along both curves and

$$
\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-7.
$$

A minus sign on a curve means its orientation is reversed. **Which statements must be true** for every such $f$? Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write points on the known curve in terms of a geometric parameter $z$:

$$
\mathbf R(z)=\langle 2(z)^4-(z)^2,(z)\rangle.
$$

For $C_1$, $z=t$ increases from $0$ to $2$. For $C_2$, $z=1-3u$ decreases from $1$ to $0$. Eliminating the parameter on $C_1$ gives $x=2y^4-y^2$. The other curve covers only the part with $0\le z\le 1$, rather than $0\le z\le 2$. A shared Cartesian equation alone is insufficient. A continuous function supported near an interior point of the omitted arc can be scaled to give any prescribed nonzero integral on the full curve, while its integral on the subarc stays zero. Thus no nonzero fixed multiple of the full integral is guaranteed on the subarc. 

Reversing $C_1$ always preserves its value:

$$
\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-7.
$$

Changing the parameter speed does not supply a multiplicative factor. 

Statement 1, $\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-7$, is **true**. Statement 2, $\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-7$, is **not guaranteed**. Statement 3, $\int_{-C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-\frac{7}{3}$, is **not guaranteed**.

question.:question/problem:
The paths $C$ and $D$ trace exactly the same geometric arc once, in the same direction. The path $D$ follows $C$ in the same direction.

The parametrization of $D$ runs 2 times as fast, with its parameter interval shortened accordingly. Suppose $f$ is continuous along the arc and

$$
\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=7.
$$

What is the value of $\int_{D} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Scalar line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of parametrization and orientation. Both paths cover the same arc once, so

$$
\int_{D} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=7.
$$

The speed change is offset by the shortened parameter interval. Reversing direction does not negate the integral, and a single traversal does not cancel it. Neither multiplying nor dividing by the parameter speed is appropriate.

Calculate

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length equals the length $L$ of the path:

$$
\int_C\,\mathrm{d}s=L.
$$

The endpoints are $A(2,-1)$ and $B(-6,-1)$. The segment is horizontal. Its endpoint distance is

$$

$$

Here the path is the segment itself, so

$$
L=d=8.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C\,\mathrm{d}s=8.
$$

Reversing the direction leaves traveled length unchanged.

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length equals the length $L$ of the path:

$$
\int_C\,\mathrm{d}s=L.
$$

The supplied radius determines the diameter:

$$
d=2r=2(5)=10.

Therefore,

$$
\oint_C\,\mathrm{d}s=10 \pi.
$$

Reversing the direction leaves traveled length unchanged. A closed path has zero net displacement, but its length is positive.

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)={e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{-t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y={e}^{-t}$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2{e}^{-t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & ={e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{e}^{-t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2{e}^{-t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot ({e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{e}^{-t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that
$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$
and
$\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{2t}\right)\cdot 1+\left(\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\right)\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{3}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4}{2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(1))] & =\frac{2}{1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+xz$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+e\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+yz+xz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+yz+xz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+yz+xz)\,k \\  & =(y+z)\,i+(x+z)\,j+(y+x)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y={e}^{t},$ and $z=e$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e)\,k \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k) \\  & =({e}^{t}+e)\cdot 1+(t+e)\cdot {e}^{t}+({e}^{t}+t)\cdot 0 \\  & ={e}^{t}+e+t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t+1} \\  & ={e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t},4t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=4t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡xy$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡xy)\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{xy}\,i+\frac{x}{xy}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\,j) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}-\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\  & =\frac{2-t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{t}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y,z)=z(x+y)$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & ={e}^{t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{3}$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)={t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]$ at $t=-1$ given that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{sin}t\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t)\text{ }\mathbf{j}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).

$$

$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1-2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{t+1}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1-2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t+{e}^{t+1}\cdot (1-2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t+{e}^{t+1}-2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t \\  & ={e}^{t+1}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t}⟩$ at the point $t=9.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right),\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y},-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=\sqrt{t}$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(9))] & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{x}^{2},2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨3{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t,2\operatorname{cos}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}t,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨3{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t,2\operatorname{cos}t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}t,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩ \\  & =3{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t+2\operatorname{cos}t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t) \\  & =3{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\operatorname{cos}t-2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))] & =3{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-2\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =3\cdot {\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}-1 \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}-4}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\hspace{-0.167em}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}t}\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =4t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (4t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\cdot 4t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}t}\cdot \frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}t} \\  & =\frac{2t\operatorname{arctan}t+1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}t}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},2t-1⟩$ at the point $t=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=2t-1$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨2{t}^{2},-2(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},2-4t⟩\cdot ⟨2t,2⟩ \\  & =2{t}^{2}\cdot 2t+(2-4t)\cdot 2 \\  & =4{t}^{3}-8t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(0))] & =4(0)^{3}-8(0)+4 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2t,\sqrt{t},3t-1⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t,y=\sqrt{t}$ and $z=3t-1$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨\sqrt{t}(3t-1),2t(3t-1),2t\sqrt{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨(3t-1)\sqrt{t},6{t}^{2}-2t,2t\sqrt{t}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},3⟩ \\  & =(3t-1)\sqrt{t}\cdot 2+(6{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+2t\sqrt{t}\cdot 3 \\  & =6t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}+6t\sqrt{t} \\  & =12t\sqrt{t}-2\sqrt{t}+\frac{3{t}^{2}-t}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(1))] & =12(1)\sqrt{1}-2\sqrt{1}+\frac{3(1)^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,4,\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩$ at the point $t=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:

$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3}),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}+{y}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨{z}^{2},3{y}^{2},2xz⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=4$ and $z=\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨(\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3})^{2},3(4)^{2},2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-3,48,2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}}⟩ \\  & =({t}^{2}-3)\cdot 1+48\cdot 0+2t\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-3}} \\  & ={t}^{2}-3+0+2{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(2))] & =3(2)^{2}-3 \\  & =12-3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t-1,3,2t⟩$ at the point $t=0.$

$$

Next, we substitute $x=t-1,$ $y=3$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨\frac{2(t-1)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(3)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(2t)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),2t⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 1+\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 0+\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2t-2+8t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10} \\  & =\frac{10t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(0))] & =\frac{10(0)-2}{5(0)^{2}-2(0)+10} \\  & =\frac{-2}{10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}(x{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}(x{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{2}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & ={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2{e}^{-t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2{e}^{-t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)={e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$

$$

$$
