\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\left((4 t^{2} \left(t + 1\right))\,i+(2 t + 1)\,j\right)\cdot\left((2)\,i+(1)\,j\right) \\ &=(4 t^{2} \left(t + 1\right))\cdot(2)+(2 t + 1)\cdot(1) \\ &=(8 t^{3} + 8 t^{2})+(2 t + 1) \\ &=8 t^{3} + 8 t^{2} + 2 t + 1\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}(8 t^{3} + 8 t^{2} + 2 t + 1)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[2 t^{4} + \frac{8 t^{3}}{3} + t^{2} + t\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((1)+(1)+(2)+\left(\frac{8}{3}\right))-((0)+(0)+(0)+(0)) \\ &=\left(\frac{20}{3}\right)-(0) \\ &=\frac{20}{3}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y)=(5 x)\,i+(5 y - 5)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j$ for $t\in[\frac{\pi}{2},2 \pi].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3 \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad y=3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(5 x)\,i+(5 y - 5)\,j \\  & =\left(5 \left(3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\right)\,i+\left(5 \left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) - 5\right)\,j \\  & =(15 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(15 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 5)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j \\  & =(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left((15 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(15 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 5)\,j\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left((3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(15 \sin{\left(t \right)})\cdot(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})+(15 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 5) \\ &{} \cdot(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(45 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(- 45 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} + 15 \sin{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=15 \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r & =\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{2 \pi}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{2 \pi}(15 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\left[- 15 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{2 \pi} \\  & =((-15))-((0)) \\  & =(-15)-(0) \\  & =-15\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ given that $$
\displaystyle F(x,y)=(-5)\left(\frac{y+1}{x}\,i-\frac{2(x-1)}{y}\,j\right)
$$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+(t-1)\,j$ for $t\in [3,4].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=t-1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(-5)\left(\frac{y+1}{x}\,i-\frac{2(x-1)}{y}\,j\right) \\  & =(-5)\left(\frac{(t-1)+1}{{t}^{2}}\,i-\frac{2({t}^{2}-1)}{t-1}\,j\right) \\  & =(-5)\left(\frac{1}{t}\,i-2(t+1)\,j\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)j \\  & =2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(-5)\left((\frac{1}{t}\,i-2(t+1)\,j)\right)\cdot (2t\,i+j) \\ &=(-5)\left(\frac{1}{t}\cdot 2t-2(t+1)\cdot 1\right) \\ &=(-5)\left(2-2(t+1)\cdot 1\right) \\ &=(-5)\left(-2t\right).\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{3}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-5)\left({\int }_{3}^{4}(-2t)\,dt\right) \\  & =(-5)\left({[-{t}^{2}]}_{3}^{4}\right) \\  & =(-5)\left([-16+9]\right) \\  & =(-5)\left(-7\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$

$$ given that $F(x,y)=(-1)\left((y\operatorname{\sin}x)\,i+(x+y)\,j\right)$ and $C$ is the path  $r(t)=\operatorname{arcsin}t\,i+2j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{1}{2}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}t,\,y=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(-1)\left(2\operatorname{\sin}(\operatorname{arcsin}t)\,i+(\operatorname{arcsin}t+2)\,j\right) \\ &=(-1)\left(2t\,i+(\operatorname{arcsin}t+2)\,j\right).\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing ${r}^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arcsin}t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(-1)\left((2t\,i+(\operatorname{arcsin}t+2)\,j)\right)\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\,i) \\ &=(-1)\left(\frac{2t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\right).\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-1)\left({\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}\,dt\right) \\  & =(-1)\left(-2\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}\,{|}_{0}^{1/2}\right) \\  & =(-1)\left(-2(\sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}}-1)\right) \\  & =(-1)\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y,z)=\left(- 2 y z\right)\,i+\left(- 2 x z\right)\,j+\left(- 2 x y\right)\,k$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(t^{2}\right)\,j+\left(t^{3}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1]$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=t,\qquad y=t^{2},\qquad z=t^{3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- 2 y z\,i+- 2 x z\,j+- 2 x y\,k \\ & =\left(- 2 \left(t^{2}\right) \left(t^{3}\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(t\right) \left(t^{3}\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(t\right) \left(t^{2}\right)\right)\,k \\ & =- 2 t^{5}\,i+- 2 t^{4}\,j+- 2 t^{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t^{2}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t^{3}\right)\,k \\ & =\,i+2 t\,j+3 t^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(- 2 t^{5}\right)\left(1\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 t^{4}\right)\left(2 t\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 t^{3}\right)\left(3 t^{2}\right) \\ & =\left(- 2 t^{5}\right)+\left(- 4 t^{5}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 6 t^{5}\right) \\ & =- 12 t^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 12 t^{5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[- 2 t^{6}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(- 2 \left(1\right)^{6}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(- 2 \left(0\right)^{6}\right)\right) \\ & =\left(-2\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y,z)=\left(x + z\right)\,i+\left(- y + z\right)\,j+\left(z^{2}\right)\,k$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=\left(- 3 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(t^{2}\right)\,j+\left(- 2 t\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,2]$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=- 3 t^{2},\qquad y=t^{2},\qquad z=- 2 t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(x + z\right)\,i+\left(- y + z\right)\,j+z^{2}\,k \\ & =\left(\left(- 3 t^{2}\right) + \left(- 2 t\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- \left(t^{2}\right) + \left(- 2 t\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(- 2 t\right)^{2}\right)\,k \\ & =t \left(- 3 t - 2\right)\,i+t \left(- t - 2\right)\,j+4 t^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- 3 t^{2}\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t^{2}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- 2 t\right)\,k \\ & =- 6 t\,i+2 t\,j+-2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(t \left(- 3 t - 2\right)\right)\left(- 6 t\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(t \left(- t - 2\right)\right)\left(2 t\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(4 t^{2}\right)\left(-2\right) \\ & =\left(12 t^{2}\right)+\left(18 t^{3}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 4 t^{2}\right)+\left(- 2 t^{3}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 8 t^{2}\right) \\ & =16 t^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{2}\left(16 t^{3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[4 t^{4}\right]_{0}^{2} \\ & =\left(4 \left(2\right)^{4}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(4 \left(0\right)^{4}\right)\right) \\ & =\left(64\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =64\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y,z)=\left(- 2 x\right)\,i+\left(- 2 z\right)\,j+\left(- 2 y\right)\,k$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=\left(2 e^{t}\right)\,i+\left(3 e^{2 t}\right)\,j+\left(e^{- 2 t}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1]$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=2 e^{t},\qquad y=3 e^{2 t},\qquad z=e^{- 2 t}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- 2 x\,i+- 2 z\,j+- 2 y\,k \\ & =\left(- 2 \left(2 e^{t}\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(e^{- 2 t}\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(3 e^{2 t}\right)\right)\,k \\ & =- 4 e^{t}\,i+- 2 e^{- 2 t}\,j+- 6 e^{2 t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 e^{t}\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(3 e^{2 t}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(e^{- 2 t}\right)\,k \\ & =2 e^{t}\,i+6 e^{2 t}\,j+- 2 e^{- 2 t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(- 4 e^{t}\right)\left(2 e^{t}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 e^{- 2 t}\right)\left(6 e^{2 t}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 6 e^{2 t}\right)\left(- 2 e^{- 2 t}\right) \\ & =\left(- 8 e^{2 t}\right)+\left(-12\right)+\left(12\right) \\ & =- 8 e^{2 t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 8 e^{2 t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[- 4 e^{2 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(- 4 e^{2 \left(1\right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(- 4 e^{2 \left(0\right)}\right)\right) \\ & =\left(- 4 e^{2}\right)+\left(4\right) \\ & =4 - 4 e^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r
$$ given that $$
\displaystyle F(x,y,z)=\left(- \frac{3 z}{x}\right)\,i+\left(- \frac{3 z}{y}\right)\,j+\left(-3\right)\,k
$$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=\left(e^{t}\right)\,i+\left(e^{t}\right)\,j+\left(t\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1]$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=e^{t},\qquad y=e^{t},\qquad z=t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- \frac{3 z}{x}\,i+- \frac{3 z}{y}\,j+-3\,k \\ & =\left(- \frac{3 \left(t\right)}{\left(e^{t}\right)}\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- \frac{3 \left(t\right)}{\left(e^{t}\right)}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(-3\right)\,k \\ & =- 3 t e^{- t}\,i+- 3 t e^{- t}\,j+-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(e^{t}\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(e^{t}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t\right)\,k \\ & =e^{t}\,i+e^{t}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(- 3 t e^{- t}\right)\left(e^{t}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 3 t e^{- t}\right)\left(e^{t}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-3\right)\left(1\right) \\ & =\left(- 3 t\right)+\left(- 3 t\right)+\left(-3\right) \\ & =- 6 t - 3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 6 t - 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[- 3 t^{2} - 3 t\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(- 3 \left(1\right)^{2} - 3 \left(1\right)\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(- 3 \left(0\right)^{2} - 3 \left(0\right)\right)\right) \\ & =\left(-6\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=- e^{- 3 t},\qquad y=- 2 e^{3 t},\qquad z=- 2 e^{3 t}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j+z\,k \\ & =\left(\left(- 2 e^{3 t}\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(- e^{- 3 t}\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(- 2 e^{3 t}\right)\right)\,k \\ & =- 2 e^{3 t}\,i+- e^{- 3 t}\,j+- 2 e^{3 t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- e^{- 3 t}\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- 2 e^{3 t}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- 2 e^{3 t}\right)\,k \\ & =3 e^{- 3 t}\,i+- 6 e^{3 t}\,j+- 6 e^{3 t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(- 2 e^{3 t}\right)\left(3 e^{- 3 t}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- e^{- 3 t}\right)\left(- 6 e^{3 t}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 e^{3 t}\right)\left(- 6 e^{3 t}\right) \\ & =\left(-6\right)+\left(6\right)+\left(12 e^{6 t}\right) \\ & =12 e^{6 t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(12 e^{6 t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[2 e^{6 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(2 e^{6 \left(1\right)}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(2 e^{6 \left(0\right)}\right)\right) \\ & =\left(2 e^{6}\right)+\left(-2\right) \\ & =-2 + 2 e^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r,
$$
where $\mathbf F(x,y)=y\,\mathbf i-x\,\mathbf j$ and $C$ is the path $\mathbf r(t)=\sin t\,\mathbf i+\cos t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\le t\le\frac\pi2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
=\int_0^{\pi/2}\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Along the path, $x=\sin t$ and $y=\cos t$, so
$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=\cos t\,\mathbf i-\sin t\,\mathbf j.
$$
Differentiate the supplied path:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf i-\sin t\,\mathbf j.
$$
Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)
&=\cos^2t+(-\sin t)(-\sin t)\\
&=\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1.
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore,
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,\mathrm dt
=\left[t\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac\pi2.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r,
$$
where $\mathbf F(x,y)=x\,\mathbf i+(y-1)\,\mathbf j$ and $C$ is the path $\mathbf r(t)=t\sin t\,\mathbf i+t\cos t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\le t\le\pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametrized line-integral formula:
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
=\int_0^\pi\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Substitute $x=t\sin t$ and $y=t\cos t$:
$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))
=t\sin t\,\mathbf i+(t\cos t-1)\,\mathbf j.
$$
Both coordinates require the product rule:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=(\sin t+t\cos t)\,\mathbf i
+(\cos t-t\sin t)\,\mathbf j.
$$
Take the dot product and expand:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)
&=t\sin t(\sin t+t\cos t)\\
&\quad +(t\cos t-1)(\cos t-t\sin t)\\
&=t\sin^2t+t^2\sin t\cos t\\
&\quad +t\cos^2t-t^2\sin t\cos t\\
&\quad -\cos t+t\sin t\\
&=t-\cos t+t\sin t.
\end{aligned}
$$
The mixed terms cancel, but the offset in the field leaves two extra terms. To integrate them, note that
$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(-t\cos t)=-\cos t+t\sin t.
$$
Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
&=\int_0^\pi(t-\cos t+t\sin t)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[\frac{t^2}{2}-t\cos t\right]_0^\pi\\
&=\frac{\pi^2}{2}-\pi(-1)-0\\
&=\frac{\pi^2}{2}+\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

where $\mathbf F(x,y)=y\,\mathbf i+(x+y)\,\mathbf j$ and $C$ is given by $\mathbf r(t)=(1+2t)\,\mathbf i+(2-t)\,\mathbf j$ for $0\le t\le1$.

*Hint: Use*
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
=\int_0^1\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt,
\qquad \mathbf r'(t)=2\,\mathbf i-\mathbf j.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Along the path, $x=1+2t$ and $y=2-t$. Substitute both coordinates into the field:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))
&=(2-t)\,\mathbf i+((1+2t)+(2-t))\,\mathbf j\\
&=(2-t)\,\mathbf i+(3+t)\,\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$
Differentiating the path gives $\mathbf r'(t)=2\,\mathbf i-\mathbf j$. Take the dot product, keeping the negative sign of the second tangent component:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)
&=2(2-t)-(3+t)\\
&=1-3t.
\end{aligned}
$$
Now evaluate the definite integral:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
&=\int_0^1(1-3t)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[t-\frac32t^2\right]_0^1\\
&=1-\frac32=-\frac12.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r,
$$
where $\mathbf F(x,y,z)=x\,\mathbf i+z\,\mathbf j+y\,\mathbf k$ and $C$ is the path
$$
\mathbf r(t)=-\sin t\,\mathbf i+\sec t\,\mathbf j+\cos t\,\mathbf k,\qquad 0\le t\le\frac\pi4.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_0^{\pi/4}\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Along the curve, $x=-\sin t$, $y=\sec t$, and $z=\cos t$. Therefore
$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=-\sin t\,\mathbf i+\cos t\,\mathbf j+\sec t\,\mathbf k.
$$
Differentiate each curve component, keeping both negative signs:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=-\cos t\,\mathbf i+\sec t\tan t\,\mathbf j-\sin t\,\mathbf k.
$$
Take the dot product before integrating:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)&=(-\sin t)(-\cos t)\\
&\quad+\cos t\sec t\tan t-\sec t\sin t\\
&=\sin t\cos t+\tan t-\tan t\\
&=\sin t\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$
The second and third terms cancel since $\cos t\sec t=1$ and $\sec t\sin t=\tan t$. Finally,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin t\cos t\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[\frac12\sin^2t\right]_0^{\pi/4}\\
&=\frac12\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2-0=\frac14.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r,
$$
where $\mathbf F(x,y,z)=y\,\mathbf i+z\,\mathbf j+x\,\mathbf k$ and $C$ is the path
$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j+t^3\,\mathbf k,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_0^1\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Along the curve, $x=t$, $y=t^2$, and $z=t^3$. Hence
$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=t^2\,\mathbf i+t^3\,\mathbf j+t\,\mathbf k.
$$
Differentiating the curve gives
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i+2t\,\mathbf j+3t^2\,\mathbf k.
$$
Match corresponding vector components in the dot product:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)&=t^2\cdot1+t^3\cdot2t+t\cdot3t^2\\
&=t^2+2t^4+3t^3.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=\int_0^1(t^2+2t^4+3t^3)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[\frac{t^3}{3}+\frac{2t^5}{5}+\frac{3t^4}{4}\right]_0^1\\
&=\frac13+\frac25+\frac34=\frac{89}{60}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

\int_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r,
$$
where $\mathbf F(x,y,z)=x\,\mathbf i+z\,\mathbf j+y\,\mathbf k$ and
$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+2t\,\mathbf j+(1-t)\,\mathbf k,\qquad 0\le t\le1.

*Hint: Use

$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_0^1\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt
$$ with $\mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-\mathbf k$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametrized line-integral formula:
$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\int_0^1\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Along the curve, $x=t$, $y=2t$, and $z=1-t$. Substitute these coordinates into the corresponding field components:
$$
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))=t\,\mathbf i+(1-t)\,\mathbf j+2t\,\mathbf k.
$$
Differentiate the curve component by component:
$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-\mathbf k.
$$
The dot product includes the negative third component:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)&=t\cdot1+(1-t)\cdot2+2t\cdot(-1)\\
&=2-3t.
\end{aligned}
$$
Finally,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r&=\int_0^1(2-3t)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[2t-\frac32t^2\right]_0^1\\
&=2-\frac32=\frac12.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

$$
{\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y)=(2 y - 1)\,i+(2 x - y + 1)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(- 2 t - 2)\,i+(- t - 1)\,j$ for $t\in[0,1].$

*Hint:* Use

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt
$$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- 2 t - 2,\quad y=- t - 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(2 y - 1)\,i+(2 x - y + 1)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(2 \left(- t - 1\right) - 1\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(2 \left(- 2 t - 2\right) - \left(- t - 1\right) + 1\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 2 t - 3)\,i+(- 3 t - 2)\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t - 2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t - 1)\,j \\  & =(-2)\,i+(-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(- 2 t - 3)\,i+(- 3 t - 2)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(-2)\,i+(-1)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t - 3)\cdot(-2)+(- 3 t - 2) \\ &{} \cdot(-1)\end{aligned} \\ &=\left({4 t + 6}\right)+\left({3 t + 2}\right) \\ &=7 t + 8\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({7 t + 8}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{\frac{7 t^{2}}{2} + 8 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((8)+\left(\frac{7}{2}\right))-((0)+(0)) \\ &=\left(\frac{23}{2}\right)-(0) \\ &=\frac{23}{2}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

$$
{\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y)=(- y)\,i+(- x - 2)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(t + 2)\,i+(2 t + 1)\,j$ for $t\in[0,1].$

*Hint:* Use

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt
$$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t + 2,\quad y=2 t + 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(- y)\,i+(- x - 2)\,j \\  & =\left(- \left(2 t + 1\right)\right)\,i+\left(- \left(t + 2\right) - 2\right)\,j \\  & =(- 2 t - 1)\,i+(- t - 4)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t + 2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 1)\,j \\  & =(1)\,i+(2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(- 2 t - 1)\,i+(- t - 4)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(1)\,i+(2)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 2 t - 1)\cdot(1)+(- t - 4)\cdot(2) \\ &=\left({- 2 t - 1}\right)+\left({- 2 t - 8}\right) \\ &=- 4 t - 9\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({- 4 t - 9}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- 2 t^{2} - 9 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((-9)+(-2))-((0)+(0)) \\ &=(-11)-(0) \\ &=-11\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

$$
{\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y)=(- 2 y)\,i+(- 2 x)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(t - 2)\,i+(2 t + 2)\,j$ for $t\in[0,1].$

*Hint:* Use

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt
$$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t - 2,\quad y=2 t + 2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(- 2 y)\,i+(- 2 x)\,j \\  & =\left(- 2 \left(2 t + 2\right)\right)\,i+\left(- 2 \left(t - 2\right)\right)\,j \\  & =(- 4 t - 4)\,i+(- 2 t + 4)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t - 2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 2)\,j \\  & =(1)\,i+(2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(- 4 t - 4)\,i+(- 2 t + 4)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(1)\,i+(2)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 4 t - 4)\cdot(1)+(- 2 t + 4)\cdot(2) \\ &=\left({- 4 t - 4}\right)+\left({- 4 t + 8}\right) \\ &=- 8 t + 4\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({- 8 t + 4}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- 4 t^{2} + 4 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((-4)+(4))-((0)+(0)) \\ &=(0)-(0) \\ &=0\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

$$
{\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y)=(- y + 1)\,i+(- x + 1)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(- t)\,i+(- t - 1)\,j$ for $t\in[0,1].$

*Hint:* Use

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt
$$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- t,\quad y=- t - 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(- y + 1)\,i+(- x + 1)\,j \\  & =\left(- \left(- t - 1\right) + 1\right)\,i+\left(- \left(- t\right) + 1\right)\,j \\  & =(t + 2)\,i+(t + 1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t - 1)\,j \\  & =(-1)\,i+(-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(t + 2)\,i+(t + 1)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(-1)\,i+(-1)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=(t + 2)\cdot(-1)+(t + 1)\cdot(-1) \\ &=\left({- t - 2}\right)+\left({- t - 1}\right) \\ &=- 2 t - 3\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({- 2 t - 3}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- t^{2} - 3 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((-1)+(-3))-((0)+(0)) \\ &=(-4)-(0) \\ &=-4\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

$$
{\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y)=(- 2 y + 2)\,i+(- 2 x - 2)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(t - 1)\,i+(2 t - 1)\,j$ for $t\in[0,1].$

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm d r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t - 1,\quad y=2 t - 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(- 2 y + 2)\,i+(- 2 x - 2)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(- 2 \left(2 t - 1\right) + 2\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(t - 1\right) - 2\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 4 t + 4)\,i+(- 2 t)\,j\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t - 1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t - 1)\,j \\  & =(1)\,i+(2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({(- 4 t + 4)\,i+(- 2 t)\,j}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({(1)\,i+(2)\,j}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 4 t + 4)\cdot(1)+(- 2 t)\cdot(2) \\ &=\left({- 4 t + 4}\right)+\left({- 4 t}\right) \\ &=- 8 t + 4\end{aligned}\end{gathered}

\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left({- 8 t + 4}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- 4 t^{2} + 4 t}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=((-4)+(4))-((0)+(0)) \\ &=(0)-(0) \\ &=0\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

$$
{\int}_{C}F\cdot\text{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y)=(- 2 x + 1)\,i+(- 2 y - 1)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j$ for $t\in[0,2 \pi].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad y=t \cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(- 2 x + 1)\,i+(- 2 y - 1)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(- 2 \left(t \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) + 1\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(- 2 \left(t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) - 1\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,i \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1)\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,i \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1)\,j\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1) \\ &{} \cdot(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1) \\ &{} \cdot(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&- 2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} +\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} + t \sin{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left({\begin{aligned}&t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{- t^{2} + t \sin{\left(t \right)} - t \cos{\left(t \right)}}\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&((- 4 \pi^{2})+(0)+(- 2 \pi)) \\ &{} -((0)+(0)+(0))\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 4 \pi^{2} - 2 \pi)-(0) \\ &=- 2 \pi \left(1 + 2 \pi\right)\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

The offset terms integrate by the reverse product rule:

$$
\begin{gathered}\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- t^{2} + t \sin{\left(t \right)} - t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&t \sin{\left(t \right)} + t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t  \\ &{} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad y=t \cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(x + 1)\,i+(y + 2)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(\left(t \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) + 1\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(\left(t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) + 2\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1)\,i \\ &{} +(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2)\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad y=t \cos{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t)) \\ \begin{aligned} &=(2 x - 1)\,i+(2 y - 2)\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left(2 \left(t \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) - 1\right)\,i \\ &{} +\left(2 \left(t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) - 2\right)\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - 1)\,i \\ &{} +(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2)\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - 1)\,i \\ &{} +(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2)\,j\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - 1) \\ &{} \cdot(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2) \\ &{} \cdot(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + 2 t \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} - t \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} +\left({\begin{aligned}&- 2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 t  \\ &{} - \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot\text{d}r \\ \begin{aligned} &=\int_{\pi}^{2 \pi}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{\pi}^{2 \pi}\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 t  \\ &{} - \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[{t^{2} - t \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)}}\right]_{\pi}^{2 \pi} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&((4 \pi^{2})+(0)+(- 4 \pi)) \\ &{} -((\pi^{2})+(0)+(2 \pi))\end{aligned} \\ &=(- 4 \pi + 4 \pi^{2})-(2 \pi + \pi^{2}) \\ &=3 \pi \left(-2 + \pi\right)\end{aligned}\end{gathered}

$$
\begin{gathered}r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) \\ \begin{aligned} &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2)\,i \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} \cdot\left({\begin{aligned}&(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i \\ &{} +(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&(- 2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2) \\ &{} \cdot(t \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} +(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)}) \\ &{} \cdot(- t \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)})\end{aligned} \\ &=\begin{aligned}&\left({\begin{aligned}&- 2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right) \\ &{} +\left({\begin{aligned}&2 t^{2} \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}  \\ &{} - 2 t \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}}\right)\end{aligned} \\ &=2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 t + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}

question.:question/problem:
Which ordinary definite integral represents $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(x+2y)\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=t\cos t\,i+t\sin t\,j$ for $t\in [0,1]$?

Use the supplied parameterization and limits. Select the integral whose integrand is $F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)$; do not evaluate it.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve, $x=t\cos t$ and $y=t\sin t$. Substitute into both mixed field components:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))&=(t\cos t+t\sin t)\,i+(t\cos t+2t\sin t)\,j\\&=t(\cos t+\sin t)\,i+t(\cos t+2\sin t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Each path component needs the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t\cos t)&=\cos t-t\sin t,\\\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t\sin t)&=\sin t+t\cos t.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
r^{\prime}(t)=(\cos t-t\sin t)\,i+(\sin t+t\cos t)\,j.
$$

Multiply matching components. Keep the two products factored:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)&=t(\cos t+\sin t)(\cos t-t\sin t)\\&\quad+t(\cos t+2\sin t)(\sin t+t\cos t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r&=\int_0^1\bigl[t(\cos t+\sin t)(\cos t-t\sin t)\\&\qquad+t(\cos t+2\sin t)(\sin t+t\cos t)\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

No antiderivative or further expansion is needed.

question.:question/problem:
Which ordinary definite integral represents $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ given that $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i-xy\,j$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=t^2\,i+t^3\,j$ for $t\in [0,1]$?

Use the supplied parameterization and limits. Select the integral whose integrand is $F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)$; do not evaluate it.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Substitute $x=t^2$ and $y=t^3$ into both components:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))&=(t^2+t^3)\,i-(t^2)(t^3)\,j\\&=(t^2+t^3)\,i-t^5\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate both path components:

$$
r^{\prime}(t)=2t\,i+3t^2\,j.
$$

The dot product includes both coordinate derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)&=(t^2+t^3)(2t)+(-t^5)(3t^2)\\&=2t^3+2t^4-3t^7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_{0}^{1}(2t^3+2t^4-3t^7)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate

\displaystyle\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r
$$ given that $F(x,y,z)=\left(- z\right)\,i+\left(- 2 y\right)\,j+\left(2 x\right)\,k$ and $C$ is the path $r(t)=\left(2 t + 1\right)\,i+\left(1 - t\right)\,j+\left(2 t\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1]$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=2 t + 1,\qquad y=1 - t,\qquad z=2 t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- z\,i+- 2 y\,j+2 x\,k \\ & =\left(- \left(2 t\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(1 - t\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 \left(2 t + 1\right)\right)\,k \\ & =- 2 t\,i+\left(2 t - 2\right)\,j+\left(4 t + 2\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t + 1\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(1 - t\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t\right)\,k \\ & =2\,i+-\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(- 2 t\right)\left(2\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 t - 2\right)\left(-1\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(4 t + 2\right)\left(2\right) \\ & =\left(- 4 t\right)+\left(2\right)+\left(- 2 t\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(4\right)+\left(8 t\right) \\ & =2 t + 6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(2 t + 6\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[t^{2} + 6 t\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(\left(1\right)^{2} + 6 \left(1\right)\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(\left(0\right)^{2} + 6 \left(0\right)\right)\right) \\ & =\left(7\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =7\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=- t - 1,\qquad y=t - 1,\qquad z=- 2 t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- 2 z\,i+- 2 x\,j+y\,k \\ & =\left(- 2 \left(- 2 t\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(- t - 1\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(t - 1\right)\right)\,k \\ & =4 t\,i+\left(2 t + 2\right)\,j+\left(t - 1\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- t - 1\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t - 1\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- 2 t\right)\,k \\ & =-\,i+\,j+-2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(4 t\right)\left(-1\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 t + 2\right)\left(1\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(t - 1\right)\left(-2\right) \\ & =\left(- 4 t\right)+\left(2\right)+\left(2 t\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(2\right)+\left(- 2 t\right) \\ & =4 - 4 t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(4 - 4 t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[- 2 t^{2} + 4 t\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(- 2 \left(1\right)^{2} + 4 \left(1\right)\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(- 2 \left(0\right)^{2} + 4 \left(0\right)\right)\right) \\ & =\left(2\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=2 t + 1,\qquad y=2 t,\qquad z=2 t + 1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =- x\,i+z\,j+- 2 y\,k \\ & =\left(- \left(2 t + 1\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(\left(2 t + 1\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(2 t\right)\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 2 t - 1\right)\,i+\left(2 t + 1\right)\,j+- 4 t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t + 1\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t + 1\right)\,k \\ & =2\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(- 2 t - 1\right)\left(2\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(2 t + 1\right)\left(2\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 4 t\right)\left(2\right) \\ & =\left(-2\right)+\left(- 4 t\right)+\left(2\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(4 t\right)+\left(- 8 t\right) \\ & =- 8 t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 8 t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & =\left[- 4 t^{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(- 4 \left(1\right)^{2}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(-\left(- 4 \left(0\right)^{2}\right)\right) \\ & =\left(-4\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x=t,\qquad y=t^{2},\qquad z=t^{3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2 y\,i+- 2 z\,j+- x\,k \\ & =\left(2 \left(t^{2}\right)\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 \left(t^{3}\right)\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\left(- \left(t\right)\right)\,k \\ & =2 t^{2}\,i+- 2 t^{3}\,j+- t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t\right)\,i \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t^{2}\right)\,j \\ &\quad {}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t^{3}\right)\,k \\ & =\,i+2 t\,j+3 t^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(2 t^{2}\right)\left(1\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 2 t^{3}\right)\left(2 t\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- t\right)\left(3 t^{2}\right) \\ & =\left(2 t^{2}\right)+\left(- 4 t^{4}\right) \\ &\quad {}+\left(- 3 t^{3}\right) \\ & =t^{2} \left(- 4 t^{2} - 3 t + 2\right)\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:

*Hint: $r^{\prime}(t)=(\cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j$. Substitute both coordinates into the field, then take the dot product.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the vector line-integral formula:

$$
\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Substitute the coordinates $x=\sin{\left(t \right)}$ and $y=\cos{\left(t \right)}$ into both field components:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))&=((\cos{\left(t \right)}))\,i\\&\quad+(- (\sin{\left(t \right)}))\,j\\&=(\cos{\left(t \right)})\,i\\&\quad+(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each path component:

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\sin{\left(t \right)})=\cos{\left(t \right)},\\y^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\cos{\left(t \right)})=- \sin{\left(t \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply matching components and add:

$$
\begin{aligned}&F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\\&=(\cos{\left(t \right)})(\cos{\left(t \right)})\\&\quad+(- \sin{\left(t \right)})(- \sin{\left(t \right)}).\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the products using $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$ where applicable:

$$
F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)=1.
$$

Keep the supplied parameter limits. The required integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{0}^{2}\bigl[(\cos{\left(t \right)})(\cos{\left(t \right)})\\&\quad+(- \sin{\left(t \right)})(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}F(r(t))&=(- 2 (\sin{\left(t \right)}))\,i\\&\quad+(- 2 (\cos{\left(t \right)}) - 1)\,j\\&=(- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i\\&\quad+(- 2 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each path component:

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\sin{\left(t \right)})=\cos{\left(t \right)},\\y^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\cos{\left(t \right)})=- \sin{\left(t \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply matching components and add:

$$
\begin{aligned}&F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\\&=(- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)})(\cos{\left(t \right)})\\&\quad+(- 2 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1)(- \sin{\left(t \right)}).\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the products using $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$ where applicable:

$$
F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)=\sin{\left(t \right)}.
$$

Keep the supplied parameter limits. The required integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{0}^{1}\bigl[(- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)})(\cos{\left(t \right)})\\&\quad+(- 2 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 1)(- \sin{\left(t \right)})\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the midline for a transformed cosine function with a minimum value of $-13$ and a maximum value of $-1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A sinusoidal graph's midline (or vertical shift) is the horizontal line that divides it vertically in half. 

The equation of the midline is given by

$$
y=\frac{{y}_{\text{min}}+{y}_{\text{max}}}{2},
$$

where ${y}_{\text{min}}$ and ${y}_{\text{max}}$ are the minimum and maximum values of the function. The midline equals the average of the maximum and minimum values. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}_{\text{min}}+{y}_{\text{max}}}{2} & =\frac{-13+(-1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{-14}{2} \\  & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=-7.$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the period of the function

$$
f(x)=3\sin\left(\frac{\pi-2x}{3}+\frac{x}{2}\right)-4.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Combine the $x$ terms inside the sine before applying the period formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\pi-2x}{3}+\frac{x}{2}
&=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{2x}{3}+\frac{x}{2}\\
&=\frac{\pi}{3}+\left(-\frac{4}{6}+\frac{3}{6}\right)x\\
&=-\frac{x}{6}+\frac{\pi}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient is $B=-\frac{1}{6}$. A negative input coefficient reverses the direction of a cycle; the period is a positive length, so use $|B|$:

$$
T=\frac{2\pi}{|B|}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{1}{6}}=12\pi.
$$

Using only one of the two original $x$ terms would miss their combined effect. The outside factor $3$ and vertical shift $-4$ do not affect the period.

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First rewrite the entire cosine argument to identify the coefficient of $x$:

$$
\frac{3x-60^{\circ}}{2}=\frac{3}{2}x-30^{\circ}.
$$

Thus $B=\frac{3}{2}$, rather than $3$. In degree measure the period is $T=\frac{360^{\circ}}{|B|}$, so

$$
T=\frac{360^{\circ}}{\frac{3}{2}}=360^{\circ}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=240^{\circ}.
$$

The factor $-2$ outside the cosine and the horizontal and vertical shifts do not change the period.

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the midline for a transformed sine function with a minimum value of $-4$ and a maximum value of $8$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The midline is the horizontal line halfway between the minimum and maximum values. Its height is their average:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \frac{y_{\text{min}}+y_{\text{max}}}{2} \\
  &= \frac{-4+8}{2} \\
  &= \frac{4}{2} \\
  &= 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=2$. The quantity $\frac{8-(-4)}{2}=6$ is the amplitude, not the height of the midline.

question.:question/problem: Find the range of $f(x)=2\sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+1$ for all real $x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The sine function takes every value from $-1$ to $1$, including both endpoints. Horizontal shifts and stretches do not change this range when $x$ can be any real number. Thus,

$$
-1\le \sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\le 1.
$$

Multiply by $2$, then add $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-2&\le 2\sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\le 2 \\
-1&\le 2\sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+1\le 3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both endpoints are attained, and every value between them is attained. Therefore, the range is $f(x)\in[-1,3]$.

question.:question/problem: Find the range of $f(x)=-3\cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-1$ for all real $x$.

$$
-1\le \cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\le 1.

Multiplying by $-3$ reverses both inequality signs. Then subtract $1$:

question.:question/problem: Find the range of $f(x)=1-2\left(2-\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)$ for all real $x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First simplify the vertical transformations. The factor $-2$ multiplies both terms inside the outer parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=1-4+2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \\
&=2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The effective vertical shift is $-3$, and the amplitude is $2$. Horizontal shifts and stretches do not change the range over all real inputs. Starting from the cosine bounds, multiply by $2$ and subtract $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-1&\le \cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\le 1 \\
-2&\le 2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\le 2 \\
-5&\le 2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-3\le -1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Cosine attains every value in $[-1,1]$, so every value between these transformed endpoints, including the endpoints, is attained. Therefore, the range is $f(x)\in[-5,-1]$.

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the midline for a transformed sine function with a minimum value of $-12$ and a maximum value of $-2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The midline is the horizontal line halfway between the minimum and maximum values. Average their heights:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \frac{y_{\text{min}}+y_{\text{max}}}{2} \\
&= \frac{-12+(-2)}{2} \\
&= -7.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=-7$. The half-range $5$ is the amplitude, rather than the vertical shift.

$$
{∬}_{S}12xyz\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}12xyz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,12xy(x+y)\sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,12xy(x+y)\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,12{x}^{2}y+12x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(12{x}^{2}y+12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4x{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6{x}^{2}+4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}\,[2{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(2+2)-0 \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-y)=-1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}3x\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,3x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le r\le 2,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,3x\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{Δ}3r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\cdot \text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{Δ}3{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}3{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [{r}^{3}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{3}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8\sqrt{3}(1-0) \\  & =8\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$

$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x+2y)=-2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x+2y)=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{1+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{9}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.

$$

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot r\text{ }\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}2r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta [{r}^{2}]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\,\text{d}r \\  & =9[-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =9\cdot (-1-1) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+\sqrt{8}y)=4,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+\sqrt{8}y)=\sqrt{8}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{4}^{2}+(\sqrt{8})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 5\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =5{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =5{∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot r\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{40}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{40}{3}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{80\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x + y$ and whose domain is the right half-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x + y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x + y)=1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{4 x}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 x)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 x)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 x}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 2,\ - \frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 x}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(4(r\cos\theta))\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{4 r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\int_{0}^{2}{4 r^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\left[\frac{4 r^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\left[(\left(\frac{32}{3}\right))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\frac{32 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =\left(\frac{32 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left[\sin{\left(\theta \right)}\right]_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =\left(\frac{32 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left[((1))-((-1))\right] \\ & =\left(\frac{32 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\cdot((1)-(-1)) \\ & =\frac{64 \sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\frac{64 \sqrt{3}}{3}$.

\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{1}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(1)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{r}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[\frac{r^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left[\theta\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ & =\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left[((2 \pi))-((0))\right] \\ & =\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\cdot((2 \pi)-(0)) \\ & =\sqrt{3} \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\sqrt{3} \pi$.

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x + y)=1.$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{4}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 2,\ 0\le\theta\le 2 \pi\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(4)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{4 r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\int_{0}^{2}{4 r}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[2 r^{2}\right]_{0}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[((8))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{8}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(8 \sqrt{3})\left[\theta\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ & =(8 \sqrt{3})\left[((2 \pi))-((0))\right] \\ & =(8 \sqrt{3})\cdot((2 \pi)-(0)) \\ & =16 \sqrt{3} \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $16 \sqrt{3} \pi$.

and

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 y)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(-1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 y)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 1,\ 0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(4(r\sin\theta))\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\int_{0}^{1}{4 r^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[\frac{4 r^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[(\left(\frac{4}{3}\right))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\frac{4 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =\left(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left[- \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =\left(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left[((0))-((-1))\right] \\ & =\left(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\cdot((0)-(-1)) \\ & =\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}$.

question.:question/problem:

This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-6x+y)=-6,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-6x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-6)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,y(6x-y)\sqrt{38}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\,(6xy-{y}^{2})\sqrt{38}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$

question.:question/problem: Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $1$, and that $P$ makes an angle of $\frac{5π}{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P$?

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r, \frac{π}{4})$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(2r, \frac{π}{3})$. Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(\sqrt{10}, \sqrt{10})$.
question.:question/worked-solution: The radius of $A$ is $r=\sqrt{10+10}=2\sqrt5$. Thus $B$ has radius $2r=4\sqrt5$ and angle $\pi/3$, giving $$B=(4\sqrt5\cos(\pi/3),4\sqrt5\sin(\pi/3))=(2\sqrt5,2\sqrt{15}).$$

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(2, θ)$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(1, θ - \frac{π}{4})$. Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2})$.
question.:question/worked-solution: The coordinates of $A$ give $\cos\theta=\sqrt2/2$ and $\sin\theta=-\sqrt2/2$, so $\theta=-\pi/4$ modulo $2\pi$. The angle of $B$ is $-\pi/2$ modulo $2\pi$, and its radius is $1$. Therefore $B=(0,-1)$.

question.:question/problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $(4,{225}^{∘}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡({225}^{∘}) \\  & =4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡({225}^{∘}) \\  & =4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-2\sqrt{2},-2\sqrt{2}).$

question.:question/problem: Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $6,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of ${315}^{∘}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$, where

$$
r=6,\,\theta ={315}^{∘}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =6\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =-3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(3\sqrt{2},-3\sqrt{2}).$

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,\frac{5\pi }{6})$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $({r}^{2},\frac{11\pi }{6}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-3,\sqrt{3}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
((\sqrt{12})^{2},\frac{11\pi }{6})=(12,\frac{11\pi }{6}).
$$

 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =12\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =6\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =12\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(6\sqrt{3},-6).$

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(2,\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(4,\theta +\frac{\pi }{3}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-\sqrt{3},-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{-1}{-\sqrt{3}}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1/\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the third quadrant, we have $\theta =\pi +{\theta }_{R}=\frac{7\pi }{6}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(4,\frac{7\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{3})=(4,\frac{3\pi }{2}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$

The diagram above shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. Determine the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(2\sqrt{2},\frac{5\pi }{6})$ and $m∠AOB=\frac{7\pi }{12}.$

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(2\sqrt{2},\frac{5\pi }{6}),$ we must have $r=2\sqrt{2}.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $2\sqrt{2},$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $2\sqrt{2}.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle clockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{5\pi }{6},$ the $\theta$-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\frac{5\pi }{6}-\frac{7\pi }{12}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(2\sqrt{2},\frac{\pi }{4})$ 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(2,2).$

question.:question/problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $(1,\pi ).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ x & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\ x & =1(-1) \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ y & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\ y & =1\cdot 0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,0).$
