question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(2,\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(2,\theta -\frac{\pi }{12}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(1,\sqrt{3}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the first quadrant, we have $\theta ={\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(2,\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{12})=(2,\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$

question.:question/problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $(10,\frac{2\pi }{3}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ x & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\ x & =10\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ y & =10\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\ y & =10\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y & =5\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-5,5\sqrt{3}).$

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,\frac{4\pi }{3})$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(\frac{r}{2},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$  Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-4,-4\sqrt{3}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-4\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(\frac{8}{2},\frac{5\pi }{6})=(4,\frac{5\pi }{6}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =-2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-2\sqrt{3},2).$

question.:question/problem:

The diagram above shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(5,\pi )$ and $m∠AOB=\frac{\pi }{3},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(5,\pi ),$ we must have $r=5.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $5,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $5.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle counterclockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta$-coordinate of $A$ is $\pi ,$ the $\theta$-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\pi +\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(5,\frac{4\pi }{3})$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =5\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =5\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

question.:question/problem:
The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(\sqrt{2},\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(2,\theta -\frac{\pi }{4}).$ Determine the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-1,1).$

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{1}{-1}\right)| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =|-\frac{\pi }{4}| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the second quadrant, we have $\theta =\pi -{\theta }_{R}=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(2,\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4})=(2,\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(0,2).$

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(6,\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(3,\theta -\frac{3\pi }{4}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(3\sqrt{2},-3\sqrt{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{-3\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{2}}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the fourth quadrant, we have $\theta =2\pi +{\theta }_{R}=\frac{7\pi }{4}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(3,\frac{7\pi }{4}-\frac{3\pi }{4})=(3,\pi ).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-3,0).$

question.:question/problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $\left(3,\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$. Find the exact Cartesian coordinates of $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, use

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

The angle $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ lies in the second quadrant and has reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$. Hence cosine is negative and sine is positive:

$$
\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\qquad
\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First calculate the $x$-coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=3\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\\
 &=3\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\\
 &=-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then calculate the $y$-coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&=3\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\\
 &=3\cdot\frac{1}{2}\\
 &=\frac{3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates are $\left(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{3}{2}\right)$. The negative $x$ and positive $y$ confirm the second quadrant.

question.:question/problem: The point $P$ has polar coordinates $\left(4,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$. Find the exact Cartesian coordinates of $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, use

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

The right triangle shows why cosine gives the horizontal component and sine gives the vertical component.

![](images/20/205b3684042b0ab0261a4d56800cd89a10a7816f8022befcf6c664337f834380.png)

Here $r=4$ and $\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$. First calculate the $x$-coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=4\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\\
 &=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\
 &=2\sqrt{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then calculate the $y$-coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\\
 &=4\cdot\frac{1}{2}\\
 &=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both coordinates are positive, as expected in the first quadrant. Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates are $\left(2\sqrt{3},2\right)$.

question.:question/problem:
The point $P$ has polar coordinates $\left(2\sqrt{3}k,\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)$, where $k$ is a positive real number. Find its exact Cartesian coordinates in terms of $k$.

The Cartesian coordinates are

$(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the same conversion formulas, keeping the radius in terms of $k$:

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

Since $k>0$, the radius $2\sqrt{3}k$ is positive. The angle $\frac{4\pi}{3}$ lies in the third quadrant and has reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$, so

$$
\cos\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)=-\frac{1}{2},\qquad
\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

First calculate the $x$-coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=2\sqrt{3}k\cos\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\\
 &=2\sqrt{3}k\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\\
 &=-\sqrt{3}k.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then calculate the $y$-coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&=2\sqrt{3}k\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\\
 &=2\sqrt{3}k\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\\
 &=-3k.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates are $\left(-\sqrt{3}k,-3k\right)$. Both coordinates are negative for every allowed $k$, as expected in the third quadrant.

question.:question/problem:
The distance from $P$ to the origin is $2$. The ray from the origin through $P$ makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ measured counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis. What are the Cartesian coordinates of $P$?

Use $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$, with $\cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$.

The diagram shows how the two coordinates relate to the radius and angle.

![A first-quadrant right triangle with radius r, angle theta, horizontal leg x equals r cosine theta, and vertical leg y equals r sine theta.](images/20/205b3684042b0ab0261a4d56800cd89a10a7816f8022befcf6c664337f834380.png)
question.:question/worked-solution:
The description gives the polar quantities $r=2$ and $\theta=30^{\circ}$. The horizontal coordinate uses cosine and the vertical coordinate uses sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=r\cos\theta=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\sqrt{3},\\
y&=r\sin\theta=2\cdot\frac{1}{2}=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both coordinates are positive because $P$ is in the first quadrant. In the order $(x,y)$, the Cartesian coordinates are $(\sqrt{3},1)$. The distance is $\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^2+1^2}=2$, as required.

question.:question/problem:
The distance from $P$ to the origin is $2\sqrt{3}$. The ray from the origin through $P$ makes an angle of $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ measured counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis. Find the exact Cartesian coordinates of $P$.

$(x,y)=(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The description gives $r=2\sqrt{3}$ and $\theta=\frac{5\pi}{6}$. The angle lies in the second quadrant with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$, so

$$
\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\qquad
\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Convert each coordinate, including the radical in the radius:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=r\cos\theta=(2\sqrt{3})\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=-\sqrt{3}\sqrt{3}=-3,\\
y&=r\sin\theta=(2\sqrt{3})\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\sqrt{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the Cartesian coordinates are $(-3,\sqrt{3})$. The signs agree with the second quadrant, and $x^2+y^2=9+3=12=(2\sqrt{3})^2$. Multiplying the two square roots in the $x$-coordinate gives $3$, rather than leaving a single factor of $\sqrt{3}$.

question.:question/problem: The distance from $P$ to the origin is $3$. The ray from the origin through $P$ makes an angle of $210^{\circ}$ measured counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis. What are the exact Cartesian coordinates of $P$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The description gives $r=3$ and $\theta=210^{\circ}$. This angle is in the third quadrant with reference angle $30^{\circ}$, so both cosine and sine are negative:

$$
\cos 210^{\circ}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\qquad
\sin 210^{\circ}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Use $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=3\cos 210^{\circ}=3\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\\
y&=3\sin 210^{\circ}=3\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates are $\left(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{3}{2}\right)$. As a check, $x^2+y^2=\frac{27}{4}+\frac{9}{4}=9=r^2$, and both coordinates have the third-quadrant signs.

question.:question/problem:
The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,0)$, where $r>0$, and Cartesian coordinates $(2,0)$. The point $B$ has polar coordinates $(2r,\frac{\pi}{3})$. Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$.

Use $x=R\cos\phi$ and $y=R\sin\phi$ for a point with polar coordinates $(R,\phi)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A=(2,0)$ lies on the positive $x$-axis, its distance from the origin is $r=2$. Thus the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(2r,\tfrac{\pi}{3})=(4,\tfrac{\pi}{3}).
$$

The lesson's right triangle shows why the Cartesian coordinates of a point are its radius times the cosine and sine of its angle:

![](images/20/205b3684042b0ab0261a4d56800cd89a10a7816f8022befcf6c664337f834380.png)

Using the radius $4$ and angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ of $B$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_B&=4\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=4\cdot\frac{1}{2}=2,\\
y_B&=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=2\sqrt{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(2,2\sqrt{3})$.

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(2,\theta)$ and Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt{3},1)$. The point $B$ has polar coordinates $(3,\theta+\frac{\pi}{3})$. Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, find the reference angle of $A$:

$$
\alpha=\arctan\left(\left|\frac{y_A}{x_A}\right|\right)=\arctan\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6}.
$$

Since $x_A<0$ and $y_A>0$, the point $A$ lies in the second quadrant. We may take

$$
\theta=\pi-\alpha=\frac{5\pi}{6}.
$$

The angle of $B$ is therefore

$$
\phi_B=\theta+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{5\pi}{6}+\frac{2\pi}{6}=\frac{7\pi}{6}.
$$

Any coterminal choice of $\theta$ gives the same Cartesian point. The polar coordinates of $B$ are $(3,\frac{7\pi}{6})$. Now convert using $x_B=3\cos\phi_B$ and $y_B=3\sin\phi_B$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_B&=3\cos\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)=3\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\\
y_B&=3\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)=3\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{3}{2})$.

question.:question/problem:
The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,\frac{\pi}{4})$, where $r>0$, and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(\frac{r}{3},\frac{7\pi}{6})$. Determine the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$.

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, recover the radius of $A$ from its Cartesian coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r&=\sqrt{x_A^2+y_A^2}\\
 &=\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^2+(\sqrt{2})^2}=\sqrt{4}=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{7\pi}{6})$. We use $x_B=R_B\cos\phi_B$ and $y_B=R_B\sin\phi_B$ with the radius and angle of $B$:

question.:question/problem:
The closed, positively oriented curve $C$ is defined as $\mathbf{r}(t)=3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as

$$
\mathbf{n}=\frac{a(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+b(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}}{||{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)||}.
$$

Find the function $a(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

$$
\mathbf{f}(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}\theta ,z⟩\hspace{2em}(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $\mathbf{r}(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
\mathbf{r}(\theta )=\mathbf{f}(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $\mathbf{r}(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
\mathbf{r}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf{r}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(\theta )=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{'}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{'}(\theta )\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{n} & =\frac{\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}}{||\overset{~}{\mathbf{n}}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{y}{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+0\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{'}(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{sin}t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=3\text{ cm}, \\ b & =AC, \\ m∠A & ={30}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

we can calculate $b=AC,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{21}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 3\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘} \\ \frac{21}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 3\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\ \frac{21}{4} & =\frac{3b}{4} \\ 3b & =21 \\ b & =7\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AC=7\text{cm}.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $△ABD$ and $△BDC$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/6e/6e070d26915bcb11118f5a23f36b80038d5dd865e32a8517a12c10939ca02f0b.png)

First, we find the area of $△ABD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & =24\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & ≈23.908\,7,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Now we find the area of $△BCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{BCD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 14\cdot 16\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & =112\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & ≈66.462\,9,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABD}+{A}_{BCD} \\  & ≈23.908\,7+66.462\,9 \\  & ≈90.371\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $90.$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/5f/5f9574fad2615ba517ed8486ab7c054b53f25184617a345afb76fca78ab9b224.png)

The area of ​​the triangle $△ABC$ is $24\sqrt{3}{\text{ in}}^{2}.$ Then, $AC=${{field-1}} $\text{in}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=8\text{ in}, \\ b & =AC, \\ m∠A & ={60}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $b=AC,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 24\sqrt{3} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} \\ 24\sqrt{3} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 8\cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ 24\sqrt{3} & =2\sqrt{3}b \\ 24\cancel{\sqrt{3}} & =2\cancel{\sqrt{3}}b \\ 2b & =24 \\ b & =12\text{ in}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AC=12\text{ in}.$

$E$ lies on $AB$. The two marked angles at $C$ are $\angle BCE=28^{\circ}$ and $\angle ECA=40^{\circ}$. The side lengths are $CA=x+2$ and $CB=2x$, and $CA+CB=23$. All lengths use the same unit.

question.:question/worked-solution:
First determine the two side lengths. Their sum is $23$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x+2)+2x&=23\\
3x+2&=23\\
x&=7.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $CA=x+2=9$ and $CB=2x=14$.

The included angle between these sides is the whole angle $\angle ACB$. Add its two marked parts:

$$
\angle ACB=28^{\circ}+40^{\circ}=68^{\circ}.
$$

Now apply the triangle area formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}

&=\frac12(9)(14)\sin68^{\circ}\\
&=63\sin68^{\circ}\\
&=58.41258283\ldots\\
&\approx58.41.
\end{aligned}
$$

The area is $58.41$ square units. Use the side lengths $9$ and $14$, rather than $x$ itself. Both the side expressions and the two angle markings must be combined before substituting into the formula.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The known sides $AB=4\sqrt2\,\text{cm}$ and $AC=6\,\text{cm}$ meet at $A$. Apply the area formula and isolate the sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal A &= \frac12(AB)(AC)\sin A \\
12 &= \frac12\cdot4\sqrt2\cdot6\sin A \\
12 &= 12\sqrt2\sin A \\

\end{aligned}
$$

Within a triangle, both $45^\circ$ and $135^\circ=180^\circ-45^\circ$ have this sine. Since $A$ is obtuse, choose $135^\circ$.

Therefore, $m\angle A=135^\circ$. Checking the area gives $\frac12\cdot4\sqrt2\cdot6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=12\,\text{cm}^2$.

question.:question/problem:
In convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AB=10$, $AD=8$, and the diagonal $AC=12$. The full angle $\angle DAB=110^\circ$ and $\angle BAC=35^\circ$.

![](images/05/05dfe4b721ff22ac11aa4e3319d0cb4caa144cb209a4f812aa30c6b6e034f8a3.png)

Find the area of $ABCD$, rounded to the nearest tenth.

Enter the rounded number using digits and a decimal point. A scientific calculator in degree mode may be used.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Diagonal $AC$ lies inside the convex quadrilateral and splits the full angle at $A$. Therefore,

$$
\angle CAD=110^\circ-35^\circ=75^\circ.
$$

![](images/7c/7c7c4df1668bad7dde4f65e0ed7af6f54fc6f5c0d435bf6f3539c274d8321f66.png)

Use the shared side $AC=12$ in both triangles. The included angle for the sides $AB$ and $AC$ is $35^\circ$, whereas the included angle for $AC$ and $AD$ is $75^\circ$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{ABC}&=\frac12(10)(12)\sin35^\circ\\
&=60\sin35^\circ\\
&\approx34.4146,\\[4pt]
A_{ACD}&=\frac12(12)(8)\sin75^\circ\\
&=48\sin75^\circ\\
&\approx46.3644.
\end{aligned}
$$

The triangles occupy the whole quadrilateral without overlapping, so add their areas:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{ABCD}&=A_{ABC}+A_{ACD}\\
&=60\sin35^\circ+48\sin75^\circ\\
&\approx80.7790.

The area of the quadrilateral $CDAB$ is $11\,\text{in}^{2}$. The sides $CD=6\,\text{in}$ and $CB=8\,\text{in}$ meet at $124^\circ$. What is the area of $\triangle DAB$, rounded to the **nearest integer**?

A scientific calculator is required.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First calculate the area of the enclosing triangle $CDB$. Use the two given sides and their included angle, with the calculator in degree mode.

$$
\begin{aligned}A_{CDB}&=\frac12\cdot CD\cdot CB\cdot\sin\angle DCB\\&=\frac12\cdot 6\cdot 8\cdot\sin124^\circ\\&\approx19.896902\,\text{in}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The enclosing triangle consists of the quadrilateral $CDAB$ and the missing triangle $DAB$. Subtract the quadrilateral area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A_{DAB}&=A_{CDB}-A_{CDAB}\\&=24\sin124^\circ-11\\&\approx8.896902\,\text{in}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Keep full precision until this subtraction is complete. Rounded to the nearest integer, the area is $9\,\text{in}^{2}$.

question.:question/problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=3.$ Given that the point $P(2,3,9)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=6x-y$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(2,3,9)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,3).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,3) & =6(2)-(3)=9\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{6xy+{y}^{2}}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,2) & =\frac{3(1)+(2)}{\sqrt{6(1)(2)+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =\frac{5}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1 \\ z &=\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=3x-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(2,-3,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=6(x-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,-3).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,-3) & =6(2-1)=6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,-3) & ={f}_{x}(2,-3)(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6x-12 \\ z & =6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=-3 \\ z &=6x-9\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=-3,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=6x-9$ (or $6x-z-9=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨6,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨6,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-i-6\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-6⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-6⟩=⟨1,0,6⟩$ is also parallel to it.

question.:question/problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z = f(x, y)$. The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y = 0$. Given that the point $P$ with $x$-coordinate $\frac{π}{2}$ lies on $C$, and that $f_{x} = y\cos x + \cos y$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution: The plane $y=0$ fixes $y$, so the slope of the intersection curve is $f_x$. At $P$, $$f_x(\pi/2,0)=0\cos(\pi/2)+\cos0=1.$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,-1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}(2xy-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,-1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1 \\ z &=-3y-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j-3\,k.$

question.:question/problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P$ with $x$-coordinate $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+xy$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-\frac{\pi }{2},2).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-\frac{\pi }{2},2) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\cdot 2 \\  & =-1-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(1,-3,8)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}+y\sqrt{x}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-3,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,-3).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-3) & =\frac{{1}^{2}+1}{{1}^{2}(-3)^{2}}+(-3)\sqrt{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}-3(1) \\  & =-\frac{25}{9}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Given that the point $P(4,-2,5)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=y\sqrt{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(4,-2,5)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(4,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)} & =(-2)\sqrt{4} \\  & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(4,-2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}(x-4) \\ z-5 & =-4(x-4) \\ z & =-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,-2,5)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=-2 \\ z &=-4x+21\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(1,2,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2xy+2$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,2,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,2)} & =2(1)(2)+2 \\  & =4+2 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,2)}(x-1) \\ z-1 & =6(x-1) \\ z & =6x-5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=2 \\ z &=6x-5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=e.$ Given that the point $P(e,2,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=e.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(e,2,3)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(e,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(e,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(e,2) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\frac{{e}^{2}}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(e,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(e,2)}(y-2) \\ z-3 & =1(y-2) \\ z & =y+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(e,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=e \\ z &=y+1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{xy}{\pi }$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\frac{\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=2 \\ z &=-2x+\pi\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\sqrt{2} \\ z &=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(2,1,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={e}^{y-1}+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,1) & ={e}^{1-1}+2(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-1) \\  & =1+4 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,1) & ={f}_{x}(2,1)(x-2) \\ z-4 & =5(x-2) \\ z & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,1,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=5x-6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=5x-6$ (or $5x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨5,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨5,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-i-5\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-5⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-5⟩=⟨1,0,5⟩$ is also parallel to it.

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,2).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-2) \\ z-3 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-2 \\ z &=2y-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-1$ (or $2y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $\mathbf{j}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,7)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$

$$

$$

$$

- For the plane $z=x+7$ (or $x-z+7=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1 \\ z &=-y-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}.$

$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2(x+y)-2$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =2(1+1)-2=2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,1) & ={f}_{x}(1,1)(x-1) \\ z-1 & =2(x-1) \\ z-1 & =2x-2 \\ z & =2x-1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,-6,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{x(y+x)}}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$

$$

$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-2 \\ z &=-y-5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-1,1⟩.$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3{e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|xy|$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$

$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,1) & ={f}_{x}(-1,1)(x-(-1)) \\ z-(-1) & =3(x+1) \\ z+1 & =3x+3 \\ z & =3x+2\end{aligned}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=3x+2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=3x+2$ (or $3x-z+2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨3,0,-1⟩.$

$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{x(y-x)}{2x(y+1)}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$

$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $y-2z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${\mathbf{n}}_{2}=⟨0,1,-2⟩.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1 \\ z &=-y-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=5.$ Given that the point $P(4,5,-2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{\sqrt{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(4,5).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=5 \\ z &=x-6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

- For the plane $y=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4 x + 8$ (or $4 x - z + 8=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨4,0,-1⟩.$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0) & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{1}{2},0) & ={f}_{x}(\frac{1}{2},0)(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=0 \\ z &=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $x-z+\frac{1}{2}=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.

question.:question/problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P$ with $y$-coordinate $\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy-\frac{\pi }{3})$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $y=\frac{\pi }{4}$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =2(x-1) \\ z & =2x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z &=2x-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2 \\ z &=4y-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

question.:question/problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{{e}^{x}-{e}^{y}}{2x}+2y$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$

question.:question/problem:
A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y)$. The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=-1$. Given that $P(-1,2,4)$ lies on $C$ and that

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The plane $x=-1$ holds $x$ constant, so $y$ varies along the section. Its tangent slope is $dz/dy=f_y(-1,2)$.

Substitute the $x$- and $y$-coordinates of $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m&=f_y(-1,2)\\
 &=3(-1)-2(2)\\
 &=-3-4\\

$$

The height $z=4$ locates the point on the surface; it is not an input to $f_y(x,y)$.

question.:question/problem:
A surface $S$ is defined by

$$
z=f(x,y)=12-3x^2-y^2.
$$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=2$. The diagram shows this section, with $x$ horizontal and $z$ vertical.

![](images/d5/d57e0d9e2dddbbfa44a0545f83aac1e2c4626d552fbb2fbd71983840e498f0d9.png)

Find the slope $m=dz/dx$ of the tangent to $C$ at $P(1,2,5)$.

$m=$ {{slope}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The plane $y=2$ holds $y$ constant, so the slope of this section is given by $f_x$, not $f_y$.

Differentiate with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=0-6x-0\\
 &=-6x.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $P$, $x=1$, so

$$
m=f_x(1,2)=-6(1)=-6.
$$

We can check this using the section itself: $g(x)=f(x,2)=8-3x^2$, and $g'(1)=-6$. The curve descends as $x$ increases through $1$, consistent with the negative slope.

question.:question/problem:
A surface $S$ is defined, for $y>0$, by

$$
z=f(x,y)=x\ln y+\frac{e^{xy}}{y}.
$$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=1$. Find the exact slope of the tangent to $C$ at the point $P$ whose $y$-coordinate is $2$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $x=1$ is fixed, $y$ varies along $C$. The required slope is $f_y(1,2)$.

Holding $x$ constant, differentiate $x\ln y$ and use the quotient rule on $e^{xy}/y$. The chain rule gives $\partial(e^{xy})/\partial y=xe^{xy}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)&=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y(xe^{xy})-e^{xy}}{y^2}\\
 &=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{e^{xy}(xy-1)}{y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate at $(x,y)=(1,2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m=f_y(1,2)&=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{e^2(2-1)}{4}\\
 &=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{e^2}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

As a check, the section is $g(y)=\ln y+e^y/y$. Its derivative is $g'(y)=1/y+e^y/y-e^y/y^2$, which gives the same slope at $y=2$.

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=e$. The point $P(e,1,2)$ lies on $C$, and

$$
f_y(x,y)=\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{y+1}}+\frac{e^y}{x}.
$$

Find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P$. Give exact answers, with $z$ expressed in terms of $y$.

$x=$
{{plane}}

$z=$
{{height}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $x=e$ is fixed, use $f_y$ for the tangent slope. Evaluating at $(e,1)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}m=f_y(e,1)&=\frac{\ln e}{\sqrt{1+1}}+\frac{e^1}{e} \\ &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Apply point-slope form at $(y_0,z_0)=(1,2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2&=\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)(y-1) \\ z&=\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)y+1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the tangent line is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=e \\ z &=\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)y+1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

At $y=1$ the height is $2$, and the coefficient of $y$ equals $f_y(e,1)$. The equivalent expression $2+(1+1/\sqrt{2})(y-1)$ is also valid for the second blank.

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-1$. Given that $P(2,-1,3)$ lies on $C$ and that $f_x=y\sqrt{x+2}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The plane fixes $y$, so the tangent slope is $f_x(2,-1)$, measured as change in $z$ per change in $x$.

$$
\begin{aligned}m&=(-1)\sqrt{2+2} \\ &=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $(x_0,z_0)=(2,3)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3&=-2(x-2) \\ z&=-2x+7.\end{aligned}
$$

Together with the fixed coordinate, the tangent line is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=-1 \\ z &=-2x+7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

At $x=2$, this gives $z=3$; its slope is $-2$, as required.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S$, defined by $z=f(x,y)$, with the plane $y=-1$. The point $P(2,-1,3)$ lies on $C$, and

$$
f_x(x,y)=2x+y.
$$

Which of the following is a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The plane $y=-1$ holds $y$ fixed, so $x$ varies and the slope in this slice is $f_x(2,-1)$:

$$
m=f_x(2,-1)=2(2)+(-1)=3.
$$

A change of $1$ in $x$ along the tangent gives a change of $3$ in $z$, with no change in $y$. Hence $\langle 1,0,3\rangle$ is a tangent vector.

Using the point-slope equation, the tangent line through $P(2,-1,3)$ is the intersection

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y&=-1 \\ z-3&=3(x-2)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The second plane can be written $3x-z-3=0$. Its normal is $\mathbf n_2=\langle 3,0,-1\rangle$, while a normal to $y=-1$ is $\mathbf n_1=\langle 0,1,0\rangle$. Thus

$$
\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2
=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k \\ 0&1&0 \\ 3&0&-1\end{vmatrix}
=\langle -1,0,-3\rangle.
$$

Its negative is the listed vector $\langle 1,0,3\rangle$. The component ratio is $v_z/v_x=3$; $\langle 3,0,1\rangle$ would instead give slope $1/3$.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S$, defined by $z=f(x,y)$, with the plane $x=-2$. The point $P(-2,-4,1)$ lies on $C$, and

$$
f_y(x,y)=\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{x(y+x)}}.
$$

Which of the following is a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The plane $x=-2$ holds $x$ fixed, so the slope in the slice is $f_y(-2,-4)$. Evaluating the given partial derivative gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
m&=\frac{-4-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-4+(-2))}} \\ &=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{12}} \\ &=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

A tangent vector is therefore $\langle 0,1,-1/\sqrt{3}\rangle$. Multiplying by the nonzero scalar $-\sqrt{3}$ gives the listed vector $\langle 0,-\sqrt{3},1\rangle$. Its ratio of $z$-change to $y$-change is $1/(-\sqrt{3})=-1/\sqrt{3}$.

The tangent line through $P(-2,-4,1)$ is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x&=-2 \\ z-1&=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(y+4)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Rearranging the second plane gives $y+\sqrt{3}z+4-\sqrt{3}=0$. Normal vectors to these planes are $\mathbf n_1=\langle 1,0,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf n_2=\langle 0,1,\sqrt{3}\rangle$. Their cross product confirms the direction:

$$
\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2
=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k \\ 1&0&0 \\ 0&1&\sqrt{3}\end{vmatrix}
=\langle 0,-\sqrt{3},1\rangle.
$$

Both signs of a direction vector are allowed, but the component ratio must be preserved. For example, $\langle 0,-1,\sqrt{3}\rangle$ has slope $-\sqrt{3}$, so it is not parallel to this tangent.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)=18-x^2-y^2$ with the plane $x=3$. The point $P(3,2,5)$ lies on $C$.

![The surface cut by the plane x=3, with the intersection curve and its tangent at P.](images/86/8619c41cd0caf04ae9ee9bcae61e31739d8da583793a67c1c87e00186c3ac417.png)

At $P$, the slope in this slice is $f_y(3,2)=-4$. Because $x$ is fixed, a tangent vector has $x$-component $0$.

Which of the following is a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $x=3$ is fixed, $y$ varies along the curve. The slope $dz/dy=-4$ means that a change of $1$ in $y$ along the tangent corresponds to a change of $-4$ in $z$. Thus a tangent vector is $\langle 0,1,-4\rangle$.

The tangent line through $P(3,2,5)$ is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x&=3 \\ z-5&=-4(y-2)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The slice $z=9-y^2$ and its tangent are shown below. The horizontal coordinate is $y$; the tangent slopes downward as $y$ increases.

![The yz slice z=9-y squared and the downward-sloping tangent at P.](images/e9/e982ef5d6d8d4fec9c64957d46f22cea2a85bd002595642f58700cf48cce4256.png)

To connect this with the plane-intersection method, rewrite the second equation as $4y+z-13=0$. Normal vectors to the two planes are $\mathbf n_1=\langle 1,0,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf n_2=\langle 0,4,1\rangle$. Their cross product is

$$
\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2
=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k \\ 1&0&0 \\ 0&4&1\end{vmatrix}
=\langle 0,-1,4\rangle.
$$

Multiplying by $-1$ gives $\langle 0,1,-4\rangle$, the listed tangent vector. Either direction along the tangent is valid; its $z$-change divided by its $y$-change must equal $-4$.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2$. The point $P(2,-1 + \frac{\pi}{4},3)$ lies on $C$, and

$$

$$

Find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P$.
question.:question/worked-solution:

The displayed quotient is evaluated at the supplied point; its denominator is nonzero. Simplifying the numerator and denominator gives the exact slope above.

A change of $1$ in $x$ along the tangent gives a change of $\frac{3}{13}$ in $z$, with no change in $y$. A tangent direction is $\langle 1,0,\frac{3}{13}\rangle$.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y&=5 \\ z-(3)&=\left(\frac{3}{13}\right)(x-(-4))\end{aligned}\right.

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized 
 by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{2}-t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\sqrt{2}]?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{2}-t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+t,$ and $y={t}^{2}-t.$ 

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =(2t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t+1)^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4t+1+4{t}^{2}-4t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\sqrt{2}[({t}^{2}+t)-({t}^{2}-t)] \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2\sqrt{2}t\cdot \sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

For a scalar line integral, substitute the parametrization and multiply by speed. Here $r'(t)=\langle2\sqrt t,t-1\rangle$, so $\|r'(t)\|=\sqrt{4t+(t-1)^2}=t+1$ on $[0,1]$. Also $3x=4t^{3/2}$. Thus $$\int_C3x\,ds=4\int_0^1(t^{5/2}+t^{3/2})\,dt=4\left(\frac27+\frac25\right)=\frac{96}{35}.$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_(C)(x^{2} + y^{2})ds,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=3(\operatorname{cos}t+t\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3(\operatorname{sin}t-t\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em}$ for $0 \le t \le 2π$.
question.:question/worked-solution: Differentiating gives $r'(t)=3t\langle\cos t,\sin t\rangle$, so the speed is $3t$ on $[0,2\pi]$. Also $x^2+y^2=9(1+t^2)$. Hence $$\int_C(x^2+y^2)\,ds=27\int_0^{2\pi}(t+t^3)\,dt=54\pi^2+108\pi^4=54\pi^2(1+2\pi^2).$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em},$ for $t\in [\sqrt{2},\sqrt{6}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$, then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=t+1.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{(t+1)-1} \\  & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =12t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4{t}^{2}+1,$ $\text{d}u=8t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{3}{2}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & ={u}^{3/2}{|}_{9}^{25} \\  & ={25}^{3/2}-{9}^{3/2} \\  & =125-27 \\  & =98\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral $$
\displaystyle \int_(C)4yz\cos xds,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\hspace{0.167em}$ for $0 < t < \frac{π}{2}$.
question.:question/worked-solution: Here $x=t$, $y=\sin t$, and $z=1$. The speed is $\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}$. Thus $$\int_C4yz\cos x\,ds=\int_0^{\pi/2}4\sin t\cos t\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}\,dt.$$ Set $u=1+\cos^2t$, so $du=-2\sin t\cos t\,dt$. The integral becomes $$2\int_1^2u^{1/2}\,du=\frac43(2\sqrt2-1).$$ The omitted endpoints have finite limits and do not change this value.

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution: Substitute $x=2t$, $y=2-t$ to get $x^3-y=8t^3+t-2$. The speed is $\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt5$. Therefore $$\int_C(x^3-y)\,ds=\sqrt5\int_{-1}^{2}(8t^3+t-2)\,dt.$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em},$ for $0\le t\le 1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ 

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2t\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{4y+1}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1}\right)\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}1+t⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}1+t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$    

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =t+(1+t)=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+1)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2t+1\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{[{t}^{2}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1+1-0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em},$ for $t\in [0,1].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$, then along the curve we have $x=3t$ and $y={t}^{3}.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =(3t)^{3}+{t}^{3} \\  & =27{t}^{3}+{t}^{3} \\  & =28{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}28{t}^{3}\cdot 3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}84{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{4},$ $\text{d}u=4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}84{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{2}21\cdot {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =21\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =14({2}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =14(2\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$

$$
