question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,-1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(2,0).$

$$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨2,0⟩-⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨3,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨3,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8x(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}),\,36{y}^{3}-24{x}^{2}y⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,-1) & =⟨8(-1)\cdot (2(-1)^{2}-3(-1)^{2}),36(-1)^{3}-24(-1)^{2}(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨8,-12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,-1) & =∇f(-1,-1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨8,-12⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =8\cdot \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}-12\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{6\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x{y}^{x-1}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,e) & =⟨{e}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡e,1{e}^{1-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,e) & =∇g(1,e)\cdot u \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{e(4)+1(-3)}{5} \\  & =\frac{4e-3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x).$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
question.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,\frac{2}{y}⟩ \\ ∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4) & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction of $∇g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)‖ & =‖⟨-1,\frac{1}{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,0,-2)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,0,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x-yz,\,2y-xz,\,2z-xy⟩ \\ ∇g(1,0,-2) & =⟨2(1)-0(-2),2(0)-1(-2),2(-2)-1(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,2,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨2,2,-4⟩.$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨16{x}^{3}-8xy,\,2y-4{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =⟨16(-1)^{3}-8(-1)(1),\,2(1)-4(-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇f(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =(-8)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)-2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(-1,3)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(2x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)j \\ ∇\,f(-1,3) & =(2(-1)-6(3))\,i+(2(3)-6(-1))j \\  & =-20\,i+12\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,3) & =∇\,f(-1,3)\cdot u \\  & =(-20\,i+12\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{-20(1)+12(1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v}=2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+\frac{y}{x})\,i+(\frac{x}{y}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1})\,i+(\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}j) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4})?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡y+4x-\frac{1}{x})i-x{sec}^{2}⁡y\text{ }j \\ -∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+4\cdot 1-\frac{1}{1})i-1\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\text{ }j \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $-4\,i-2\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ at the point $A(1,e)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,e).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,e⟩-⟨1,e⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}}}⟨-3,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-3,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{2x}{y}⟩ \\ ∇f(1,e) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡e,\,\frac{2(1)}{e}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{2}{e}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,e) & =∇f(1,e)\cdot u \\  & =⟨2,\frac{2}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,0⟩ \\  & =2(-1)+\frac{2}{e}(0) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)={x}^{y}$ increase most rapidly at the point $(2,1)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y})\,j \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,i+{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(1){2}^{1-1}\,i+({2}^{1})\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,j \\  & =i+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $i+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}.$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?
question.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})i-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})j \\  & =-2x{y}^{3}\,i-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,j \\ -∇f(2,-1) & =-2(2)(-1)^{3}\,i-3(2)^{2}(-1)^{2}j \\  & =4\,i-12\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction of $-∇f(2,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇f(2,-1)‖ & =‖4\,i-12\,j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-12)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{160} \\  & =4\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $g(x,y)=(x^2+y)^2$ at the point $A(1,-2)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative at a point $A$ in the direction of a nonzero vector $\mathbf v$ is

$$
D_{\mathbf u}g(A)=\nabla g(A)\cdot\mathbf u,
\qquad \mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}.
$$

The direction must be represented by a unit vector.

The direction is from $A$ towards $B$, so subtract the coordinates in that order and normalize:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf v&=\overrightarrow{AB}=\langle -2-1,2-(-2)\rangle=\langle -3,4\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{(-3)^2+4^2}=5,\\
\mathbf u&=\left\langle -\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the chain rule to both partial derivatives, then evaluate at $A$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_x(x,y)&=2(x^2+y)(2x)=4x(x^2+y),\\
g_y(x,y)&=2(x^2+y),\\
\nabla g(1,-2)&=\langle 4(1)(1-2),2(1-2)\rangle\\
&=\langle -4,-2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}g(1,-2)&=\langle -4,-2\rangle\cdot\left\langle -\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right\rangle\\
&=\frac{(-4)(-3)+(-2)(4)}{5}\\
&=\frac{12-8}{5}=\frac{4}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x^2+2xy$ at the point $(1,2)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v=2\mathbf i-\mathbf j$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative at a point $A$ in the direction of a nonzero vector $\mathbf v$ is

$$
D_{\mathbf u}f(A)=\nabla f(A)\cdot\mathbf u,
\qquad \mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}.
$$

The direction must be represented by a unit vector.

First, normalize the supplied direction vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{5},\\
\mathbf u&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\langle 2,-1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now compute the partial derivatives and evaluate the gradient at $(1,2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x+2y,\\
f_y(x,y)&=2x,\\
\nabla f(1,2)&=\langle 2(1)+2(2),2(1)\rangle=\langle 6,2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the dot product gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}f(1,2)&=\langle 6,2\rangle\cdot\frac{\langle 2,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{5}}\\
&=\frac{6(2)+2(-1)}{\sqrt{5}}\\
&=\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}}=2\sqrt{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the directional derivative of the function $h(x,y)=\dfrac{x^2+y}{x-y}$ at the point $A(2,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-1,3)$.

The required directional derivative is {{field-1}}. Give an exact value.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative at a point $A$ in the direction of a nonzero vector $\mathbf v$ is

$$
D_{\mathbf u}h(A)=\nabla h(A)\cdot\mathbf u,
\qquad \mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}.
$$

The direction must be represented by a unit vector.

First find the direction from $A$ towards $B$ and its unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf v&=\overrightarrow{AB}=\langle -1-2,3-1\rangle=\langle -3,2\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{(-3)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13},\\
\mathbf u&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\langle -3,2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2-1=1\ne 0$, the function is differentiable near $A$. Use the quotient rule for each partial derivative. In the $y$ derivative, the derivative of the denominator $x-y$ is $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_x(x,y)&=\frac{2x(x-y)-(x^2+y)}{(x-y)^2},\\
h_y(x,y)&=\frac{(x-y)+(x^2+y)}{(x-y)^2},\\
h_x(2,1)&=\frac{4(1)-5}{1^2}=-1,\\
h_y(2,1)&=\frac{1+5}{1^2}=6.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the gradient at the starting point $A$, then take the dot product with the unit direction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}h(2,1)&=\langle -1,6\rangle\cdot\frac{\langle -3,2\rangle}{\sqrt{13}}\\
&=\frac{(-1)(-3)+6(2)}{\sqrt{13}}\\
&=\frac{15}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{15\sqrt{13}}{13}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=xy^2-3\ln(x+z)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,2,2)$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The point is in the domain because $x+z=3>0$. A differentiable function decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to its gradient.

Compute all three partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_x&=y^2-\frac{3}{x+z},\\
g_y&=2xy,\\
g_z&=-\frac{3}{x+z}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The logarithm contributes to the $x$ and $z$ components, but not the $y$ component. At the given point,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla g(1,2,2)&=\left\langle 2^2-\frac{3}{1+2},\,2(1)(2),\,-\frac{3}{1+2}\right\rangle\\
&=\langle 3,4,-1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Reverse every component to obtain the direction of fastest decrease:

$$
-\nabla g(1,2,2)=\langle -3,-4,1\rangle.
$$

Any positive multiple of this vector represents the same direction.

question.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=x^2+xy+2y^2$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,-1)$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
A differentiable function increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient.

Compute the partial derivatives while holding the other variable constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x+y,\\
f_y(x,y)&=x+4y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate at the given point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f(1,-1)&=(2(1)+(-1))\mathbf{i}+(1+4(-1))\mathbf{j}\\
&=\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f$ increases most rapidly in the direction of $\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$. A direction vector need not have unit length; any positive multiple points in the same direction.

question.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $h(x,y,z)=(x+y)e^{xz-y}+\ln(x+z)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,1,1)$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The point is in the domain because $x+z=2>0$. The direction of fastest decrease is opposite to the gradient.

Differentiate before substituting the point. The product rule is needed for the $x$ and $y$ partial derivatives, and the exponential requires the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_x&=e^{xz-y}+(x+y)z e^{xz-y}+\frac{1}{x+z},\\
h_y&=e^{xz-y}-(x+y)e^{xz-y},\\
h_z&=(x+y)x e^{xz-y}+\frac{1}{x+z}.
\end{aligned}
$$

In the $y$ partial derivative, the minus sign comes from $\partial(xz-y)/\partial y=-1$. The logarithm contributes only to the $x$ and $z$ partial derivatives.

At $(1,1,1)$, the exponential is $e^{1(1)-1}=1$ and $x+y=x+z=2$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla h(1,1,1)&=\left\langle 1+2(1)+\frac12,\,1-2,\,2(1)+\frac12\right\rangle\\
&=\left\langle \frac72,-1,\frac52\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Negate all three components:

$$
-\nabla h(1,1,1)=\left\langle -\frac72,1,-\frac52\right\rangle.
$$

Thus $h$ decreases most rapidly in this direction. Multiplying this vector by a positive number does not change its direction.

question.:question/problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=2x^2-3y^2$. What is the rate of change of $g$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v=\langle 4,-3\rangle$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change is the directional derivative $D_{\mathbf u}g(1,1)$, where $\mathbf u$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v$.

First normalize the direction vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{4^2+(-3)^2}=5,\\
\mathbf u&=\left\langle\frac45,-\frac35\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Next compute the gradient and evaluate it at the given point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla g(x,y)&=\langle 4x,-6y\rangle,\\
\nabla g(1,1)&=\langle 4,-6\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally take the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}g(1,1)&=\nabla g(1,1)\cdot\mathbf u\\
&=4\left(\frac45\right)+(-6)\left(-\frac35\right)\\
&=\frac{16+18}{5}=\frac{34}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The positive sign means that $g$ increases in this direction.

question.:question/problem:
At a point $P$, a differentiable function $f(x,y)$ has gradient $\nabla f(P)=\langle 2,-1\rangle$.

Which expression gives the rate of change of $f$ at $P$ in the direction of $\mathbf v=\langle 3,4\rangle$? You do not need to evaluate the expression.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change in a direction is the directional derivative

$$
D_{\mathbf u}f(P)=\nabla f(P)\cdot\mathbf u,
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the specified direction. Since $\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$,

$$
\mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}=\left\langle\frac35,\frac45\right\rangle.
$$

Thus the required expression is

$$
\langle 2,-1\rangle\cdot\left\langle\frac35,\frac45\right\rangle
=\frac{2(3)+(-1)(4)}{5}.
$$

Dividing by $5$ makes the rate a change per unit distance; using $\mathbf v$ without normalizing would give a rate for a different speed of travel.

question.:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x,y)=2xy+e^{2x-y}$. What is the signed rate of change of $f$ at the point $(1,2)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?
question.:question/worked-solution:
First compute the gradient, using the chain rule for the exponential term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2y+2e^{2x-y},\\
f_y(x,y)&=2x-e^{2x-y},\\
\nabla f(1,2)&=\langle 4+2,2-1\rangle=\langle 6,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The direction of steepest decrease is opposite to the gradient. The corresponding unit vector is

$$
\mathbf u=-\frac{\nabla f(1,2)}{\|\nabla f(1,2)\|}
=\frac{\langle-6,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{37}}.
$$

The rate in that direction is

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}f(1,2)&=\langle6,1\rangle\cdot\frac{\langle-6,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{37}}\\
&=\frac{-36-1}{\sqrt{37}}=-\sqrt{37}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, $D_{\mathbf u}f=\|\nabla f\|\cos\theta$ is smallest when $\theta=\pi$. The magnitude of the decrease is $\sqrt{37}$, but the signed rate of change is $-\sqrt{37}$.

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $2kg$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F$, measured in Newtons $(N)$.
At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t) = 4t - 3t^{2}$ meters per second.
Calculate the magnitude of the force at time $t = 2$ seconds.
question.:question/worked-solution: Acceleration is $a(t)=v'(t)=4-6t$. At $t=2$, $a=-8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Newton's second law gives $F=2(-8)=-16\,\mathrm N$, so the requested magnitude is $16\,\mathrm N$.

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $5kg$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F$, measured in Newtons.
At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t) = t^{3} - 2e^{t}$ meters per second.
Find an expression for the force acting on the body at time $t$.
question.:question/worked-solution: Acceleration is $v'(t)=3t^2-2e^t$. Multiply by the mass $5\,\mathrm{kg}$: $$F(t)=5(3t^2-2e^t)=15t^2-10e^t,$$ measured in newtons.

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}$ meters.
Find the expression for the force acting on the body at time $t.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2 \\  & =2-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =4\cdot (2-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =8-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $8kg$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F$, measured in Newtons $(N)$.
At time $t > 0$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t) = 2\sqrt{t}$ meters.
Calculate the magnitude of the force at time $t = 4$ seconds.
question.:question/worked-solution: Differentiate position twice: $s'(t)=t^{-1/2}$ and $s''(t)=-\tfrac12t^{-3/2}$. Thus $F(t)=8s''(t)=-4t^{-3/2}\,\mathrm N$. At $t=4$, the force is $-1/2\,\mathrm N$, whose magnitude is $1/2\,\mathrm N$.

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t\ge 0$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t)=2{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-36t+2$ meters per second.
Calculate the time at which the force acting on the body has zero magnitude.
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration. 

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-36t+2) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-6t-36\end{aligned}
$$

Since the mass is always positive, the force has zero magnitude when the acceleration equals zero. So, we set $a(t)=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2}-6t-36 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}-t-6 & =0 \\ (t-3)(t+2) & =0 \\ t & =-2,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\ge 0,$ we disregard the negative solution. 

Therefore, the force has zero magnitude at $t=3\,\text{s}.$

At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t)=4\sqrt{t}-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-3)$ meters per second.
Calculate the magnitude of the force at time $t=4$ seconds.
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\sqrt{t}-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-3)) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{5}{t-3}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the acceleration at $t=4\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4}}-\frac{5}{4-3} \\  & =1-5 \\  & =-4\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force, in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =8\cdot (-4) \\  & =-32.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of the force is

$$
|F|=|-32|=32\,\text{N}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $5\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t)=t-4\sqrt{t}$ meters.
Find the expression for the force acting on the body at time $t.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4\sqrt{t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4{t}^{1/2}) \\  & =1-4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {t}^{-1/2} \\  & =1-2{t}^{-1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2{t}^{-1/2}) \\  & =0-2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\cdot {t}^{-3/2} \\  & ={t}^{-3/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{t\sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force in Newtons is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =5\cdot \left(\frac{1}{t\sqrt{t}}\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{t\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+\frac{4}{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the acceleration at $t=2\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}a(2) & =2-\frac{4}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force in Newtons is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2) & =ma(2) \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of the force is

$$
|F(2)|=|2|=2\,\text{N}.
$$

\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+{e}^{5-t}) \\  & =4t-{e}^{5-t}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{e}^{5-t}) \\  & =4-(-{e}^{5-t}) \\  & =4+{e}^{5-t}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the acceleration at $t=5\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =4+{e}^{5-5} \\  & =4+1 \\  & =5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force in Newtons is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =4\cdot (5) \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $2{x}^{2}\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $2t\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 2t\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & ={t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0={0}^{2}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)={2}^{2}=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =16\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(3{t}^{2}+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. question.:question/worked-solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$

$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (3{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & ={t}^{3}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0={0}^{3}+0+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}+t.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)={1}^{3}+1=2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)={2}^{3}+2=10\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {10}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =150-6 \\  & =144\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $2t\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. $$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $6x\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =3(4-1) \\  & =9\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=2$ using the work-energy principle:

$$

$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=2$ is $5\,m/s.$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(3{x}^{2}+1)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, the particle was initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the particle's initial velocity.

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

$$

and final velocity, at $t=4$, is

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $8\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

$$

and final velocity, at $t=2,$ is

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(4-{x}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $6\sqrt{x}\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=4.$

\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}6\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{x}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =4(8-1) \\  & =28\,J\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(\frac{1}{x}+{x}^{3})\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=e.$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(8-x)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=3.$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $2{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $3.5\,kg$ at a rate of $2{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=3.5\cdot 2{x}^{3}=7{x}^{3}\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{2}7{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}(16-0) \\  & =28\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+x)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, the particle was initially at $x=1,$ and the particle has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ at $x=4,$ calculate the particle's initial velocity.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{2}{x}){|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(8-\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{2}-2) \\  & =9\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ at $x=4.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 9 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {3}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 9 & =\frac{27}{2}-\frac{3}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =3 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm \sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $\sqrt{3}\,m/s.$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude ${t}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{1}{4}(0)^{4}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)=\frac{1}{4}({2}^{4})=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =32\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(1+{t}^{2})\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. $$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=0+\frac{1}{3}({0}^{3})+C\,⟹\,C=0.

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=t+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=1\,s$ is

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $2{e}^{-t}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 2{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =-2{e}^{-t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
0=-2{e}^{-0}+C\,⟹\,C=2.

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=2-2{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=1\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)=2-2{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}=\frac{3}{2}\,m/s.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. $$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{1}{6}({0}^{3})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{1}{6}({1}^{3})=\frac{1}{6}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{1}{6}({2}^{3})=\frac{4}{3}\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{24} \\  & =\frac{21}{8}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{8}{5}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $3t\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 3t\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\frac{3}{2}({0}^{2})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=2\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\frac{3}{2}({1}^{2})=\frac{3}{2}\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(2)=\frac{3}{2}({2}^{2})=6\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {6}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{8}{5}\cdot {\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{144}{5}-\frac{9}{5} \\  & =27\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(8-{x}^{3})\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(8-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[8x-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =8(2)-\frac{1}{4}({2}^{4})-(8(1)-\frac{1}{4}({1}^{4})) \\  & =16-4-8+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{17}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{3}{2}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(1+2t)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (1+2t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =t+{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=0+{0}^{2}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=t+{t}^{2}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)=2+{2}^{2}=6\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot 36 \\  & =27\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{t+1}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=3\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+1|=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|3+1|=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2} \\  & =8{ln}^{2}⁡2-2{ln}^{2}⁡2 \\  & =6{ln}^{2}⁡(2)\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The displacement of the particle is given by $({t}^{3}+2)\,m,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=2\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by $x(t)={t}^{3}+2,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+2) \\  & =3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(2)=3(2)^{2}=12\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=3$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(3)=3(3)^{2}=27\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (27)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (12)^{2} \\  & =729-144 \\  & =585\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(3\sqrt{x}+2)\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3\sqrt{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{1/2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3/2}+2x]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2({4}^{3/2})+2(4)-(2({1}^{3/2})+2(1)) \\  & =16+8-2-2 \\  & =20\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $0.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(5-x)\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $0.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(5-x)\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=0.5\cdot (5-x)=(2.5-0.5x)\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(2.5-0.5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{5}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(2)-\frac{1}{4}({2}^{2})-(\frac{5}{2}(1)-\frac{1}{4}({1}^{2})) \\  & =5-1-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is $(3t-1)\,m/s,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by $v(t)=3t-1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=3(1)-1=2\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=3$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(3)=3(3)-1=8\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot (8)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot (2)^{2} \\  & =96-6 \\  & =90\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $3\sqrt{t}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=1\,s.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 3\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =2{t}^{3/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=2({0}^{3/2})+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{3/2}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=1\,s$ is

v=v(1)=2({1}^{3/2})=2\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =6\,J.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2})\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity $v=5\,m/s$ at $x=2,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =16+16-0 \\  & =32\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=5\,m/s$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 32 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {5}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 32 & =50-2{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2{v}_{0}^{2} & =18 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =9 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $3\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=5-3=2\,m/s.
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{1}{2}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at $x=1,$ and the particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=4,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[3x+\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(12+\frac{1}{4})-(3+1) \\  & =\frac{33}{4}\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=7\,m/s$ at $x=4.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=1$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{33}{4} & =\frac{49}{4}-\frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{4}{v}_{0}^{2} & =4 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=1$ is $4\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=1$ to $x=4$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=7-4=3\,m/s.
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(2-x)\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $0.25\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The displacement of the particle is given by $({t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+2)\,m,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+2) \\  & =4{t}^{3}-4t\end{aligned}

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=4(1)^{3}-4(1)=0\,m/s,

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=4(2)^{3}-4(2)=24\,m/s.

$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $3{x}^{2}\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at $x=0,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{3}-0 \\  & =8\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at $x=0.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=2$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 8 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 8 & =2{v}_{1}^{2}-8 \\ 2{v}_{1}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =8 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=2$ is $2\sqrt{2}\,m/s.$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=-\frac{1}{0+1}+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1-\frac{1}{t+1}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=3\,s$ is

$$
v=v(3)=1-\frac{1}{3+1}=\frac{3}{4}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot \frac{9}{16} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}({2}^{3})-({0}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}({0}^{3})) \\  & =4+\frac{8}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{20}{3}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+5\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf{F}$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{a}^{b}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(5\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}t\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}t)+(-5\operatorname{cos}t)\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}t \\  & =-25{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t-25{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t \\  & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-25)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & =-25t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-25(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-50\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\frac{5}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation $25{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $5,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+5\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf{F}$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{a}^{b}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{5}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}t \\  & =-1+5 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & =4t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi )-0 \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf{F}$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{a}^{b}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t)+\left(-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\right)\cdot \operatorname{cos}t \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-2(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\frac{3}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{2}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36$ oriented counterclockwise.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

It is given by the formula

$$
\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{a}^{b}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{3}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{2}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}t)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}t \\  & =-2-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}$ is a conservative vector field on ${R}^{2},$ then the circulation $Γ=0$ for any *closed* path $C\in {R}^{2},$ that is 

$$

$$

We notice that $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x+y}.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$\mathbf{F}$ is **not** conservative” is false. The vector field $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative since the partial derivatives are equal and continuous everywhere on ${R}^{2}.$

- Statement “$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}=0
$$ for any piecewise smooth path $C\in {R}^{2}$” is false. The result $Γ=0$ applies to closed curves only.

\displaystyle {∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}\ne 0
$$ for some closed paths $C\in {R}^{2}$” is false. The circulation $Γ=0$ for any closed path $C\in {R}^{2}.$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ oriented counterclockwise.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-4(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=-y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=5$ oriented counterclockwise.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $\sqrt{5}$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

$$

$$
x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =5{sin}^{2}⁡t+5{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =5.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\,\text{d}t \\  & =5t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =5(2\pi )-0 \\  & =10\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$
