question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+t[(3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}] \\  & =2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+t(3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}) \\  & =3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3t$ and $y=2-t$ along the segment.

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =(3t)^{2}-(2-t) \\  & =9{t}^{2}+t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x, y, z) = x + y + z$, traversed along the line segment from $(1, 0, 1)$ to $(2, 3, 0)$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Parametrize the segment by

$$
r(t)=\langle1+t,3t,1-t\rangle,\qquad0\le t\le1.
$$

The speed is $|r'(t)|=\sqrt{1+9+1}=\sqrt{11}$, and $f(r(t))=2+3t$. Thus

$$
\int_C f\,ds=\sqrt{11}\int_0^1(2+3t)\,dt.
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})+t[3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-(\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})] \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})-t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i} \\  & =(1-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1-t$ and $y=3$ along the segment.

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\mathbf{i} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}((1-t)+3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}(4-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}(4-t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}(4-t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx-{x}^{2}\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(0,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx-{x}^{2}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-{sin}^{3}⁡t-{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t+{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(-1,0)$ to the point $N(2,4),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=-\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{b}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}+t(2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-(-\mathbf{i})) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}+t(3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(3t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=3t-1$ and $y(t)=4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t(3)-(3t-1)(4)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\,dt \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above, and let $C$ be the path along the segment $\overline{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B$. Which of the following statements are true?

\displaystyle \int_{-C}F \cdot dr > 0

question.:question/worked-solution:
Along the segment from $A$ to $B$, both the field arrows and the direction of traversal point right. Their dot product is positive, so

Reversing the path changes the sign of a vector line integral:

Therefore statement I only is true.

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$

$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement $$

$$ is false, while statement $$

$$ is true. Since the force $\mathbf{F}$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/20/20121d30445c9e756f1c2c024713bc6cd6f0464cfcfc24df68bc30c766c4988e.png)

\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

$$ is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $\mathbf{F}$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/0f/0ff98536c275458d68deabda91f56bf63e7c8f59f5ea79c68292332d8cd58d4f.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0;
$$ $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ only.

question.:question/problem:
![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf{F}$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive” is true, while statement “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero” is false. From the diagram below it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

- Statement “The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive” is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive”; “The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive” only.

question.:question/problem:
![](images/77/772added7ce46ba0ec25de66dfd03e0107787d851006f261ac8843eba008a2d2.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf{F}$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $\mathbf{F}$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement “The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is positive” is false, while statement “The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is zero” is true. From the diagram below we see that $\mathbf{F}$ acts perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $\mathbf{F}$ through $C.$

![](images/d7/d7a469a331a3cda238fcefb9e7163743483975c4ecc7b962d6d5f8d79736693c.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s=0.
$$

- Statement “The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $-C$ is negative” is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/29/29f144d6f3ce8233a034025fe933bc57dbea5476c50a259853a98bd2a2b3a47b.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is zero” only.

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is a stream function for the vector field
$\mathbf{F}(x,y)={x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-2x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2xy.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y.
$$

question.:question/problem:

Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${\mathbf{n}}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

Now, since the vector field $\mathbf{F}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is parallel to ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net outflow through ${C}_{2}$ will cancel with the net inflow through ${C}_{4}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s\hspace{1em}⟹\hspace{1em}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s=0.
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/c4/c4e47604540f3cfb3f73af34b0d3eb64bb649e9a42004d22eccc2dd9007de4fb.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=16.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(2x\,i+y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+2\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 16+2\cdot 8=48.
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

question.:question/problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $ψ(x, y) = 2x\sin y - e^{y}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For the stream-function convention $F=\psi_y i-\psi_x j$, differentiate

$$
\psi_y=2x\cos y-e^y,\qquad\psi_x=2\sin y.
$$

Therefore

$$
F(x,y)=(2x\cos y-e^y)i-2\sin y\,j.
$$

Its divergence is $2\cos y-2\cos y=0$, as expected for a stream function.

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0+0=0
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=y+2y\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)=2x\,i-y\,j$ doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2+(-1)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ only.

\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $\mathbf{F}(x,y)={x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf{F}$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-2x)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2xy.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y.
$$

Finally, we find the level curve of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ that passes through $P.$
First, we find the value of the stream function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(-1,-1) & =(-1)^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =1\cdot (-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is the $-1$-level curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the streamline that passes through $P(-1,-1)$ is $y=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.$

question.:question/problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $ψ(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}) \\  & =2y{e}^{xy}+{y}^{2}x{e}^{xy} \\  & =y{e}^{xy}(2+yx), \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}{e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}) \\  & =-({y}^{3}{e}^{xy}+2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y) & =P\,i+Q\,j \\  & =y{e}^{xy}(2+yx)\,i-({y}^{3}{e}^{xy}+2x)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

I. $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=4xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{y}^{4}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$

II. $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}(3x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3y\operatorname{sin}(3x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$

III. $\mathbf{F}(x,y)={e}^{xy}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-y{e}^{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=4y+4{y}^{3}\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field II has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)=0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=y{e}^{xy}+(-{e}^{x})\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

question.:question/problem:
![](images/0e/0e4a78829ce8d1135d46dda1db59c968c0306937d9c5a45b24fa41648a679ea4.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,
$$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{2}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =⟨2,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨2-t,t⟩ \\  & =(2-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=2-t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{2}(t)) & =(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(2-t+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2-t-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{2}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{2}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{2}^{'}(t) & =(2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =-2+(2-2t) \\  & =-2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{2}}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{2}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =2-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-(1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(2,4),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t\cdot 1+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t+2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}]-[0] \\  & =2+8 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/51/512905447203d1d3a96781d20d586f9c4cf5cc9392fab50607b6fc77e9b00121.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y={x}^{2}$ from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,4),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,4)$ to the point $B(0,4).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-2,
$$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

${C}_{1}$ is the section of parabola $y={x}^{2}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t) &=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t)) & =x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =(t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =t+2{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{1}}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t+2{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}-2 \\  & =[2+8]-2 \\  & =10-2 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x, y) = 2xy$ along the line segment from $(1, 2)$ to $(2, 1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Parametrize the segment by $x=1+t$, $y=2-t$, $0\le t\le1$. Its speed is $\sqrt2$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C2xy\,ds
&=2\sqrt2\int_0^1(1+t)(2-t)\,dt\\
&=2\sqrt2\left[2t+\frac{t^2}2-\frac{t^3}3\right]_0^1
=\frac{13\sqrt2}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_{C}\sin \left(\frac{πy}{4}\right)ds
$$ along the line segment from $(1, 0, 1)$ to $(2, 2, 3)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use $r(t)=\langle1+t,2t,1+2t\rangle$, $0\le t\le1$. Its speed is $3$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\sin\left(\frac{\pi y}4\right)\,ds
&=3\int_0^1\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}2\right)\,dt\\
&=-\frac6\pi\left[\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}2\right)\right]_0^1
=\frac6\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x, y) = 2x - 3y$ along the line segment from $(1, 0)$ to $(-1, 0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The segment lies on $y=0$. Parametrize it by $x=1-2t$, $y=0$, $0\le t\le1$, giving $ds=2\,dt$. Then

$$
\int_C(2x-3y)\,ds=\int_0^1(2-4t)\,2\,dt
=\left[4t-4t^2\right]_0^1=0.
$$

The positive and negative contributions cancel. The arc-length factor is positive even though $x$ decreases.

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(0,1)$ to the point $N(3,3),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx-y\,dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =\mathbf{j}+t(3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\mathbf{j}+t(3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=3t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx-y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3t)^{2}\cdot 3-(1+2t)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}27{t}^{2}-2-4t\,dt \\  & ={[9{t}^{3}-2t-2{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[9(1)^{3}-2(1)-2(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=(x+1)^{2}$ traversed from the point $P(0,1)$ to point $Q(1,4),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y}=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=(x+1)^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) &=x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+1)^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{i}+2(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1+2(t+1)}{(t+1)^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{t+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{1+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)]-[-\frac{1}{0+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)] \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2]-[-1+0] \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dy-x\,dx}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},
$$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dy-x\,dx}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {y}^{′}\,\text{d}t-x\cdot {x}^{′}\,\text{d}t}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {y}^{′}-x\cdot {x}^{′}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[-1-1] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ for $f(x, y, z) = y\sqrt{x^{2} + z^{2}}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $x$ and $y$ as constants and apply the chain rule:
$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=y\cdot\frac12(x^2+z^2)^{-1/2}\cdot 2z=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{x^2+z^2}}.
$$
The formula holds when $x^2+z^2>0$. At $x=z=0$, this partial derivative exists only when $y=0$.

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ for $f(x, y) = x^{2} + xy\sin y$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $x$ as constant. The product rule gives
$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=0+x\left(\sin y+y\cos y\right)=x(\sin y+y\cos y).
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x, y) = \frac{\cos x}{x + y}$, evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(π, 0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the quotient rule while holding $y$ fixed,
$$
f_x(x,y)=\frac{-(x+y)\sin x-\cos x}{(x+y)^2}.
$$
At $(\pi,0)$, the denominator is nonzero and
$$
f_x(\pi,0)=\frac{-\pi\sin\pi-\cos\pi}{\pi^2}=\frac1{\pi^2}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x, y) = \frac{e^{y^{2}}}{x^{2} - 2y}$. The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by
$\frac{∂f}{∂y} = (h(x, y)e^{y^{2}})/((x^{2} - 2y)^{2})$.
Find the function $h(x, y)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The quotient rule gives
$$
f_y=\frac{(2ye^{y^2})(x^2-2y)-e^{y^2}(-2)}{(x^2-2y)^2}
=\frac{(2x^2y-4y^2+2)e^{y^2}}{(x^2-2y)^2}.
$$
Thus $h(x,y)=2x^2y-4y^2+2$. The derivative is defined where $x^2-2y\ne0$.

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})-{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product, the chain, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})-{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) & =(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot {e}^{xy}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}))-{x}^{2}\cdot (2y) \\  & =(1\cdot {e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy))-2{x}^{2}y \\  & =({e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y))-2{x}^{2}y \\  & =({e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot 1)-2{x}^{2}y \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy}-2{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,1)} & ={e}^{1\cdot 1}+1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 1}-2\cdot {1}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =e+e-2 \\  & =2e-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(1,0,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)) \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-(0) \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2y) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2(1)^{2}(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}y,$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(1,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y) & ={e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)+{x}^{2}\cdot (1) \\  & =x{e}^{xy}\cdot (1)+{x}^{2} \\  & =x{e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}+{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ for $f(x, y) = e^{4x - x^{4}y}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Treat $x$ as constant and apply the chain rule:
$$
f_y=e^{4x-x^4y}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(4x-x^4y)=-x^4e^{4x-x^4y}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(0,1),$ $(1,0),$ $(-1,3),$ and $(0,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=2x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(0,1) & =(0+1,2(0)+1) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1+0,2(1)+0) \\  & =(1,2) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(-1,3) & =(-1+3,2(-1)+3) \\  & =(2,1) \\ {\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(0,2) & =(0+2,2(0)+2) \\  & =(2,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}1\le u\le 2,\hspace{1em}1\le v\le 2\}
$$

![](images/3a/3a831bbc56c0ce5e749fcf45bd65825f297d7732158b8f9e371f2178e61b92c0.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{2x+y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨xz,\hspace{0.222em}2y,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨uv,\hspace{0.222em}u+v,\hspace{0.222em}1-v⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}au{v}^{2}+b{v}^{2}+cuv-u+v\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(1-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨v,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(1-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ v & 1 & 0 \\ u & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}v & 0 \\ u & -1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}v & 1 \\ u & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,v,v-u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨xz,\,2y,\,1⟩{|}_{x=uv\,y=u+v\,z=1-v} \\  & =⟨uv\cdot (1-v),\,2(u+v),\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨uv-u{v}^{2},\,2u+2v,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨uv-u{v}^{2},\,2u+2v,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,v,\,v-u⟩ \\  & =(uv-u{v}^{2})\cdot (-1)+(2u+2v)\cdot v+1\cdot (v-u) \\  & =u{v}^{2}-uv+2uv+2{v}^{2}+v-u \\  & =u{v}^{2}+2{v}^{2}+uv-u+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1\cdot u{v}^{2}+2\cdot {v}^{2}+1\cdot uv-u+v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=1+2+1=4.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨2x+y,\hspace{0.222em}2z,\hspace{0.222em}y+z⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨-{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2}⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨8uv,\hspace{0.222em}4uv,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨8uv,\hspace{0.222em}4uv,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨2x+y,\hspace{0.222em}2z,\hspace{0.222em}y+z⟩{|}_{x=-{u}^{2}\,y=2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =⟨2(-{u}^{2})+(2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}2({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}(2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2})+{v}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2{u}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨8uv,\hspace{0.222em}4uv,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩ \\  & =(-{v}^{2})\cdot 8uv+2{v}^{2}\cdot 4uv+2{u}^{2}\cdot 4uv \\  & =-8u{v}^{3}+8u{v}^{3}+8{u}^{3}v \\  & =8{u}^{3}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}8{u}^{3}v}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3x+y+z,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{y}{2}-2,\hspace{0.222em}-3x-z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u-1,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}2-3u-2v⟩
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-3⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨3x+y+z,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{y}{2}-2,\hspace{0.222em}-3x-z⟩|}_{x=u-1\,y=2v\,z=2-3u-2v} \\  & =⟨3(u-1)+(2v)+(2-3u-2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{2v}{2}-2,\hspace{0.222em}-3(u-1)-(2-3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}v-2,\hspace{0.222em}2v+1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}v-2,\hspace{0.222em}2v+1⟩\cdot ⟨6,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\  & =(-1)\cdot 6+(v-2)\cdot 2+(2v+1)\cdot 2 \\  & =-6+2v-4+4v+2 \\  & =6v-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3x+y+z,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{y}{2}-2,\hspace{0.222em}-3x-z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(6v-8)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(6v-8)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}(6v-8)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & =[u]_{-1}^{1}\cdot [3{v}^{2}-8v]_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨2x,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{xz}{3}-2y,\hspace{0.222em}2z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨2u-1,\hspace{0.222em}uv,\hspace{0.222em}3v⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 2\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨3v,\hspace{0.222em}-6,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨3v,\hspace{0.222em}-6,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨2x,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{xz}{3}-2y,\hspace{0.222em}2z⟩|}_{x=2u-1\,y=uv\,z=3v} \\  & =⟨2(2u-1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{(2u-1)(3v)}{3}-2uv,\hspace{0.222em}2(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨4u-2,\hspace{0.222em}-v,\hspace{0.222em}6v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨4u-2,\hspace{0.222em}-v,\hspace{0.222em}6v⟩\cdot ⟨3v,\hspace{0.222em}-6,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩ \\  & =(4u-2)\cdot 3v+(-v)\cdot (-6)+6v\cdot 2u \\  & =12uv-6v+6v+12uv \\  & =24uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨2x,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{xz}{3}-2y,\hspace{0.222em}2z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}24uv\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}24uv\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}[12{u}^{2}v]_{0}^{1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}12v\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & =[6{v}^{2}]_{-1}^{2} \\  & =6({2}^{2}-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,0),$ $(2,-1),$ $(2,2),$ and $(1,3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x-1,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(2(1)-1,1+0) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-1) & =(2(2)-1,2+(-1)) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,2) & =(2(2)-1,2+2) \\  & =(3,4) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2(1)-1,1+3) \\  & =(1,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](images/1d/1d5943d2cf79e7c77f6db3e939242d7e31068f46506fa618abd24b6ac813d32a.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{v}^{2}\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 21\cdot 4\,\text{d}v \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the change of variables 

$$
u=3x-2y,\,v=y+2z,\,w=z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}(3x-2y)^{2}(y+2z)\,dV,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le 3x-2y\le 3,\,0\le y+2z\le 2,\,0\le 2z\le 1\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=3x-2y,\,v=y+2z,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is 

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 3,\,0\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le \frac{1}{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(3x-2y)^{2}(y+2z)\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}{u}^{2}v\cdot |\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{3}{u}^{2}v\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{2}v\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{u}^{2}\,du\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}v\,dv\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1/2}dw \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{u=0}^{u=3}\cdot {[\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{v=0}^{v=2}\cdot [w]_{w=0}^{w=1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (9-0)\cdot (2-0)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le x\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}-1\le 2y+z\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}1\le y-2z\le 4\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le 2y+z\le 1,\,1\le y-2z\le 4,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=2y+z,\,w=y-2z.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Δ} & =\{(u,v,w)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}-1\le v\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}1\le w\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}dV & ={∭}_{Δ}1\cdot |-\frac{1}{5}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{5}\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}du\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}dv\cdot {\int }_{1}^{4}dw \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[u]_{0}^{1}\cdot [v]_{-1}^{1}\cdot [w]_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1))\cdot (4-1) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$

$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y-x.\end{aligned}
$$

.

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{y-x}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 2,\,0\le x-y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf{T}:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $\mathbf{T}$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{1+(x-y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,du]dv \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{2}du]dv \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}[u]_{0}^{2}\,dv \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,dv \\  & =2[\operatorname{arctan}⁡v]_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

the triple integral

can be written in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w$ as
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y,\,w=\sqrt{z}
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 2,\,1\le {w}^{2}\le uv\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}(-1-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{w}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=-w.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}3\sqrt{z}\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}3w\cdot |-w|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}3{w}^{2}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{uv}3{w}^{2}\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=y+z,\,w=z,
$$

which of the following could be the missing part of the expression below?

$$
{∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,dV={\int }_{3\pi /4}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}\,dw\,dv\,du
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=y+z,\,w=z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,\frac{3\pi }{4}\le u\le \pi ,\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,-1\le w\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(1-0) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot |\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /4}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$
