$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{36}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}y}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})-y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}y}\cdot y\cdot 2x-y\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-\frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2xy-1}) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1) & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}(2x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot (2x\cdot 1-0) \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{\sqrt{2xy-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy),$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{4},2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot (2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y\cdot (1) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{4},2) & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {2}^{2}+2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot 2) \\  & =2\pi +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =2\pi +2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{x+y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}⁡y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,\pi /2)} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-(\pi +\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{\operatorname{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1-0}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(0,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{x}{y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\cdot (y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x}{(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(0,2)} & =\frac{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡0-0\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡0)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2+0}{(2+0)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{x+y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{2(x+y)\sqrt{x+y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{x+y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x+y)\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x+y})}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y))}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot 1)}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{6(x+y)-(3x+y)}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\right)}{x+y} \\  & =\frac{3x+5y}{2(x+y)\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=3x+5y.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2x{y}^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}y}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2h(x,y)}{{x}^{3}y}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{2x{y}^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}y}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-1)\cdot {x}^{2}y-(2x{y}^{2}-1)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)}{({x}^{2}y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{y}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}y-(2x{y}^{2}-1)\cdot 2xy}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2xy}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy-2{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy(1-x{y}^{2})}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-x{y}^{2})}{{x}^{3}y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
h(x,y)=1-x{y}^{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ for $f(x,y)={x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x{y}^{3}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{y}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{y}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) & =(\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))-{y}^{3}\cdot (1) \\  & =((4{x}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{4}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x))-{y}^{3} \\  & =4{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{x}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{y}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{x-{y}^{2}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{h(x,y)}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{x-{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot (x-{y}^{2})-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x-{y}^{2})}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2y\cdot (x-{y}^{2})-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot (-2y)}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy-2{y}^{3}+2{x}^{2}y+2{y}^{3}}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy+2{x}^{2}y}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy(1+x)}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=2xy(1+x).
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\sqrt{y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(\frac{1}{4},4).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product, the chain, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) & =(\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)))+\sqrt{y}\cdot (1) \\  & =(1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\cdot \frac{1}{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy))+\sqrt{y} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x))+\sqrt{y} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1+\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{1}{4},4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1/4,4)} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4)+1+\sqrt{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(2,\sqrt{5}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain, the sum, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) & =1\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot ({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot ({x}^{2}\cdot 0+2y) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,\sqrt{5}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\sqrt{5})} & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}+\frac{{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+5}+\frac{5}{\sqrt{4+5}} \\  & =3+\frac{5}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y,$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(2,\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & =x(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y))+\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =x(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y))+\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =x(\operatorname{cos}⁡y-y\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi )} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =2(-1-\pi \cdot 0)+(-1) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}3u+2v \\ u+3v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=3u+2v$ and $y(u,v)=u+3v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot 3-1\cdot 2 \\  & =9-2 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}uv \\ \frac{v}{u}\end{bmatrix}
$$

 

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=uv$ and $y=\frac{v}{u}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}v & u \\ -\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\, & \frac{1}{u}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v\cdot \frac{1}{u}\text{ }-u\cdot \left(-\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{2v}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,3)}=\frac{2(3)}{-2}=-3.
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{u-v} \\ \operatorname{ln}(uv)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u-v}$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(uv).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v} \\ \frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u-v}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{v}\right)-(-{e}^{u-v})\cdot \frac{1}{u} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{v}+\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,1)}=\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}+\frac{{e}^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}=2.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $$
\displaystyle T(\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix})=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{u+v} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(uv)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(uv).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{v}\right)-{e}^{u+v}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{u}\right) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u+v}}{v}-\frac{{e}^{u+v}}{u} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u+v}(u-v)}{vu}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $$
\displaystyle T(\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix})=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ 4u+6v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y=4u+6v.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =4 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \,\text{ }4\, & \,\text{ }6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\cdot 6-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot 4 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2} \\ {u}^{2}-{v}^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & 2v \\ 2u & -2v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-2v\cdot 2u \\  & =-4uv-4uv \\  & =-8uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,1)}=-8(-2)(1)=16.
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}}{2} \\ uv\end{bmatrix}
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\frac{{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}}{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}u & -v \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =u\cdot u-(-v)\cdot v \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,-2)}=(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}=5.
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{v}^{2}+uv \\ v-u\end{bmatrix}
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={v}^{2}+uv$ and $y(u,v)=v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v+u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}v & 2v+u \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v\cdot 1-(2v+u)\cdot (-1) \\  & =v+2v+u \\  & =3v+u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(8,-2)}=3(-2)+8=2.
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}u \\ \operatorname{sin}v\end{bmatrix}
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\pi /6 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡v-0\cdot 0 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\pi /6 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u+v,\,y=u,\,z=v
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u+v,\hspace{0.222em}u,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =(x+2y-z)\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=u-v\,y=2u+2v\,z=2v} \\  & =(u-v)+2(2u+2v)-(2v) \\  & =5u+v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}(5u+v)\cdot 6\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}(5u+v)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2}({\int }_{0}^{1}(5u+v)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{5{u}^{2}}{2}+vu]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}v \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{5}{2}+v)\text{d}v \\  & =6{[\frac{5v}{2}+\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =6[5+2] \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(xy+z)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u+v,\,y=u-v,\,z=0
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u+v,\hspace{0.222em}u-v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+0+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =xy+z\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u-v\,z=0} \\  & =(u+v)(u-v) \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le u\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(xy+z)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\cdot 2\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}({\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}-{v}^{2}u]}_{0}^{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{3}-{v}^{2})\text{d}v \\  & =2{[\frac{v}{3}-\frac{{v}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2[\frac{2}{3}-\frac{8}{3}] \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u,\,y=u+v,\,z=2v
$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}u+v,\hspace{0.222em}2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}-2,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}-2,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =2xz\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}4uv\cdot 3\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}4uv\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}({x}^{2}-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=2u+v,\,y=2u-2v,\,z=u+2v
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $1\le v\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨2u+v,\hspace{0.222em}2u-2v,\hspace{0.222em}u+2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-2,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\hspace{0.222em}-3,\hspace{0.222em}-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨6,\hspace{0.222em}-3,\hspace{0.222em}-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+9+36} \\  & =\sqrt{81} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-{z}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u-2v\,z=u+2v} \\  & =(2u+v)^{2}-(u+2v)^{2} \\  & =3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}-1\le u\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}1\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-{z}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}(3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2})\cdot 9\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =9{∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}(3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =9{\int }_{1}^{2}({\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{u}^{2}-3{v}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =9{\int }_{1}^{2}{[{u}^{3}-3{v}^{2}u]}_{-1}^{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v \\  & =9{\int }_{1}^{2}(2-6{v}^{2})\text{d}v \\  & =9\cdot [2v-2{v}^{3}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =9\cdot (-12) \\  & =-108.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨2x,\hspace{0.222em}2y,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-uv,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2}⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨-2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}-2{u}^{2}⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨-2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}-2{u}^{2}⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨2x,\hspace{0.222em}2y,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩{|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=-uv\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =⟨2{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-2uv,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨2{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-2uv,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}-2{u}^{2}⟩ \\  & =2{u}^{2}\cdot (-2{v}^{2})+(-2uv)\cdot (-4uv)+{v}^{2}\cdot (-2{u}^{2}) \\  & =-4{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+8{u}^{2}{v}^{2}-2{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨y+z,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2}⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨y+z,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩|}_{x=u-v\,y=2\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =⟨2+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}u-v+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨2+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}u-v+{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\  & =(2+{v}^{2})\cdot 0+(u-v+{v}^{2})\cdot (-2v)+1\cdot 0 \\  & =-2uv+2{v}^{2}-2{v}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨y+z,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2uv+2{v}^{2}-2{v}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2uv+2{v}^{2}-2{v}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[-{u}^{2}v+2u{v}^{2}-2u{v}^{3}]_{u=0}^{u=1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-v+2{v}^{2}-2{v}^{3})\text{d}v \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{v}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨{x}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}x+y,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨3u{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}u-v,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}-2\le u\le 0,\hspace{0.222em}0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-6uv-3{v}^{2}⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-6uv-3{v}^{2}⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨{x}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}x+y,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩|}_{x=3u{v}^{2}\,y=u-v\,z=2} \\  & =⟨{(3u{v}^{2})}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}3u{v}^{2}+u-v,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\  & =⟨9{u}^{2}{v}^{4},\hspace{0.222em}3u{v}^{2}+u-v,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨9{u}^{2}{v}^{4},\hspace{0.222em}3u{v}^{2}+u-v,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\cdot ⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-6uv-3{v}^{2}⟩ \\  & =9{u}^{2}{v}^{4}\cdot 0+(3u{v}^{2}+u-v)\cdot 0+2\cdot (-6uv-3{v}^{2}) \\  & =-6(2uv+{v}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{x}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}x+y,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-6(2uv+{v}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & =-6{\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2uv+{v}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =-6{\int }_{-2}^{0}{[u{v}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{v=0}^{v=1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =-6{\int }_{-2}^{0}(u+\frac{1}{3})\text{d}u \\  & =-6{[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}u]}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =-6(-2+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}z,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}uv⟩
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}2u & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-v,\hspace{0.222em}-2{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}z,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=v\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}uv,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}uv,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩\cdot ⟨-v,\hspace{0.222em}-2{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩ \\  & =3\cdot (-v)+uv\cdot (-2{u}^{2})+v\cdot 2u \\  & =-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3,\hspace{0.222em}z,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-3uv-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{4}v+{u}^{2}v]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-6v)\text{d}v \\  & =[-3{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}v-u,\hspace{0.222em}-2uv⟩
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-2uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}-2v⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-2uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & -1 & -2v \\ -1 & 1 & -2u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2v \\ 1 & -2u\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2v \\ -1 & -2u\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2u+2v,\hspace{0.222em}2u+2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩|}_{x=u-v\,y=v-u\,z=-2uv} \\  & =⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}v-u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨u-v,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}v-u⟩\cdot ⟨2u+2v,\hspace{0.222em}2u+2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\  & =(u-v)\cdot (2u+2v)+0\cdot (2u+2v)+(v-u)\cdot 0 \\  & =2({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}-u{v}^{2}]}_{u=0}^{u=1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{3}-{v}^{2})\text{d}v \\  & =2{[\frac{1}{3}v-\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨-x-z,\hspace{0.222em}x-y,\hspace{0.222em}-z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u+v,\hspace{0.222em}v-u,\hspace{0.222em}-v⟩
$$

for $-1\le u\le 0$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨-x-z,\hspace{0.222em}x-y,\hspace{0.222em}-z⟩|}_{x=u+v\,y=v-u\,z=-v} \\  & =⟨-(u+v)-(-v),\hspace{0.222em}u+v-(v-u),\hspace{0.222em}-(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-u,\hspace{0.222em}2u,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨-u,\hspace{0.222em}2u,\hspace{0.222em}v⟩\cdot ⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\  & =(-u)\cdot 1+2u\cdot 1+v\cdot 2 \\  & =-u+2u+2v \\  & =u+2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x-z,\hspace{0.222em}x-y,\hspace{0.222em}-z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(u+2v)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u+2v)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[uv+{v}^{2}]_{v=0}^{v=1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(u+1)\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}+u]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-3xy⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}1-2u⟩
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u{v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(1-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-2⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u{v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-1),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(1-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨2uv,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {v}^{2} & 0 & -2 \\ 2uv & 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}{v}^{2} & -2 \\ 2uv & 0\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}{v}^{2} & 0 \\ 2uv & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & ={⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-3xy⟩|}_{x=u{v}^{2}\,y=-1\,z=1-2u} \\  & =⟨1-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-3(u{v}^{2})(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}3u{v}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨1-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}3u{v}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\  & =(1-2u)\cdot 0+2\cdot (-4uv)+3u{v}^{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =-8uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}-3xy⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-8uv)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}uv\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}u\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u{\int }_{0}^{1}v\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.167em} \\  & =-8\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{2}+y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨-u,\hspace{0.222em}-u,\hspace{0.222em}-v⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -0 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}{z}^{2}+y)\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=-u\,y=-u\,z=-v} \\  & =(-u)^{2}\cdot (-v)^{2}-u \\  & ={u}^{2}{v}^{2}-u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}({u}^{2}{v}^{2}-u)\sqrt{2}\hspace{0.167em}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$

over the parametric surface

$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-2u,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & -2u & 1 \\ 0 & 2v & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-2u & 1 \\ 2v & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2u \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨-2v,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-2v)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+4{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =(-x-y-z)\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}-{u}^{2}\,z=u} \\  & =-u-({v}^{2}-{u}^{2})-u \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}({u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u)\sqrt{8}v\hspace{0.167em}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

over the parametric surface
