$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-{v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨v,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-{v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ v & -1 & 0 \\ u & 0 & -2v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}v & 0 \\ u & -2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}v & -1 \\ u & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2v,\hspace{0.222em}2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}u⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2v,\hspace{0.222em}2{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}u⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(2v)^{2}+(2{v}^{2})^{2}+(u)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+{u}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =(x-{y}^{2}z)\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=uv\,y=-u\,z=-{v}^{2}} \\  & =uv-(-u)^{2}\cdot -{v}^{2} \\  & =uv+{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}(uv+{u}^{2}{v}^{2})\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+{u}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u+v,\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}+2v,\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{3}+3v⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}a{u}^{2}+bu+c\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}+2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{3}+3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}2u,\hspace{0.222em}3{u}^{2}⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}+2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{3}+3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 2u & 3{u}^{2} \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}2u & 3{u}^{2} \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3{u}^{2} \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2u \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6u-6{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}3{u}^{2}-3,\hspace{0.222em}2-2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩{|}_{x=u+v\,y={u}^{2}+2v\,z={u}^{3}+3v} \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\cdot ⟨6u-6{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}3{u}^{2}-3,\hspace{0.222em}2-2u⟩ \\  & =1\cdot (6u-6{u}^{2})+0\cdot (3{u}^{2}-3)+2\cdot (2-2u) \\  & =6u-6{u}^{2}+4-4u \\  & =-6{u}^{2}+2u+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-6)\cdot {u}^{2}+2\cdot u+4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=-6+2+4=0.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨x-\frac{1}{z},\hspace{0.222em}y+\frac{1}{z},\hspace{0.222em}z⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u{e}^{v},\hspace{0.222em}u{e}^{-v},\hspace{0.222em}u⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}a{e}^{v}+b{e}^{-v}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u{e}^{v}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u{e}^{-v}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{v},\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{-v},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u{e}^{v}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u{e}^{-v}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨u{e}^{v},\hspace{0.222em}-u{e}^{-v},\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {e}^{v} & {e}^{-v} & 1 \\ u{e}^{v} & -u{e}^{-v} & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{-v} & 1 \\ -u{e}^{-v} & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{v} & 1 \\ u{e}^{v} & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{v} & {e}^{-v} \\ u{e}^{v} & -u{e}^{-v}\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨u{e}^{-v},\hspace{0.222em}u{e}^{v},\hspace{0.222em}-2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨x-\frac{1}{z},\hspace{0.222em}y+\frac{1}{z},\hspace{0.222em}z⟩{|}_{x=u{e}^{v}\,y=u{e}^{-v}\,z=u} \\  & =⟨u{e}^{v}-\frac{1}{u},\hspace{0.222em}u{e}^{-v}+\frac{1}{u},\hspace{0.222em}u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨u{e}^{v}-\frac{1}{u},\hspace{0.222em}u{e}^{-v}+\frac{1}{u},\hspace{0.222em}u⟩\cdot ⟨u{e}^{-v},\hspace{0.222em}u{e}^{v},\hspace{0.222em}-2u⟩ \\  & =(u{e}^{v}-\frac{1}{u})\cdot u{e}^{-v}+(u{e}^{-v}+\frac{1}{u})\cdot u{e}^{v}+u\cdot (-2u) \\  & ={u}^{2}-{e}^{-v}+{u}^{2}+{e}^{v}-2{u}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{v}-{e}^{-v}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1\cdot {e}^{v}+(-1)\cdot {e}^{-v}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=1-1=0.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨{z}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{y}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}x⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}u⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨{z}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{y}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}x⟩{|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=v\,z=u} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩ \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot (-1)+{v}^{2}\cdot 0+{u}^{2}\cdot 2u \\  & =2{u}^{3}-{u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}2{u}^{3}-{u}^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x=u{v}^{2}+w,\,y={u}^{3}+v,\,z=uv.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =3{u}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{v}^{2} & 2uv & 1 \\ 3{u}^{2} & 1 & 0 \\ v & u & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}3{u}^{2} & 1 \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3{u}^{3}-v.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u{e}^{w} \\ w-u \\ w{e}^{u}-3v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u{e}^{w},\,y(u,v,w)=w-u,\,z(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u}-3v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{w} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =u{e}^{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-3, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{w} & 0 & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ w{e}^{u} & -3 & {e}^{u}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-3)(-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{w} & u{e}^{w} \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3({e}^{w}+u{e}^{w}) \\  & =3{e}^{w}(1+u).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2} \\ u+3w \\ -v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=u+3w,\,z(u,v,w)=-v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =3 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-1, & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & 2v & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)(-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =6u-0 \\  & =6u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}(u\hspace{0.167em}v\hspace{0.167em}w) \\ u+2w \\ uv\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(u\,v\,w),\,y(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,z(u,v,w)=uv.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =\frac{1}{w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} & \frac{1}{w} \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ v & u & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ v & u\end{vmatrix}+2(-1)^{2+3}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v} \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{w}(u-0)-2(1-1) \\  & =\frac{u}{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=z,\,w=4y-2{z}^{2}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & -4z\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 4 & -4z\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-4) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=z-y,\,v=x+z,\,w=-3x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =-3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0+3)+1(0-0) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=y-3z,\,v=x+2z,\,w=3x-y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)={e}^{x},\,v(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y},\,w(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & ={e}^{x} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & ={e}^{x+y+z} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & ={e}^{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{x}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{x}({e}^{2x+2y+z}-0) \\  & ={e}^{3x+2y+z}.\end{aligned}

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x+2y+z} & ={e}^{x+(x+y)+(x+y+z)} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x+y+z} \\  & =uvw\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{uvw}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x \\ z-y \\ xy\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=x,\,v(x,y,z)=z-y,\,w(x,y,z)=xy.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ y & x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-x) \\  & =-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =-u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}uv \\ u+v \\ w\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=uv,\,y(u,v,w)=u+v,\,z(u,v,w)=w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}v & u & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}v & u \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ v-u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}v{e}^{u} & {e}^{u} \\ {e}^{v} & u{e}^{v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v{e}^{u}\cdot u{e}^{v}-{e}^{v}\cdot {e}^{u} \\  & =uv{e}^{u+v}-{e}^{u+v} \\  & =(uv-1){e}^{u+v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,1)} & =(uv-1){e}^{u+v}\,{|}_{u=-1\,v=1} \\  & =(-1\cdot 1-1){e}^{-1+1} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-2|\cdot \delta A \\  & =2\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|6|\cdot \delta A \\  & =6\,\delta A.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,4)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{u}^{2}}{v} \\ uv\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot \underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{2u}{v} & -\frac{{u}^{2}}{{v}^{2}} \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2u}{v}\cdot u-v\cdot \left(-\frac{{u}^{2}}{{v}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{2}}{v}+\frac{{u}^{2}}{v} \\  & =\frac{3{u}^{2}}{v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(2,4)} & =\left(\frac{3{u}^{2}}{v}\right)\,{|}_{u=2\,v=4} \\  & =\frac{3(2)^{2}}{4} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|3|\cdot \delta A \\  & =3\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf{F}$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{a}^{b}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t)+0\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}t \\  & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}(2t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & =[\frac{\operatorname{sin}(2t)}{2}]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf{F}$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$

$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,z={t}^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot (\operatorname{cos}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(t)\cdot \operatorname{cos}(t)+(-\operatorname{sin}(t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}(t))+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t \\  & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(\pi t)+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}(t)+2{t}^{3} \\  & =1+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=(1-{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf{F}$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$

$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(1-{t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}(\pi t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =-2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(\mathbf{i}-\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot (-2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =1\cdot (-2t)+0\cdot 2t+\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t) \\  & =-2t+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}(2\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Γ}={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2t+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}(2\pi t))\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={[-{t}^{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-1-\frac{1}{4})-(-1-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =0\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=(2{t}^{3}-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+({t}^{3}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2{t}^{3}-2t,\,y=3{t}^{2}+3t,\,z={t}^{3}-t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =({t}^{3}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(6{t}^{2}-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(6t+3)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(3{t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(({t}^{3}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot ((6{t}^{2}-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(6t+3)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(3{t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =({t}^{3}-t)\cdot (6{t}^{2}-2)+0\cdot (6t+3)+(3{t}^{2}+3t)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1) \\  & =6{t}^{5}+9{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(6{t}^{5}+9{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{6}+\frac{9{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(1-\frac{9}{5}+\frac{1}{4}+1-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=4.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-x{e}^{z},\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{z}⟩{|}_{z=4} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-x{e}^{4}}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{0}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{{e}^{4}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-x{e}^{4})-0\cdot 0+{e}^{4})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ with radius $2$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{4}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{4}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={e}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}r\,\text{d}r \\  & ={e}^{4}[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=2} \\  & ={e}^{4}(2\pi -0)\cdot (2-0) \\  & =4\pi {e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=x.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=x.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)=1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}z,\hspace{0.222em}x⟩{|}_{z=x} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{0}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{x}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{x}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot 1-x\cdot 0+x))\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=({t}^{2}+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}+t,\,y={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,z=2{t}^{2}+2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+({t}^{2}+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(4t+2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2{t}^{2}+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+({t}^{2}+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot ((2t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(4t+2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})(2t+1)+(2{t}^{2}+2t)(3{t}^{2}+2t)+({t}^{2}+t)(4t+2) \\  & =2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2t+11{t}^{2}+17{t}^{3}+8{t}^{4})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}+\frac{11}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{17}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{8}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(1-\frac{11}{3}+\frac{17}{4}-\frac{8}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+yz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-t,\,y=2{t}^{2}+1,\,z={t}^{2}-1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+yz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(2{t}^{2}+1)({t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(3{t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot ((3{t}^{2}-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}+1)(3{t}^{2}-1)+3(4t)+(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}-1)(2t) \\  & =-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-1+10t+{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+6{t}^{4}+4{t}^{5})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={[-t+5{t}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}+\frac{6}{5}{t}^{5}+\frac{2}{3}{t}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-1+5+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3})-(1+5-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{6}{5}+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-2+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{16}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{e}^{z-2y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{e}^{z-2y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)-2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}(\pi t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}(\pi t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =(2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}(\pi t))-2\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t)+1\cdot 2\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi {\operatorname{sin}}^{2}(\pi t)-2\pi {\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(\pi t)+2\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-2\pi +2\pi \operatorname{cos}(\pi t))\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =[-2\pi t+2\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2\pi (1)+0)-(-2\pi (-1)+0) \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=4$ and ${b}^{2}=2.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=4,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{4}=2.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=2,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{2}.$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=2,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot 2=4,$ and the minor axis has length $2b=2\cdot \sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}.$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=3$ and ${b}^{2}=12.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=3,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{3}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=12,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=2\sqrt{3},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=\sqrt{3}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 2\sqrt{3}=4\sqrt{3},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3}.$

question.:question/problem: Find the possible values of the constant $p$ given that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 6 & -5 & 2p-4\end{bmatrix}$ is singular.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 6 & -5 & 2p-4\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -5 & 2p-4\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 6 & 2p-4\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 6 & -5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2p-4+10)-0+(-10-6) \\  & =2p-4+10-10-6 \\  & =2p-10\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix is singular, the determinant is $0.$ So,  we have:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}2p-10 & =0 \\ 2p & =10 \\ p & =\frac{10}{2} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $p=5.$

Let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 & 3 \\ -3y & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & y & -5\end{vmatrix} & =4\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ y & -5\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}-3y & 1 \\ 2 & -5\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}-3y & -2 \\ 2 & y\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4\cdot (10-y)-2\cdot (15y-2)+3\cdot (-3{y}^{2}+4) \\  & =40-4y-30y+4-9{y}^{2}+12 \\  & =-9{y}^{2}-34y+56\end{aligned}

Since the determinant of the matrix is $81,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{y}^{2}-34y+56 & =81 \\ -9{y}^{2}-34y-25 & =0 \\ 9{y}^{2}+34y+25 & =0 \\ y & =\frac{-34\pm \sqrt{{34}^{2}-4\cdot 9\cdot 25}}{2\cdot 9} \\  & =\frac{-34\pm \sqrt{256}}{18} \\  & =\frac{-34\pm 16}{18} \\  & =\frac{-17\pm 8}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $y=-\frac{25}{9}$ and $y=-1.$

question.:question/problem:
Given that
$$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}-k & 0 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2k & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$
and $det(A)=-30,$ find the value of $k.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}-k & 0 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2k & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-k\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2k & 1\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2k & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-k\cdot 3+0-3\cdot (-6k) \\  & =-3k+18k \\  & =15k\end{aligned}
$$

Since the determinant of the matrix is $-30,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}15k & =-30 \\ k & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that $M=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & p & 0 \\ p-3 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ and $det(M)=-23,$ find all the possible values of $p.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & p & 0 \\ p-3 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}p & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}-(-3)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ p-3 & -1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & p \\ p-3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0+3\cdot (-1)+2\cdot (3p-{p}^{2}) \\  & =-3-2{p}^{2}+6p \\  & =-2{p}^{2}+6p-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since the determinant of the matrix is $-23,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{p}^{2}+6p-3 & =-23 \\ 2{p}^{2}-6p-20 & =0 \\ {p}^{2}-3p-10 & =0 \\ p & =\frac{-(-3)\pm \sqrt{(-3)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot (-10)}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{3\pm \sqrt{49}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3\pm 7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the solutions are $p=-2$ and $p=5.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{c}=⟨-2,0,0⟩$ and $\mathbf{d}=⟨4,-1,0⟩.$ Find the scalar projection of $\mathbf{c}$ onto $\mathbf{d}.$

$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the triangle spanned by $\mathbf{r}=⟨1,-2,3⟩$ and $\mathbf{t}=⟨0,1,-2⟩.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}\times \mathbf{t} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-2)\cdot (-2)-3\cdot 1)\mathbf{i}-(1\cdot (-2)-3\cdot 0)\mathbf{j}+(1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨1,2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the corresponding parallelogram is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{r}\times \mathbf{t}\hspace{0.167em}| \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of the triangle is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the $△\,LMN$, if $L(0,0,1)$, $M(2,1,1)$, $N(3,1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{LM}$ and $\overset{\to }{LN}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{LM} & =\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{l} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨2,1,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{LN} & =\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{l} \\  & =(3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-\mathbf{k} \\  & =3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨3,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{LM}\times \overset{\to }{LN} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(1\cdot 0-0\cdot 1)\mathbf{i}-(2\cdot 0-0\cdot 3)\mathbf{j}+(2\cdot 1-1\cdot 3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{LM}$ and $\overset{\to }{LN}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{LM}\times \overset{\to }{LN}| \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,LMN$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{g}=\begin{bmatrix}{r}^{2} \\ -1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{h}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ {r}^{2} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Given that $\mathbf{g}⊥\mathbf{h}$ and $r<0$, find the value of $r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We know that $\mathbf{g}⊥\mathbf{h}$ ($\mathbf{g}$ and $\mathbf{h}$ are perpendicular) if and only if $\mathbf{g}\cdot \mathbf{h}=0.$

Computing the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{g}\cdot \mathbf{h} & ={g}_{x}\cdot {h}_{x}+{g}_{y}\cdot {h}_{y}+{g}_{z}\cdot {h}_{z} \\  & ={r}^{2}\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot {r}^{2}+(-6)\cdot 2 \\  & =3{r}^{2}-{r}^{2}-12 \\  & =2{r}^{2}-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{g}\cdot \mathbf{h} & =0 \\ 2{r}^{2}-12 & =0 \\ 2{r}^{2} & =12 \\ {r}^{2} & =6 \\ r & =\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the positive solution since we are told that $r<0.$ Therefore, $r=-\sqrt{6}.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨2,1,-1⟩$ and $\mathbf{b}=⟨1,4,2⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{b}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}-{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{a}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{b}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a} & =\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+1\cdot 4+(-1)\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{a}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b} & =\frac{\mathbf{b}\cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\hspace{0.167em}|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{b}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}-{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{a}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b} & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{6}-4\sqrt{21}}{\sqrt{126}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{c}=⟨4,3,0⟩$ and $\mathbf{d}=⟨2,1,2⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{d}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{c}-{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{c}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{d}.$

Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{d}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{c} & =\frac{\mathbf{c}\cdot \mathbf{d}}{|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{d}\hspace{0.167em}|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}+{d}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 2+3\cdot 1+0\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{c}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{d} & =\frac{\mathbf{c}\cdot \mathbf{d}}{|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{c}\hspace{0.167em}|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{c}_{x}^{2}+{c}_{y}^{2}+{c}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{11}{\sqrt{25}} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}.\end{aligned}

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{d}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{c}-{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{c}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{d} & =\frac{11}{3}-\frac{11}{5} \\  & =11(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =11(\frac{5}{15}-\frac{3}{15}) \\  & =\frac{22}{15}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨-1,2,\sqrt{11}⟩$ and $\mathbf{b}=⟨4,3,\sqrt{11}⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{b}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}-{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{a}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{b}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a} & =\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 4+2\cdot 3+\sqrt{11}\cdot \sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(\sqrt{11})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{13}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{a}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b} & =\frac{\mathbf{b}\cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\hspace{0.167em}|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{13}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(\sqrt{11})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{13}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{13}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{b}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}-{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{a}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b} & =\frac{13}{6}-\frac{13}{4} \\  & =13(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =13(\frac{2}{12}-\frac{3}{12}) \\  & =-\frac{13}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{p}=⟨1,4,2\sqrt{2}⟩$ and $\mathbf{q}=⟨1,1,\sqrt{2}⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{q}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{p}+{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{p}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{q}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{\mathbf{q}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{p} & =\frac{\mathbf{p}\cdot \mathbf{q}}{|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{q}\hspace{0.167em}|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}+{q}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1+2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{4}} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{u}=⟨2,1,-1⟩$ and $\mathbf{v}=⟨1,2,0⟩.$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{f}=⟨1,1,-2⟩$ and $\mathbf{g}=⟨3,2,1⟩.$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{h}=⟨2,0,3⟩$ and $\mathbf{l}=⟨4,1,3⟩.$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the $△\,RST$, if $R(3,-2,1)$, $S(2,-2,2)$, $T(1,-3,3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{RS}$ and $\overset{\to }{RT}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{RS} & =\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{r} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-1,0,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{RT} & =\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{r} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-2,-1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{RS}\times \overset{\to }{RT} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 1)\mathbf{i}-((-1)\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot 1)\mathbf{j}+((-1)\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{RS}$ and $\overset{\to }{RT}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{RS}\times \overset{\to }{RT}| \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,RST$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/6f/6f827dac7ecaf3a659245d1178aa39a519ae3a40339c917004247f12554c871a.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and a square $C$ with side length $8$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${\mathbf{n}}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/0b/0b753318ebad9270c3fc8788d0e3949ffb29a800eb3f8dd6fb67cb271be68033.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${\mathbf{n}}_{1}=\mathbf{i},$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot {\mathbf{n}}_{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot \mathbf{i}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=4\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-4,4].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-4}^{4}4\cdot ||{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)||\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-4}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =8(4-(-4)) \\  & =8\cdot 8 \\  & =64.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{p}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{q}=\begin{bmatrix}15 \\ \sqrt{2} \\ x\end{bmatrix}.$ Given that the scalar projection of $\mathbf{p}$ onto $\mathbf{q}$ is $0,$ find the value of $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{p}$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{q}$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
\mathbf{p}⊥\mathbf{q}\hspace{2em}⟹\hspace{2em}\mathbf{p}\cdot \mathbf{q}=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{p}\cdot \mathbf{q} & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =(-2)\cdot 15+0\cdot \sqrt{2}+5\cdot x \\  & =5x-30.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{p}\cdot \mathbf{q} & =0 \\ 5x-30 & =0 \\ 5x & =30 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\displaystyle \int x{5}^{x}\text{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={5}^{x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}-\int \frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{5}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{x{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}-\int \frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}-\frac{{5}^{x}}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5))^{2}}+C \\  & =\frac{{5}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(x-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5})+C\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:

Using the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-2)\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 1)\mathbf{i}-((-4)\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 1)\mathbf{j}+((-4)\cdot (-2)-0\cdot (-2))\mathbf{k} \\  & =4\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}+8\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨4,-4,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the corresponding parallelogram is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{8}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -2 & -1 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ -4 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ -4 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 0)\mathbf{i}-((-2)\cdot (-2)-(-4)\cdot 0)\mathbf{j}+((-2)\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-1))\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}-8\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨2,-4,-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the corresponding parallelogram is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-8)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of the triangle is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{2\sqrt{21}}{2}=\sqrt{21}.
$$

First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(-3\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-4\mathbf{k})-(-2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-1,3,-3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(-2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(-2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{k}) \\  & =2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨2,-2,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & 3 & -3 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(3\cdot 3-(-2)\cdot (-3))\mathbf{i}-((-1)\cdot 3-2\cdot (-3))\mathbf{j}+((-1)\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =3\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}-4\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨3,-3,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC}| \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,ABC$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{\sqrt{34}}{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{LM}\times \overset{\to }{LN} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -3 & 3 & 1 \\ -5 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ -5 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ -5 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(3\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 2)\mathbf{i}-((-3)\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-5))\mathbf{j}+((-3)\cdot 2-3\cdot (-5))\mathbf{k} \\  & =-5\mathbf{i}-8\mathbf{j}+9\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-5,-8,9⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,LMN$ is

Let's also compute $LM$ since it appears in the formula:

$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that the length of the altitude $CK$ can be related to the area of $△\,ABC$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}CK\cdot AB
$$

So, to find $CK,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(4\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =3\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+0\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨3,2,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨1,3,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2\cdot 1-0\cdot 3)\mathbf{i}-(3\cdot 1-0\cdot 1)\mathbf{j}+(3\cdot 3-2\cdot 1)\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+7\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨2,-3,7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{7}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{62}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,ABC$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{\sqrt{62}}{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $AB$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =|\overset{\to }{AB}| \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}CK\cdot AB,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{62}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}CK\cdot \sqrt{13} \\ CK & =\frac{\sqrt{62}}{\sqrt{13}} \\ CK & =\frac{\sqrt{806}}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{GI}\times \overset{\to }{GH} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(3\cdot 3-1\cdot 1)\mathbf{i}-(1\cdot 3-1\cdot 2)\mathbf{j}+(1\cdot 1-3\cdot 2)\mathbf{k} \\  & =8\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-5\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨8,-1,-5⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,GHI$ is

$$

$$

Let's also compute $GI$ since it appears in the formula:

$$

$$
