$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{RS} & =\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{r} \\  & =(7\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+5\mathbf{k})-(4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+6\mathbf{k}) \\  & =3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨3,-1,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{RT} & =\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{r} \\  & =(6\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k})-(4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+6\mathbf{k}) \\  & =2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨2,3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{RS}\times \overset{\to }{RT} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 3 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)(-2)-(-1)\cdot 3)\mathbf{i}-(3(-2)-(-1)\cdot 2)\mathbf{j}+(3\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot 2)\mathbf{k} \\  & =5\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+11\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨5,4,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,RST$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $RS$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}RS & =|\overset{\to }{RS}| \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{11}.\end{aligned}

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}TK\cdot RS,$ we get

$$

To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3 \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{36} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -5 \\ \frac{y+5}{2\sqrt{7}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+5)^{2}}{(2\sqrt{7})^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+5)^{2}}{28} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{36}+\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{28} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{36}+\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{28}=1.

$$

Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{x} & ⇒ & v={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot {e}^{x}-\int {e}^{x}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =2x{e}^{x}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x{e}^{x}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{x}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(1\cdot {e}^{1}-0\cdot {e}^{0})-2({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2e-2(e-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 4x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x & =4x\cdot (-\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))-\int (-\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))\cdot 4\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{4}{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{4}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{4}{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{4}{\pi }(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0))+\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)) \\  & =-\frac{4}{\pi }(-1-0)+\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}(0-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 9x\cdot {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =9x\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x})-\int (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x})\cdot 9\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}9x{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =-3x{e}^{-3x}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-3{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3x{e}^{-3x}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-{e}^{-3x}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-3(1\cdot {e}^{-3}-0\cdot {e}^{0})-({e}^{-3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-3{e}^{-3}-({e}^{-3}-1) \\  & =1-4{e}^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+1)^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1) & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (1+0) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)$ for $g(x,y,z)=(x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z+(z+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z+(z+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}((z+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =(x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡z)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z+y) \\  & =(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot 1 \\  & =(x+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Unfortunately, this limit takes the indeterminate form because the numerator and denominator both evaluate to zero at the given point:

$$
\lim_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}}{z{x}^{2}-z{y}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot {1}^{2}+1\cdot (-1)-(-1)^{2}}{1\cdot {1}^{2}-1\cdot (-1)^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}}{z{x}^{2}-z{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+2xy-xy-{y}^{2}}{z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2x(x+y)-y(x+y)}{z(x+y)(x-y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{(2x-y)(x+y)}{z(x+y)(x-y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2x-y}{z(x-y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2x-y}{z(x-y)} & =\frac{2(1)-(-1)}{1(1-(-1))} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{3}{2}.$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $∇h(x,y)$ at $(1,1)$ if $h(x,y)=4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =⟨{h}_{x}(x,y),\,{h}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y,\,\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ ∇h(1,1) & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡1,\,\frac{4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{4}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the gradient of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},0)$ if $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The function 

$$
f(x,y,z)=\frac{{x}^{2}+yz+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-xy+xz-yz}
$$

is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(-1,1,0)$ does not cause the denominator to become zero, so we can calculate the limit by substituting  $(-1,1,0)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}+yz+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-xy+xz-yz} & =\frac{(-1)^{2}+(1)(0)+(0)^{2}}{(-1)^{2}-(-1)(1)+(-1)(0)-(1)(0)} \\  & =\frac{1+0+0}{1+1+0-0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3xy-2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-xy}=\frac{2\cdot {1}^{2}+3\cdot 1\cdot 2-2\cdot {2}^{2}}{2\cdot {1}^{2}-1\cdot 2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first factoring the denominator, and then canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3xy-2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-xy} & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+4xy-xy-2{y}^{2}}{x(2x-y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2x(x+2y)-y(x+2y)}{x(2x-y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{(2x-y)(x+2y)}{x(2x-y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{x+2y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{x+2y}{x} & =\frac{1+2\cdot 2}{1} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $5.$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point  where $(x,y)=(1,1)$, can be found by computing $∇g(1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{g}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\,i+\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j \\ ∇g(1,1) & =\frac{1}{(1)}\,i+\frac{1}{(1)}\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇g(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}g(1,1)}{‖\mathrm{∇}g(1,1)‖} & =\frac{\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $2xy+6{y}^{2}=x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(8,-3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy+6{y}^{2} & =x-2 \\ 2xy+6{y}^{2}-x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy+6{y}^{2}-x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(8,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(8,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(8,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,j \\  & =(2y-1)\,i+(2x+12y)\,j \\ ∇f(8,-3) & =(2(-3)-1)\,i+(2(8)+12(-3))\,j \\  & =-7\,i-20\,j \\  & =⟨-7,-20⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(8,-3)=⟨-7,-20⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(8,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-8}{-7} & =\frac{y-(-3)}{-20} \\ -20(x-8) & =-7(y+3) \\ -20x+7y+160+21 & =0 \\ -20x+7y+181 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $∇f(x,y)$ at $(2,1)$ if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =2x\sqrt{y+3} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Given  $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})$, find $∇g(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x-\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\cdot 2y \\  & =\frac{1}{y}-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+{g}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(\frac{1}{y}-2y\operatorname{sin}({y}^{2}))\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $∇f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(2,3,1)$ if $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot yz \\  & =\frac{1}{2x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot xz \\  & =\frac{1}{2y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot xy \\  & =\frac{1}{2z}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{f}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2z}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,1) & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 2}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\cdot 3}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2\cdot 1}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{6}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y=8xy+2-8e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =8xy+2-8e \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy & =2-8e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=2-8e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf{t}(1,e)={f}_{y}(1,e)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(1,e)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf{t}(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{2x}{y}-8x)i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡y-8y)\,j \\ t(1,e) & =(\frac{2(1)}{e}-8(1))i-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-8(e))\,j \\  & =(\frac{2}{e}-8)i+(8e-2)j\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, our tangent vector is $(\frac{2}{e}-8)\mathbf{i}+(8e-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the value of $$
\displaystyle \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{vmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 8\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 8\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(32-0)+1(0-0)+2(0-0) \\  & =1\cdot 32 \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(1,2)$ to the point $B(3,4),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+t(3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-(\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+t(2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(1+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2+2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=1+2t$ and $y(t)=2+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+2t)\cdot 2+(2+2t)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6+8t\,dt \\  & ={[6t+4{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[6(1)+4(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/73/73c6a8268a179f72611fb65e099d1249d48501e4fd4731d03747800e1944fd97.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,2)$ to the point $D(1,3).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{7}{2},
$$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(2x-3y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+t(⟨1,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\  & =⟨t,1+t⟩ \\  & =t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(2t-3(1+t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+(1+t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(-3-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t) & =((-3-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =-3-t+2t+1 \\  & =t-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\mathbf{F}({\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{1}}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}_{1}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-2t]}_{0}^{1}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-2-0]+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ traversed from the point $P(0,0)$ to point $Q(1,1),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}4y{e}^{xy}\,dx+dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt[3]{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) &=x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}={t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4y{e}^{xy}\,dx+dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4y{e}^{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4y{e}^{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t\cdot {e}^{{t}^{3}\cdot t}\cdot 3{t}^{2}+1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{4}}+1\,dt \\  & ={[3{e}^{{t}^{4}}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[3{e}^{(1)^{4}}+(1)]-[3{e}^{(0)^{4}}+(0)] \\  & =[3e+1]-[3] \\  & =3e-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-2}^{0}x{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-x} & ⇒ & v=-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot (-{e}^{-x})-\int (-{e}^{-x})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{0}x{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =-x{e}^{-x}{|}_{-2}^{0}+{\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x{e}^{-x}{|}_{-2}^{0}-{e}^{-x}{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =[-0{e}^{-0}-2{e}^{2}]-[{e}^{0}-{e}^{2}] \\  & =-2{e}^{2}-1+{e}^{2} \\  & =-1-{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xyz-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,0,\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =yz\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =yz\cdot 1-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =yz-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}yz-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) & =yz-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xz) \\  & =yz-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)\cdot (z) \\  & =yz-z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz) \\  & =z(y-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,0,\pi )} & =\pi (0-\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )) \\  & =\pi (0-(-1)) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}(xy),\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)+f(x,y)\mathrm{∇}g(x,y) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}(xy))(y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j})+xy(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\  & =[y\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+y\text{ }\mathbf{i}]+[x\operatorname{ln}(xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j}] \\  & =y(\operatorname{ln}(xy)+1)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x(\operatorname{ln}(xy)+1)\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y}
$$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y}=\frac{2\cdot 0+0}{3\cdot 0+0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$” is false. Taking $\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)\,\hspace{0.222em}\hspace{0.222em}y=x}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2x+x}{3x+x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x}{4x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=-x$” is true. Taking $\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)\,\hspace{0.222em}\hspace{0.222em}y=-x}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{-2x+x}{3x-x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{-x}{2x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit exists and is equal to $0$” is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\frac{2y+x}{3x+y}=\text{DNE}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,1,-1).$  

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,k \\  & =({y}^{2}+2xz)\text{ }i+(2xy+{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2yz+{x}^{2})\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,1,-1) & =((1)^{2}+2(-1)(-1))\,i+(2(-1)(1)+(-1)^{2}))\,j+(2(1)(-1)+(-1)^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i-1j-1\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$

question.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{49}=1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=4$ and ${b}^{2}=49.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=4,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{4}=2.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=49,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{49}=7.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=7,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=2.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 7=14,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 2=4.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $M$ given below?

Select all that apply.

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 4 & -2\end{vmatrix}-(-2)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-4-12)+2(-2+6)+1(4+4) \\  & =1\cdot (-16)+2\cdot 4+1\cdot 8 \\  & =-16+8+8 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $det(M)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, only statements “$M$ is a singular matrix” and $det(M)=0$ are true.

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the $△\,WXY$, if $W(2,-3,1)$, $X(-2,1,2)$, $Y(3,-1,3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{WX}$ and $\overset{\to }{WY}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{WX} & =\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{w} \\  & =(-2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-4\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-4,4,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{WY} & =\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{w} \\  & =(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})-(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨1,2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{WX}\times \overset{\to }{WY} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -4 & 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-4 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(4\cdot 2-1\cdot 2)\mathbf{i}-((-4)\cdot 2-1\cdot 1)\mathbf{j}+((-4)\cdot 2-1\cdot 4)\mathbf{k} \\  & =6\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j}-12\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨6,9,-12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{WX}$ and $\overset{\to }{WY}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{WX}\times \overset{\to }{WY}| \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{9}^{2}+{12}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{261}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,WXY$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{\sqrt{261}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the $△\,NPQ$, if $N(1,0,1)$, $P(2,2,3)$, $Q(2,1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{NP}$ and $\overset{\to }{NQ}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{NP} & =\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{n} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨1,2,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{NQ} & =\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{n} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨1,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{NP}\times \overset{\to }{NQ} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2\cdot 0-1\cdot 2)\mathbf{i}-(1\cdot 0-1\cdot 2)\mathbf{j}+(1\cdot 1-1\cdot 2)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-2,2,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{NP}$ and $\overset{\to }{NQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{NP}\times \overset{\to }{NQ}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,NPQ$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the $△\,FGH$, if $F(1,1,2)$, $G(2,2,3)$, $H(1,0,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{FG}$ and $\overset{\to }{FH}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{FG} & =\mathbf{g}-\mathbf{f} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{FH} & =\mathbf{h}-\mathbf{f} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{FG}\times \overset{\to }{FH} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(1\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 1)\mathbf{i}-(1\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 1)\mathbf{j}+(1\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 1)\mathbf{k} \\  & =\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{FG}$ and $\overset{\to }{FH}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{FG}\times \overset{\to }{FH}| \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,FGH$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the $△\,CDE$, if $C(1,-2,3)$, $D(1,-3,3)$, $E(1,1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{CD}$ and $\overset{\to }{CE}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{CD} & =\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{c} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{CE} & =\mathbf{e}-\mathbf{c} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}) \\  & =3\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{CD}\times \overset{\to }{CE} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)\cdot (-2)-3\cdot 0)\mathbf{i}-(0\cdot (-2)-0\cdot 0)\mathbf{j}+(0\cdot 3-0\cdot (-1))\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\mathbf{i} \\  & =⟨2,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{CD}$ and $\overset{\to }{CE}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{CD}\times \overset{\to }{CE}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,CDE$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=1.
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the length of the altitude $MH$ of the $△\,LMN$, if $L(3,3,2)$, $M(1,1,2)$, $N(2,2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that the length of the altitude $MH$ can be related to the area of $△\,LMN$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}MH\cdot LN
$$

So, to find $MH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{LM}$ and $\overset{\to }{LN}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{LM} & =\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{l} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨-2,-2,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{LN} & =\mathbf{n}-\mathbf{l} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-1,-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{LM}\times \overset{\to }{LN} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -2 & -2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-2)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 0)\mathbf{i}-((-2)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 0)\mathbf{j}+((-2)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot (-2))\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨2,-2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{LM}$ and $\overset{\to }{LN}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{LM}\times \overset{\to }{LN}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,LMN$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2}=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $LN$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}LN & =|\overset{\to }{LN}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}MH\cdot LN,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}MH\cdot LN \\ \sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}MH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ 2\sqrt{2} & =MH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ MH & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ MH & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the length of the altitude $VH$ of the $△\,TUV$, if $T(3,2,3)$, $U(0,1,0)$, $V(2,1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that the length of the altitude $VH$ can be related to the area of $△\,TUV$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}VH\cdot TU
$$

So, to find $VH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{TU}$ and $\overset{\to }{TV}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{TU} & =\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{t} \\  & =\mathbf{j}-(3\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-3,-1,-3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{TV} & =\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{t} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-1,-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{TU}\times \overset{\to }{TV} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -3 & -1 & -3 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -3 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -3 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot (-3))\mathbf{i}-((-3)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot (-3))\mathbf{j}+((-3)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot (-1))\mathbf{k} \\  & =-2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-2,0,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{TU}$ and $\overset{\to }{TV}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{TU}\times \overset{\to }{TV}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,TUV$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2}=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $TU$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}TU & =|\overset{\to }{TU}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}VH\cdot TU,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}VH\cdot TU \\ \sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}VH\cdot \sqrt{19} \\ 2\sqrt{2} & =VH\cdot \sqrt{19} \\ VH & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{19}} \\ VH & =\frac{2\sqrt{38}}{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the length of the altitude $ZH$ of the $△\,WYZ$, if $W(2,3,2)$, $Y(1,2,1)$, $Z(1,-1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that the length of the altitude $ZH$ can be related to the area of $△\,WYZ$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot WY
$$

So, to find $ZH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{WY}$ and $\overset{\to }{WZ}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{WY} & =\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{w} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-1,-1,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{WZ} & =\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{w} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-1,-4,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{WY}\times \overset{\to }{WZ} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -4 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -4 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)\cdot (-1)-(-4)\cdot (-1))\mathbf{i}-((-1)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot (-1))\mathbf{j}+((-1)\cdot (-4)-(-1)\cdot (-1))\mathbf{k} \\  & =-3\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-3,0,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{WY}$ and $\overset{\to }{WZ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{WY}\times \overset{\to }{WZ}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,WYZ$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $WY$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}WY & =|\overset{\to }{WY}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot WY,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot WY \\ \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}ZH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ 3\sqrt{2} & =ZH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ ZH & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ ZH & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the length of the altitude $GH$ of the $△\,GSM$, if $S(1,-1,2)$, $G(-2,0,2)$, $M(1,1,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that the length of the altitude $GH$ can be related to the area of $△\,GSM$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}GH\cdot SM
$$

So, to find $GH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{SG}$ and $\overset{\to }{SM}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{SG} & =\mathbf{g}-\mathbf{s} \\  & =(-2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨-3,1,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{SM} & =\mathbf{m}-\mathbf{s} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})-(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =2\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,2,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{SG}\times \overset{\to }{SM} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(1\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 0)\mathbf{i}-((-3)\cdot (-2)-0\cdot 0)\mathbf{j}+((-3)\cdot 2-0\cdot 1)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-2\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j}-6\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-2,-6,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{SG}$ and $\overset{\to }{SM}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{SG}\times \overset{\to }{SM}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-6)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{76} \\  & =2\sqrt{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,GSM$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{2\sqrt{19}}{2}=\sqrt{19}.
$$

Let's also compute $SM$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}SM & =|\overset{\to }{SM}| \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}GH\cdot SM,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}GH\cdot SM \\ \sqrt{19} & =\frac{1}{2}GH\cdot 2\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{19} & =GH\cdot \sqrt{2} \\ GH & =\frac{\sqrt{19}}{\sqrt{2}} \\ GH & =\frac{\sqrt{38}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the length of the altitude $DH$ of the $△\,DMA$, if $D(-1,2,1)$, $M(-1,0,-1)$, $A(1,-2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that the length of the altitude $DH$ can be related to the area of $△\,DMA$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot MA
$$

So, to find $DH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{MD}$ and $\overset{\to }{MA}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{MD} & =\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{m} \\  & =(-\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{k}) \\  & =2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,2,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{MA} & =\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{m} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{k}) \\  & =2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{MD}\times \overset{\to }{MA} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot 2)\mathbf{i}-(0\cdot 2-2\cdot 2)\mathbf{j}+(0\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 2)\mathbf{k} \\  & =8\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}-4\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨8,4,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{MD}$ and $\overset{\to }{MA}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{MD}\times \overset{\to }{MA}| \\  & =\sqrt{{8}^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{96} \\  & =4\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,DMA$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{4\sqrt{6}}{2}=2\sqrt{6}.
$$

Let's also compute $MA$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}MA & =|\overset{\to }{MA}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot MA,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot MA \\ 2\sqrt{6} & =\frac{1}{2}DH\cdot 2\sqrt{3} \\ 2\sqrt{6} & =DH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ DH & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ DH & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$, can be found by computing $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\text{ }i+2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x+3y-2xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(1-2y)\text{ }i+(3-2x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(\frac{3}{2},1) & =(1-2(1))\text{ }i+(3-2\left(\frac{3}{2}\right))\text{ }j \\  & =-i\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(\frac{3}{2},1)}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(\frac{3}{2},1)‖} & =\frac{-\mathbf{i}}{1}=-\mathbf{i}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}+x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0)$, can be found by computing $∇f(0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,0) & =({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }j \\  & =2i+2j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(0,0)}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(0,0)‖} & =\frac{2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =2(2)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =4\,i \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨4,0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-2)0-(y-0)4 & =0 \\ -4y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $2x+y-1=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y-1 & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\ -1 & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}-2x-y)\,j \\  & =(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-2)\,i+(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-1)\,j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}-{0}^{2}}}-2)\,i+(-\frac{0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}-{0}^{2}}}-1)\,j \\  & =-i-j \\  & =⟨-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-1,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-1} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ 1-x & =-y \\ x-y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve ${y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}=4xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,-3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =4xy \\ {y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,j \\  & =(6x-4y)\,i+(2y-4x)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,-3) & =(6(-1)-4(-3))\,i+(2(-3)-4(-1))\,j \\  & =6\,i-2\,j \\  & =⟨6,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,-3)=⟨6,-2⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{6} & =\frac{y-(-3)}{-2} \\ (-2)(x+1) & =6(y+3) \\ -2x-2 & =6y+18 \\ 6y+2x+20 & =0 \\ 3y+x+10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{4}{5}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $3{x}^{2}-xz=6-3xyz$ at the point $(1,0,-3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-xz & =6-3xyz \\ 3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)k \\  & =(6x-z+3yz)\text{ }i+3xz\text{ }j+(-x+3xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,-3) & =(6(1)-(-3)+3(0)(-3))\text{ }i+3(1)(-3)\text{ }j+(-1+3(1)(0))\text{ }k \\  & =9\,i-9\,j-k \\  & =⟨9,-9,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y-0}{-9}=\frac{z-(-3)}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y}{-9}=\frac{z+3}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given $h(x,y,z)=xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)$, find $∇h(x,y,z).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)) \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}⁡(z) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)) \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(z) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)) \\  & =xy\cdot \frac{1}{z} \\  & =\frac{xy}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+{h}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+{h}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{k} \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}(z)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\operatorname{ln}(z)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+\frac{xy}{z}\text{ }\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $∇g(x,y,z)$ given that  $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+yz{e}^{xyz} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}+xz{e}^{xyz} \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+xy{e}^{xyz}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,  the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+yz{e}^{xyz})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(2{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}+xz{e}^{xyz})\text{ }\mathbf{j}+(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+xy{e}^{xyz})\text{ }\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=(2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\frac{1}{xy},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}h(x,y)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=h\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)+f(x,y)\mathrm{∇}h(x,y) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}((2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j})+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(\frac{2xy+{y}^{2}}{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{j})+(-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(\frac{2x+y}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{x+2y}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j})+(-\frac{x+y}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{x+y}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(-\frac{x+y}{x}+\frac{2x+y}{x})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(-\frac{x+y}{y}+\frac{x+2y}{y})\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\  & =\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Suppose $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{p}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{3}$ and the angle between vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ is $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Find the scalar projection of $\mathbf{p}$ onto $\mathbf{q}.$

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xy$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as 

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xy)\,j \\  & =(2x{y}^{2}+y)\,i+(2y{x}^{2}+x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,2) & =(2(1)(2)^{2}+(2))\,i+(2(2)(1)^{2}+(1))\,j \\  & =10\,i+5\,j \\  & =⟨10,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨10,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2xy+9.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2xy+9 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,2)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf{t}(-1,2)={f}_{y}(-1,2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(-1,2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf{t}(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy-9)\,j \\  & =(2y-2x)\,i-(2x-2y)\,j \\ t(-1,2) & =(2(2)-2(-1))\,i-(2(-1)-2(2))\,j \\  & =6\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $6\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+6\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$

question.:question/problem:
At which points on the curve ${y}^{2}+2xy={x}^{2}+8$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{j}?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy & ={x}^{2}+8 \\ {y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=8.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf{t}(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf{t}(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{t}(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})\mathbf{i}-\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2})\mathbf{j} \\  & =2(y+x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2(y-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $\mathbf{j}$, we must have $\mathbf{t}\cdot \mathbf{j}=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{t}(x,y)\cdot \mathbf{j} & =0 \\ (2(y+x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2(y-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot \mathbf{j} & =0 \\ -2(y-x) & =0 \\ y & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2xy-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ (x)^{2}+2x(x)-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =8 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=2$, we get $y=2$ and the corresponding point is $(2,2).$

- If $x=-2$, we get $y=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,-2).$

question.:question/problem:
At which points on the curve ${x}^{2}+2xy=-5y+4$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{j}?$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2xy & =-5y+4 \\ {x}^{2}+2xy+5y & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy+5y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf{t}(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf{t}(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{t}(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+5y)\mathbf{i}-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+5y)\mathbf{j} \\  & =(2x+5)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-(2x+2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $\mathbf{j}$, we must have $\mathbf{t}\cdot \mathbf{j}=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{t}(x,y)\cdot \mathbf{j} & =0 \\ ((2x+5)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-(2x+2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot \mathbf{j} & =0 \\ -(2x+2y) & =0 \\ x & =-y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-y$ into the equation of our curve gives:    

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2xy+5y & =4 \\ (-y)^{2}+2(-y)y+5y & =4 \\ {y}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+5y & =4 \\ -{y}^{2}+5y-4 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-5y+4 & =0 \\ (y-1)(y-4) & =0 \\ y & =1\,\text{or}\,y=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $y=1$, we get $x=-1$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,1).$

- If $y=4$, we get $x=-4$ and the corresponding point is $(-4,4).$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4xy=1-3x.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4xy & =1-3x \\ 2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4xy+3x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4xy+3x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf{t}(1,1)={f}_{y}(1,1)\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(1,1)\mathbf{j}
$$

 

So, we calculate $\mathbf{t}(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4xy+3x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-4xy+3x)j \\  & =(4y{x}^{3}-4x)i-(6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4y+3)j \\ t(1,1) & =(4(1)(1)^{3}-4(1))i-(6(1)^{2}(1)^{2}-4(1)+3)j \\  & =-5\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-5\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate  $$
\displaystyle \int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\displaystyle \int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,2)}\operatorname{ln}(4-x-y).$

Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x-y).

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous except when $4-x-y$  is negative or zero. However, at the point $(1,2)$,  the expression  $4-x-y$ is positive, so we can calculate the limit by substituting  $(1,2)$ into the function: 

$$

question.:question/problem: Find  $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,2)}\frac{x{z}^{2}-y{z}^{2}}{yz-xz}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,2)}\frac{x{z}^{2}-y{z}^{2}}{yz-xz}=\frac{1\cdot {2}^{2}-1\cdot {2}^{2}}{1\cdot 2-1\cdot 2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,2)}\frac{x{z}^{2}-y{z}^{2}}{yz-xz} & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,2)}\frac{(x-y){z}^{2}}{(y-x)z} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,2)}-\frac{(x-y){z}^{2}}{(x-y)z} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,2)}(-z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,2)}(-z) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy+{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}=\frac{(-1)^{2}+2\cdot (-1)\cdot 1+{1}^{2}}{{1}^{2}-(-1)^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy+{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}} & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}\frac{(x+y)^{2}}{(y-x)(y+x)} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}\frac{(x+y)(x+y)}{(y-x)(x+y)} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+y}{y-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+y}{y-x} & =\frac{(-1)+1}{1-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{0}{2} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $0.$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2}}{x-y-2}=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2}}{x-y-2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{1+2}}{3-1-2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2}}{x-y-2} & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{2}-(\sqrt{y+2})^{2}}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{x-y-2}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2}} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{1+2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{x}-y}=\frac{{1}^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{x}-y} & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}\frac{({y}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{x}+y)}{(\sqrt{x}-y)(\sqrt{x}+y)} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}\frac{({y}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{x}+y)}{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}\frac{-(x-{y}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+y)}{x-{y}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}-(\sqrt{x}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}-(\sqrt{x}+y) & =-(\sqrt{1}+1) \\  & =-(1+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$
The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
The limit exists and is equal to $2$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}
$$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2\cdot {0}^{2}-0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$” is true. Taking $\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)\,\hspace{0.222em}\hspace{0.222em}y=x}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x(2x-1)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{2x-1} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 0}{2\cdot 0-1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$” is also true. Taking $\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)\,\hspace{0.222em}\hspace{0.222em}y={x}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit exists and is equal to $2$” is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\text{DNE}
$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot 0\cdot {0}^{3}}{{0}^{6}+8\cdot {0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)\,\hspace{0.222em}\hspace{0.222em}y=x}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{6}+8{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{2}({x}^{4}+8)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}+8} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)\,\hspace{0.222em}\hspace{0.222em}y={x}^{3}}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{6}}{{x}^{6}+8{x}^{6}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2{x}^{6}}{9{x}^{6}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

question.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=16$ and ${b}^{2}=9.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=16,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be  $a=\sqrt{16}=4.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=9,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{9}=3.$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=4,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=3.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot 4=8,$ and the minor axis has length $2b=2\cdot 3=6.$

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$

$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=16$ and ${b}^{2}=25.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=16,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{16}=4.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=25,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{25}=5.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=5,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=4.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 5=10,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 4=8.$
