question.:question/problem: For the function $g(x,y,z)=\sqrt{x}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂g}{∂z}$ at the point $(3,\frac{1}{2},1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the constant multiple and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(y{z}^{2})}^{2}}}\right)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}{z}^{4}}}\right)\cdot y\cdot 2z \\  & =-\frac{2yz\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}{z}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,\frac{1}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}{|}_{(3,\,1/2,\,1)} & =-\frac{2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(1)\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{1-{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}(1)^{4}}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\cdot \frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\cdot \frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y) & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))}{x+y}\cdot (x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))}{x+y}\cdot (x\cdot 0+1) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{3}y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{3}y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{x}^{3}y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{x}^{3}y) & =\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot (1+y\cdot 3{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1+3{x}^{2}y}{x+{x}^{3}y}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the function $$
\displaystyle f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y},
$$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(\pi ,-\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi ,-\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,-\pi )} & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(-1)(-1)}{(-1-0)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{e}^{y-x}},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient and chain rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{e}^{y-x}}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y-x}-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y-x})}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot {e}^{y-x}-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y-x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y-x)}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x{e}^{y-x}-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y-x}\cdot (-1)}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{y-x}}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x+{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{e}^{y-x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,-1)} & =\frac{2(1)+{1}^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{{e}^{-1-1}} \\  & =\frac{2+1-1}{{e}^{-2}} \\  & =2{e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $$
\displaystyle f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y}.
$$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{h(x,y)}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ for $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+{y}^{5}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+{y}^{5}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) & =(\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))+{y}^{5}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =((1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x))+{y}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =(1+{y}^{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2}),$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{4},1)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})) & =(2x)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =2x\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =2x\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot (1) \\  & =2x\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi /4,1)} & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {1}^{2})+{\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {1}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot 1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}\cdot (\sqrt{2})^{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}+4\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(0,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{y})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x(\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y}+{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x((2y)\cdot {e}^{y}+{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{y}) \\  & =(2y+{y}^{2}){e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(0,2)} & =(2\cdot 2+{2}^{2}){e}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =8{e}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =8{e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ given that $g(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the constant multiple and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(xy)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(xy)^{2}}}\cdot (x) \\  & =\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot 1 \\  & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+y{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(-1,1)} & =3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+(1){e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =3+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-{e}^{2y}{z}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{3}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}{z}^{4}) \\  & =4{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-{z}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-{z}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}) & =4{x}^{3}\cdot 2y-{z}^{4}\cdot {e}^{2y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2y) \\  & =4{x}^{3}\cdot 2y-{z}^{4}\cdot {e}^{2y}\cdot 2 \\  & =8{x}^{3}y-2{z}^{4}{e}^{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}_{y}(x,y,z)=8{x}^{3}y-2{z}^{4}{e}^{2y}.
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{z}^{3}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{3}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{3})-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)) \\  & ={z}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & ={z}^{3}\cdot 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\cdot 2x \\  & ={z}^{3}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1,2)} & ={2}^{3}-2(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) \\  & =8-2(1)(-1) \\  & =8+2 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y)) \\  & =\frac{2}{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{2}{x+2y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y).$

The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}(xz+2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{cos}(xz+2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+x\operatorname{cos}(xz+2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $h(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right),$ find $∇h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2}}\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2}}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y,z)={x}^{y}+{y}^{z},$ find $∇f(x,y,z).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & =y{x}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+z{y}^{z-1} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{y}+{y}^{z}) \\  & ={y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}x+z{y}^{z-1})\mathbf{j}+{y}^{z}\operatorname{ln}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $∇h(x,y,z)$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,\pi )$ if $h(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =x{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)+{e}^{xy}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))(z) \\  & ={e}^{xy}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,j+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\,i+{e}^{xy}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j-y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\,k \\  & ={e}^{xy}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\,i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)\,k) \\ ∇h(\frac{1}{2},1,\pi ) & ={e}^{(1/2)(1)}(1\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\pi )\,i+(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(1\pi ))\,j-1\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\pi )\,k) \\  & =\sqrt{e}(-i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-0\,k) \\  & =-\sqrt{e}(i+\frac{1}{2}\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the gradient of the product $g(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x,y) & ={e}^{x-y},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}g(x,y)={e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & ={x}^{2}-3xy,\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}h(x,y)=(2x-3y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-3x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $g(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[gh]=h∇g+g∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}[g(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)\mathrm{∇}g(x,y)+g(x,y)\mathrm{∇}h(x,y) \\  & =({x}^{2}-3xy)({e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})+{e}^{x-y}((2x-3y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-3x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(({x}^{2}-3xy){e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-({x}^{2}-3xy){e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})+((2x-3y){e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-3x{e}^{x-y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & ={e}^{x-y}({x}^{2}-3xy+2x-3y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{e}^{x-y}({x}^{2}-3xy+3x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & ={e}^{x-y}(({x}^{2}-3xy+2x-3y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-({x}^{2}-3xy+3x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{x-y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-2,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(-2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-2,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{x+y}{x-y}\right)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{x+y}{x-y}\right)\,j \\  & =\frac{1(x-y)-(x+y)(1)}{(x-y)^{2}}\,i+\frac{1(x-y)-(x+y)(-1)}{(x-y)^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{2y}{(x-y)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2x}{(x-y)^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(-2,-1) & =-\frac{2(-1)}{(-2-(-1))^{2}}\,i+\frac{2(-2)}{(-2-(-1))^{2}}\,j \\  & =2\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(-2,-1)}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(-2,-1)‖} & =\frac{2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}(2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(\mathbf{i}-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(2,-2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{y}{x}\right))j \\  & =\frac{\left(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}{1+{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2}}\,i+\frac{\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)}{1+{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =-\frac{(-2)}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{8}\,i+\frac{2}{8}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(2,-2)}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(2,-2)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})}{‖\frac{1}{4}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(3{x}^{2}yz-y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{3}z-x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+({x}^{3}y-2xyz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,1) & =(3(1)^{2}(-2)(1)-(-2)(1)^{2})\,i+((1)^{3}(1)-(1)(1)^{2})\,j+((1)^{3}(-2)-2(1)(-2)(1))\,k \\  & =-4\,i+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1).$

question.:question/problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}={x}^{2}-6x+12$ at the point $(2,0,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-6x \\ 4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x & =12\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=12.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)k \\  & =(6-2x)\,i-8y\,j+8z\,k \\ ∇f(2,0,1) & =(6-2(2))\,i-8(0)\text{ }j+8(1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+8\,k \\  & =⟨2,0,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(2,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r} & =⟨2,0,1⟩+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{∇}f(2,0,1)=⟨2,0,1⟩+t\hspace{0.167em}⟨2,0,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz=-3$ at the point $(2,-1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,-1,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)k \\  & =({e}^{x+y+z}-2yz)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y+z}-2xz)\text{ }j+({e}^{x+y+z}-2xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,-1,-1) & =({e}^{2-1-1}-2(-1)(-1))\text{ }i+({e}^{2-1-1}-2(2)(-1))\text{ }j+({e}^{2-1-1}-2(2)(-1))\text{ }k \\  & =({e}^{0}-2)\text{ }i+({e}^{0}+4)\text{ }j+({e}^{0}+4)\text{ }k \\  & =-i+5\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨-1,5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-1)}=\frac{y-(-1)}{5}=\frac{z-(-1)}{5} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-1)}=\frac{y+1}{5}=\frac{z+1}{5} \\ 2-x=\frac{y+1}{5}=\frac{z+1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}3u-5v \\ \operatorname{ln}(u+v)\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=3u-5v$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(u+v).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-5 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u+v} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u+v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & -5 \\ \frac{1}{u+v} & \frac{1}{u+v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot \left(\frac{1}{u+v}\right)-(-5)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{u+v}\right) \\  & =\frac{8}{u+v}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}(\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix})=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{u+v} \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x={e}^{u+v}$ and $y={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ \,\text{ }2u\, & \,\text{ }2v\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot 2v-{e}^{u+v}\cdot 2u \\  & =2{e}^{u+v}(v-u).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}(u+v) \\ \operatorname{sin}(u-v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{bmatrix}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & -\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v))-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is 

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=2.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}uv \\ u+v\end{bmatrix}.

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}v & u \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v\cdot 1-1\cdot u \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}v-u & >0 \\ v & >u\end{aligned}

Notice that the equation

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}(u-v) \\ v-{u}^{2}\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot \underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{u-v} & -\frac{1}{u-v} \\ -2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{u-v}\cdot 1-(-2u)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{u-v}\right) \\  & =\frac{1-2u}{u-v} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(2,1)} & ={\left(\frac{1-2u}{u-v}\right)\,|}_{u=2\,v=1} \\  & =\frac{1-2(2)}{2-1} \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-3|\cdot \delta A \\  & =3\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-3,3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u+{v}^{2} \\ \operatorname{sin}(u+v)\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot \underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot 2v \\  & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\,{|}_{u=-3\,v=3} \\  & =(1-2(3))\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\cdot \delta A \\  & =5\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given  $g(x,y,z)={e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)$, find $∇g(x,y,z).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}-1) \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1)) \\  & =2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{k} \\  & =2z{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+2y{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{cos}({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+2x{e}^{2xz}\operatorname{sin}({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }\mathbf{k} \\  & =2{e}^{2xz}\text{ }(z\operatorname{sin}({y}^{2}-1)\mathbf{i}+y\operatorname{cos}({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+x\operatorname{sin}({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }\mathbf{k})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given $h(x,y,z)=xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$, find  $∇h(x,y,z).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{yz}{xyz} \\  & =yz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{xz}{xyz} \\  & =xz(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+xyz\frac{xy}{xyz} \\  & =xy(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+{h}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+{h}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }\mathbf{k} \\  & =yz(\operatorname{ln}(xyz)+1)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+xz(\operatorname{ln}(xyz)+1)\text{ }\mathbf{j}+xy(\operatorname{ln}(xyz)+1)\text{ }\mathbf{k} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}(xyz)+1)(yz\text{ }\mathbf{i}+xz\text{ }\mathbf{j}+xy\text{ }\mathbf{k}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}=1$ at the point $(2,1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$     

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1,2).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1,2):$    

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2x}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,2) & =\frac{2\cdot 2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }k \\  & =4\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =⟨4,\,\frac{1}{2},\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-1}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{z-2}{-2} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=2y-2=\frac{2-z}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}v\operatorname{tan}\left(\frac{u}{2}\right) \\ \operatorname{sin}v\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $$
\displaystyle x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)
$$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(u/2)} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right) \\ \,0\, & \,\text{ }\text{ }\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given  $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y$, find $∇f(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\  & =(y\operatorname{cos}(xy)+2x\operatorname{ln}y)\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(x\operatorname{cos}(xy)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y})\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4)$, can be found by computing $∇f(5,4).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(5,4) & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}}j \\  & =\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{∇}f(5,4)}{‖\mathrm{∇}f(5,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}\mathbf{i}-\frac{4}{3}\mathbf{j}}{\sqrt{{\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right)}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}\mathbf{i}-\frac{4}{3}\mathbf{j}}{\frac{\sqrt{41}}{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{41}(5\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}=1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If we set $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{9}x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(3,0) & =\frac{2}{9}(3)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\,i \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,0)=⟨\frac{2}{3},0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-3)0-(y-0)\frac{2}{3} & =0 \\ -\frac{2}{3}y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)={x}^{2}+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & ={x}^{2}+y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2x)\,i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,0) & =(-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-2\cdot (-1))\,i+(-(-1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-j \\  & =⟨2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,0)=⟨2,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x+1}{2} & =-y \\ x+1 & =-2y \\ x+2y+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $∇h(x,y,z)$ at the point $(1,-1,\pi )$ if $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

 
Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\text{ }i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\text{ }j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\text{ }k \\ ∇h(1,-1,\pi ) & =(-1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\text{ }i+(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\text{ }j+(1)(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\text{ }k \\  & =(-\pi )(-1)\text{ }i+\pi (-1)\text{ }j-(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =\pi \text{ }i-\pi \text{ }j+\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y)=4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y+0-2x \\  & =2(2y-x) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4x+2y-0 \\  & =2(2x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=2(2y-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2(2x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$

Now, we solve $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=\mathbf{0}:$

$$
2(2y-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2(2x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=0\text{ }\mathbf{i}+0\text{ }\mathbf{j}
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j},$ we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2y-x &=0 \\ 2x+y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=2y.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2y)+y & =0 \\ 5y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get $x=2\cdot 0=0.$

Therefore, $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=\mathbf{0}$ at the point $(0,0).$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y,z)=\mathbf{0}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0+0-1-0-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{1}{y}+0-0-1-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y+z\operatorname{ln}⁡z-x-y-z) \\  & =0+0+\operatorname{ln}⁡z+z\cdot \frac{1}{z}-0-0-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z+1-1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{ln}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{ln}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$ 

Now, we solve $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y,z)=\mathbf{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{ln}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{ln}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} & =0\text{ }\mathbf{i}+0\text{ }\mathbf{j}+0\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, and $\mathbf{k}$, we obtain:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x &=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y &=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=1.$  Similarly, from the second and third equations, we obtain $y=1$ and $z=1.$

Hence, $\mathrm{∇}g(x,y,z)=\mathbf{0}$ at the point $(1,1,1).$

question.:question/problem:
Find the gradient of the product $g(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x,y) & ={e}^{xy},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}h(x,y)=2x\text{ }\mathbf{i}+2y\text{ }\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $g(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[gh]=h\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}[g(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)\mathrm{∇}g(x,y)+g(x,y)\mathrm{∇}h(x,y) \\  & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(y{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{j})+{e}^{xy}(2x\text{ }\mathbf{i}+2y\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})y{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})x{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{j})+(2x{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+2y{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =({x}^{2}y+{y}^{3}+2x){e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}-{v}^{2} \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T},$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -2v \\ 2u & 2v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2u\cdot 2v-(-2v)\cdot 2u \\  & =4uv+4uv \\  & =8uv.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/62/62f33dab4305a41a0bc180231fef7015361dec4aac63f14c31fd48a39b8fcd68.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{2}{y}$ traversed between the points $(2,1)$ and $(\frac{1}{3},6),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{2}{t}.
$$

 

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨\frac{2}{t},\hspace{0.222em}t⟩,\hspace{2em}1\le t\le 6
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 6$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\right)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{{t}^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4+{t}^{4}}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=4x{y}^{2},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =4\left(\frac{2}{t}\right)(t)^{2} \\  & =8t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4x{y}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{6}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{6}8t\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{1}^{6}\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+4}}{t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-2y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-2y)) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(x-2y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-2y)) \\  & =-2{sec}^{2}⁡(x-2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & ={\operatorname{sec}}^{2}(x-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2{\operatorname{sec}}^{2}(x-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =1 \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-4,1),$ $(1,1),$ and $(3,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-4,1) & =i+2\cdot 1\,j=i+2\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =i+2\cdot 1\,j=i+2\,j \\ ∇f(3,-1) & =i+2\cdot (-1)\,j=i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{b}=-3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =\mathbf{0}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{0}) \\  & =t(\mathbf{b}) \\  & =t(-3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =-3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-3t$ and $y=4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =-3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & ={e}^{-3t+4t} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z},$ traversed along the line segment from $(3,-2,3)$ to $(5,-1,7)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,-2,3)$ to $(5,-1,7).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=3\mathbf{i}-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=5\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+7\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\mathbf{a}+t\hspace{0.167em}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\  & =(3\mathbf{i}-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})+t[(5\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+7\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})] \\  & =(3\mathbf{i}-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})+t(2\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k}) \\  & =(2t+3)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(4t+3)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t+3,y=t-2,$ and $z=4t+3$ along the segment.

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+3)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{21}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\sqrt{2(2t+3)+(t-2)-(4t+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{t+1}\cdot \sqrt{21}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{21}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{t+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.222em}2\operatorname{sin}t⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.222em}2\operatorname{sin}t⟩,\hspace{2em}\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}t}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{e}^{2\operatorname{cos}t}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=-2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-8{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}({e}^{x}+y)\,dx-x\,dy,
$$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,\sqrt{3})$ to the point $B(-\sqrt{3},0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =x(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({e}^{x}+y)\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+3\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(0,-3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by

question.:question/problem:
If $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+y\,\text{d}y+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z
$$ is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ for some piecewise smooth curve $C,$ then $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x+Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y+R\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}z
$$

In our case, $P={x}^{2},Q=y,R={z}^{3}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{z}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x+y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y+{z}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\mathbf{F}={x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{z}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-x+y,$ find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-x+y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-x+y)\,j \\  & =({y}^{2}-1)\text{ }i+(2xy+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =((-1)^{2}-1)\,i+(2(1)(-1)+1)\,j \\  & =0\,i-j \\  & =⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-(-1)⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: At which point on the curve $2{x}^{2}=y+1$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2} & =y+1 \\ 2{x}^{2}-y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf{t}(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf{t}(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{t}(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{f}_{x}(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\mathbf{i}-4x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j},$ we must have $\mathbf{t}\cdot (\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{t}(x,y)\cdot \mathbf{(}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) & =0 \\ (-\mathbf{i}-4x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) & =0 \\ -1-4x & =0 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2} & =y+1 \\ 2{\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2} & =y+1 \\ \frac{1}{8} & =y+1 \\ y & =-\frac{7}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the corresponding point is $(-\frac{1}{4},-\frac{7}{8}).$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by 

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}+v \\ uv\end{bmatrix},
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}+v \\ uv\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{u}^{2} & 1 \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot u-v\cdot 1 \\  & ={u}^{3}-v.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}-v & <0 \\ v & >{u}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v={u}^{3}
$$

defines a cubic function, and the coordinates of, say, $(-1,1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

Notice that the equation

\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2} \\ v-u\end{bmatrix}.

question.:question/problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-2,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{u+v} \\ {u}^{3}+v\end{bmatrix}?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot \underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ 3{u}^{2} & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot 1-3{u}^{2}\cdot {e}^{u+v} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2}) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,2)} & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2})\,{|}_{u=-2\,v=2} \\  & ={e}^{-2+2}(1-3(-2)^{2}) \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-11|\cdot \delta A \\  & =11\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x-{y}^{2}+1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $ψ(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x-{y}^{2}+1) \\  & =-2y, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x-{y}^{2}+1) \\  & =-2x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x-{y}^{2}+1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y) & =P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-(2x-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Construct the vector field that has the stream function $ψ(x,y)=5{y}^{3}x-{x}^{3}-xy.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ if the following equations hold:

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}
$$

Computing the partial derivatives of the function $ψ(x,y),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{∂ψ}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{y}^{3}x-{x}^{3}-xy) \\  & =15x{y}^{2}-x, \\ Q & =-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x} \\  & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{y}^{3}x-{x}^{3}-xy) \\  & =-(5{y}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field with the stream function $ψ(x,y)=5{y}^{3}x-{x}^{3}-xy$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y) & =P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(15x{y}^{2}-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-(5{y}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following represents the streamlines of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=2x\mathbf{i}-2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ over the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $\mathbf{F}$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=2x\mathbf{i}-2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$

 is a vector field with simply connected domain $D,$ where $P(x,y)=2x$ and $Q(x,y)=-2y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf{F}$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2-2=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=2xy+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy.
$$

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function $ψ(x,y)=2xy$ given by the equations $ψ(x,y)=c.$

Notice that the range of $ψ(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =c \\ 2xy & =c \\ y & =\frac{c}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of hyperbolas with asymptotes $y=0$ and $x=0$ and, for $c=0,$ the lines $y=0$ and $x=0.$ Therefore, the correct graph (along with the vector field $\mathbf{F}$) is as follows:

![](images/24/24c6dadd4f980121a36929a9cdb800f7da8fac8eb84af40d595af89aa77b11ea.png)

question.:question/problem: Which of the following represents the streamlines of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ over the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $\mathbf{F}$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}
$$

 is a vector field with simply connected domain $D,$ where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\mathbf{F}$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=-2x.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=-{x}^{2}+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f(x)=-{x}^{2}$ or $g(y)={y}^{2},$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function $ψ(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$ given by the equations $ψ(x,y)=c.$

Notice that the range of $ψ(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =c \\ {y}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =c\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of hyperbolas with asymptotes $y=x$ and $x=-x$ and, for $c=0,$ the lines $y=x$ and $y=-x.$ Therefore, the correct graph (along with the vector field $\mathbf{F}$) is as follows:

![](images/9b/9b0d2f98a0b71beb773b802908f01691924492a5f3abff3db75be4a0ae458e7d.png)

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=2x{y}^{2}+xy+2x$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}+xy+2x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}+xy+2x)\,j \\  & =(2{y}^{2}+y+2)\,i+(4xy+x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(2(1)^{2}+(1)+2)\,i+(4(1)(1)+(1))\,j \\  & =5\,i+5\,j \\  & =⟨5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨5,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$
