Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=3x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/09/0950c559d5d6df93cf40afd8fdbd07f090f864fa462083bfd496246e7f2bded9.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/95/958965484cd271c5eb7ccfc8bf913386e57b9b733719885d232e562063969ca8.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=-x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-{\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =-2\cdot 4 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=-8.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(-x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+2\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-2}^{2}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=16.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot (-8)+2\cdot 16=16.
$$

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=5$ and the vertical radius has length $b=7.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{7}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{49} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}xy,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}2uv⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}auv+b{u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}2uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2v \\ 0 & 1 & 2u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2v \\ 1 & 2u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2v \\ 0 & 2u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2v,\,-2u,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨{x}^{2},\,xy,\,z⟩{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=2uv} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2},\,uv,\,2uv⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨{u}^{2},\,uv,\,2uv⟩\cdot ⟨-2v,\,-2u,\,1⟩ \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot (-2v)+uv\cdot (-2u)+2uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-2{u}^{2}v-2{u}^{2}v+2uv \\  & =2uv-4{u}^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\cdot uv+(-4)\cdot {u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2-4=-2.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3x,\hspace{0.222em}-{y}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨3uv,\hspace{0.222em}u,\hspace{0.222em}-v⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}3v,\hspace{0.222em}-3u⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-1,\,3v,\,-3u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨3x,\,-{y}^{2},\,2⟩|}_{x=3uv\,y=u\,z=-v} \\  & =⟨3(3uv),\,-{u}^{2},\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨9uv,\,-{u}^{2},\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨9uv,\,-{u}^{2},\,2⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,3v,\,-3u⟩ \\  & =9uv\cdot (-1)+(-{u}^{2})\cdot 3v+2\cdot (-3u) \\  & =-9uv-3{u}^{2}v-6u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3x,\,-{y}^{2},\,2⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-9uv-3{u}^{2}v-6u)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-9uv-3{u}^{2}v-6u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{9}{2}{u}^{2}v-{u}^{3}v-3{u}^{2}]}_{u=0}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{11}{2}v-3)\text{d}v \\  & ={[-\frac{11}{4}{v}^{2}-3v]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{11}{4}-3 \\  & =-\frac{23}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3z,\hspace{0.222em}-2x,\hspace{0.222em}-y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨-v,\hspace{0.222em}-u,\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2}⟩
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-1,\,2u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & 2u \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2u \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2u \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩|}_{x=-v\,y=-u\,z={u}^{2}} \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,-2(-v),\,-(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩ \\  & =3{u}^{2}\cdot 0+2v\cdot (-2u)+u\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv-u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4uv+u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{u}^{2}v+\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{u=0}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}(2v+\frac{1}{2})\text{d}v \\  & =-{[{v}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}v]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x=v+w,\,y=u+w,\,z=u+v.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)(0-1)+(1-0) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x=au,\,y=bv,\,z=cw.
$$

You may assume that $a$, $b$ and $c$ are fixed constants.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =a & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =b & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =c\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}a & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & b & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & c\end{vmatrix} \\  & =a(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}b & 0 \\ 0 & c\end{vmatrix} \\  & =a(bc-0) \\  & =abc.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{u}+v \\ v+w \\ vw\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u}+v,\,y(u,v,w)=v+w,\,z(u,v,w)=vw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}(v-w).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ {e}^{u}(v-w) & =0 \\ v-w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v-w=0$ defines the plane $v=w.$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${\mathbf{T}}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{\mathbf{T}}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{z}{y} \\ y \\ xz\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}.$

*Hint: You can assume that $y,z\ne 0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{y},\,v(x,y,z)=y,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z(0-\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =-\frac{z}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z}{y} & =-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=x,\,v=2y,\,w=3z.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=(x-y)^{2}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)^{2}) \\  & =2(x-y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)^{2}) \\  & =-2(x-y)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =2(x-y)\,i-2(x-y)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(2,1),$ $(1,2),$ and $(1,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,1) & =2\cdot (2-1)\,i-2\cdot (2-1)\,j=2\,i-2\,j \\ ∇f(1,2) & =2\cdot (1-2)\,i-2\cdot (1-2)\,j=-2\,i+2\,j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =2\cdot (1-(-1))\,i-2\cdot (1-(-1))\,j=4\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/b3/b3c874f3c4564795a2ddcfb4c2896c1bc0ef1b4b7b3d8e8318f42d15643942d7.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $UVWU,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction?
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup \{-{C}_{2}\}\cup \{-{C}_{3}\},
$$

where $-{C}_{2}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/4d/4d4c2c86ed8506ff034141ac20a5a56587a80370384ceeaf08c66f2ce3e8a315.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(4,-2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(4,-2)$ to the point $B(4,0).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{8}{3},
$$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{y}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the section of the curve $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t)=t\,i-\sqrt{t}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 4.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-\sqrt{t}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =t\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{t})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j) \\  & =t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2})\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{0}^{4}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{4}^{3/2}}{3}-0)+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)={e}^{y+z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{x+z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{e}^{x+y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ and let $C$ be a path in ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}.$ Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y+R(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{e}^{y+z}\,\text{d}x+{e}^{x+z}\,\text{d}y+{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=-y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [0,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,z=2.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =-y\,i+x\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,k \\  & =-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+0\,k) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+0\cdot 0 \\  & =2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi (2-0) \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$

where $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=⟨x+y,\hspace{0.222em}-x+y,\hspace{0.222em}-2z⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(x-1) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{x+y}_{P},\,\underbrace{-x+y}_{Q},\,\underbrace{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot 2(x-1)-(-x+y)\cdot 2(y+1)-2((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2((x+y)(1-x)+(x-y)(y+1)-(x-1)^{2}-(y+1)^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4(-{r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{r}^{3}+2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-{r}^{3}\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi {r}^{3}-2\pi r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8\pi {[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\pi (-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [0,1).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=2z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{2}-{t}^{3},\,z={t}^{2}-t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2z\,i+3y\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,j+(2t-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}-2t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,j+(2t-1)\,k) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (2t-3{t}^{2})+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =(-3{t}^{3}+5{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =2t-9{t}^{2}+13{t}^{3}-6{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-9{t}^{2}+13{t}^{3}-6{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}+\frac{13}{4}{t}^{4}-\frac{6}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-3+\frac{13}{4}-\frac{6}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=(2{t}^{3}-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(-t-{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2{t}^{3}-2t,\,y=t+{t}^{2},\,z=-t-{t}^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =(t+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+{t}^{2})\,j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t-{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =(6{t}^{2}-2)\,i+(1+2t)\,j+(-1-2t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,k)\cdot ((6{t}^{2}-2)\,i+(1+2t)\,j+(-1-2t)\,k) \\  & =(t+{t}^{2})\cdot (6{t}^{2}-2)+0\cdot (1+2t)+(2{t}^{3}-2t)\cdot (-1-2t) \\  & =2{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}+{t}^{4}+\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(-\frac{2}{5}+1-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the intersection of the half-cone $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $y=1+x,$ $x=0,$ and $y=0.$ Given that the curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-{z}^{3},\hspace{0.222em}0⟩,$ the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$ can be written as 

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨0\,-{z}^{3},\,0⟩{|}_{z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\  & =⟨0,\,-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2},\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{0}_{P},\,\underbrace{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}}_{Q},\,\underbrace{0}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/ab/ab155520a21d38483e8b0978a04972e1a96c8d273d23ca7aa36bb1846189b4c8.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1+x}\,y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}(2\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{sin}(2\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [0,1)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =z\,j-y\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t))\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k) \\  & =0\cdot (2t-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\cdot (-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t))+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t))\cdot 2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(2\pi t)-2\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(2\pi t) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi )\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2\pi [t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2\pi (1-0) \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=4 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & ⇒ & v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 4x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =4x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot 4\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}-4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+4(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1-0\cdot 0)+4(0-1) \\  & =2\pi -4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$ find the lengths of its major and minor axes.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=13$ and ${b}^{2}=36.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=13,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{13}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=36,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{36}=6.$

Thus, the semi-major axis has length $b=6,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=\sqrt{13}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 6=12,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{13}=2\sqrt{13}.$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}xz,\hspace{0.222em}yz⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}v⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}auv+b{u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2u,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2u & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2u \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\,-1,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,xz,\,yz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y={u}^{2}\,z=v} \\  & =⟨v,\,uv,\,{u}^{2}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨v,\,uv,\,{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨2u,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =v\cdot 2u+uv\cdot (-1)+{u}^{2}v\cdot 0 \\  & =2uv-uv+0 \\  & =uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1\cdot uv+0\cdot {u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=1+0=1.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}y,\hspace{0.222em}-z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u+v,\hspace{0.222em}v-u,\hspace{0.222em}uv⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 0,\,0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}=⟨-u-v,\hspace{0.222em}v-u,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-u-v,\,v-u,\,2⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨x,\,y,\,-z⟩|}_{x=u+v\,y=v-u\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,-uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,-uv⟩\cdot ⟨-u-v,\,v-u,\,2⟩ \\  & =(u+v)\cdot (-u-v)+(v-u)\cdot (v-u)+(-uv)\cdot 2 \\  & =-{u}^{2}-2uv-{v}^{2}+{v}^{2}-2uv+{u}^{2}-2uv \\  & =-6uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x,\,y,\,-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-6uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{0}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{1}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{-2}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-6\cdot [\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =-6\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find  $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xz+xy+yz}{x+z}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{x\to (1,1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xz+xy+yz}{x+z}=\frac{{1}^{2}+1\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+1\cdot (-1)}{1+(-1)}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xz+xy+yz}{x+z} & =\lim_{x\to (1,1,-1)}\frac{x(x+z)+y(x+z)}{x+z} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (1,1,-1)}\frac{(x+y)(x+z)}{x+z} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (1,1,-1)}(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,1,-1)}x+y & =1+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $2.$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,-3,2)}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{zx+zy}{\sqrt{x+y+4}-2}=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,\frac{zx+zy}{\sqrt{x+y+4}-2}=\frac{2\cdot 3+2\cdot (-3)}{\sqrt{3+(-3)+4}-2}=\frac{6-6}{\sqrt{4}-2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,\frac{zx+zy}{\sqrt{x+y+4}-2} & =\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,\frac{(zx+zy)(\sqrt{x+y+4}+2)}{(\sqrt{x+y+4}-2)(\sqrt{x+y+4}+2)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,\frac{(zx+zy)(\sqrt{x+y+4}+2)}{(\sqrt{x+y+4})^{2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,\frac{(zx+zy)(\sqrt{x+y+4}+2)}{x+y+4-4} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,\frac{z(x+y)(\sqrt{x+y+4}+2)}{x+y} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,z(\sqrt{x+y+4}+2)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (3,-3,2)}\,z(\sqrt{x+y+4}+2) & =2(\sqrt{3-3+4}+2) \\  & =2(\sqrt{4}+2) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $8.$

question.:question/problem: Find $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1)}\frac{x(xy-1)}{y}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{x(xy-1)}{y}.
$$

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(2,1)$ does not cause the denominator to vanish, so we can calculate the limit by substituting $(2,1)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{x(xy-1)}{y} & =\frac{2(2\cdot 1-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{2(1)}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-2,-2)}\sqrt{xy}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=\sqrt{xy}.
$$

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous except when the expression under the radical   is negative. However, for the point $(-2,-2)$ the product $x\cdot y$ is not negative, so we can calculate the limit by substituting  $(-2,-2)$ into the function: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (-2,-2)}\sqrt{xy}=\sqrt{(-2)\cdot (-2)}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Determine $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & =\frac{({0}^{2})(0)}{{0}^{4}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0+0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=0}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}(0)}{{x}^{4}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}({x}^{2})}{{x}^{4}+({x}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}+{x}^{4}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{{x}^{4}}}{2\cancel{{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

question.:question/problem: Determine $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x+y}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x+y} & =\frac{{1}^{3}+2(1)^{2}(-1)+1(-1)^{2}}{1+(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1-2+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x+y} & =\lim_{x\to (1,-1)}\frac{x({x}^{2}+2xy+{y}^{2})}{x+y} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (1,-1)}\frac{x(x+y)(x+y)}{x+y} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (1,-1)}\frac{x(x+y)\cancel{(x+y)}}{\cancel{x+y}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (1,-1)}x(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (1,-1)}x(x+y) & =1(1-1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $0.$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (4,-4,-2)}\frac{\sqrt[3]{x-y}}{z}=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function 

$$
f(x,y,z)=\frac{\sqrt[3]{x-y}}{z}
$$

is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(4,-4,-2)$ does not cause the  denominator to vanish, so we can calculate the limit by substituting  $(4,-4,-2)$ into the function: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (4,-4,-2)}\frac{\sqrt[3]{x-y}}{z} & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{4-(-4)}}{(-2)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{8}}{-2} \\  & =\frac{2}{-2} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{\sqrt{6+y}-x}{6+y-{x}^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{6+3}-3}{6+3-{3}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{\sqrt{6+y}-x}{6+y-{x}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{(\sqrt{6+y}-x)(\sqrt{6+y}+x)}{(6+y-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{6+y}+x)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{(\sqrt{6+y})^{2}-{x}^{2}}{(6+y-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{6+y}+x)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{6+y-{x}^{2}}{(6+y-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{6+y}+x)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6+y}+x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (3,3)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6+y}+x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6+3}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{6}.$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}^{2}⁡(3x-{y}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(0,\sqrt{\pi }).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}^{2}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(3x-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot (3x\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot (3x\cdot 0-2y) \\  & =4y\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,\sqrt{\pi }):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(0,\sqrt{\pi })} & =4(\sqrt{\pi })\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(0)-{(\sqrt{\pi })}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(0)-{(\sqrt{\pi })}^{2}) \\  & =4\sqrt{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{3xy-1}{2x-3y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(0,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{3xy-1}{2x-3y}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(3xy-1)\cdot (2x-3y)-(3xy-1)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-3y)}{(2x-3y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3x\cdot (2x-3y)-(3xy-1)\cdot (-3)}{(2x-3y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}-9xy+9xy-3}{(2x-3y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}-3}{(2x-3y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(0,-1)} & =\frac{6(0)^{2}-3}{(2(0)-3(-1))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{xy}}{xy}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y){e}^{xy}}{{x}^{2}y}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{{e}^{xy}}{xy}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})\cdot xy-{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)}{(xy)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)\cdot xy-{e}^{xy}\cdot y}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot xy-y{e}^{xy}}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{xy}(xy-1)}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(xy-1){e}^{xy}}{{x}^{2}y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=xy-1.
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(4,1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}) \\  & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(4y-x{z}^{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(4y-x{z}^{4}) & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}(4y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{4})) \\  & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot (0-{z}^{4}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)) \\  & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot (-{z}^{4})\cdot 1 \\  & =-{z}^{4}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(4,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}{|}_{(4,1,1)} & =-(1)^{4}{e}^{4(1)-4(1)^{4}} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=(2y+1)^{2x+1},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(2,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((2y+1)^{2x+1}) \\  & =(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}((2y+1))\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\cdot (2\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)) \\  & =(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\cdot (2\cdot 1+0) \\  & =2(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,0)} & =2\cdot (2\cdot 2+1)\cdot (2\cdot 0+1)^{2\cdot 2} \\  & =2\cdot 5\cdot {1}^{4} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule and the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}) & ={y}^{2}(\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}})) \\  & ={y}^{2}((2x)\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})) \\  & ={y}^{2}(2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot (2x)) \\  & ={y}^{2}(2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}+2{x}^{3}{e}^{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =2{y}^{2}(x+{x}^{3}){e}^{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ for $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}^{2}⁡(3x-{y}^{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}^{2}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2}))\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(3x-{y}^{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2}))\cdot 3 \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4})) \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4}))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product and the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4})) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4})) \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot (1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4})+y\cdot \frac{1}{{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{4})) \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4})+\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}\cdot (4{y}^{3}))) \\  & ={x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{4})+4)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)-xy.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)-xy) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂x}(yx)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂x}(yx) & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(yx) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\cdot 1-y\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{x}-y\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{y}},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(3,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{y}}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{y}-({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{y})}{{(\sqrt{y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2y\cdot \sqrt{y}-({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}})}{y} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{4{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}}\right)}{y} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}}{2y\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(3,1)} & =\frac{{3}^{2}+3(1)^{2}}{2(1)\sqrt{1}} \\  & =\frac{9+3}{2} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{6x+11y}{\sqrt{y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{h(x,y)}{2y\sqrt{y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{6x+11y}{\sqrt{y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(6x+11y)\cdot \sqrt{y}-(6x+11y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{y})}{{(\sqrt{y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(11\cdot \sqrt{y}-(6x+11y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}})}{y} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{22y-(6x+11y)}{2\sqrt{y}}\right)}{y} \\  & =\frac{11y-6x}{2y\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=11y-6x.
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}))) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(x{y}^{2})}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the constant multiple rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,3)} & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{1+{1}^{2}\cdot {3}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{9}{1+81} \\  & =\frac{9}{82}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $∇f(x,y)$ at $(e,1)$ if $f(x,y)={x}^{y}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}) \\  & =y{x}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y}) \\  & ={x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\text{ }i+{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\text{ }j, \\ ∇f(e,1) & =1(e)^{1-1}\,i+{e}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡e\,j \\  & =i+e\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ and $h(x,y)=y{e}^{x}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=f\,∇\,h+h\,∇\,f\,\,
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y})={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y})=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{x})=y{e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{x})={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j=y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+{e}^{x}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =x{e}^{y}(y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+{e}^{x}\text{ }j)+y{e}^{x}({e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =xy{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+xy{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(x+1)y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+x(1+y){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate $∇h(x,y)$ at $(1,-1)$ if $h(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}+xy}.$
Given $h(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x.$ Find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $\mathrm{∇}h(x,y,z)=\mathbf{0}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =2x-2{y}^{2} \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =4z-4yx \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+4yz-2{z}^{2}-2{y}^{2}x) \\  & =4y-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=2(x-{y}^{2})\,i+4(z-yx)\,j+4(y-z)\,k.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-{y}^{2})\,i+4(z-yx)\,j+4(y-z)\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-{y}^{2} &=0, \\ z-yx &=0, \\ y-z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The first equation gives $x={y}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain $z={y}^{3}.$ Substituting $z={y}^{3}$ into the third equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=-1,$ we get $x=(-1)^{2}=1$ and $z=(-1)^{3}=-1.$

- For $y=0,$ we obtain $x={0}^{2}=0$ and $z={0}^{3}=0.$

- For $y=1,$ gives $x={1}^{2}=1$ and $z={1}^{3}=1.$

Finally, $∇h(x,y,z)=0$ at three points: $(1,-1,-1),$ $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,1).$

question.:question/problem:
Given $h(x,y,z)=xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}.$ Find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $\mathrm{∇}h(x,y,z)=\mathbf{0}.$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}) \\  & =xy{e}^{x}+y{e}^{x}+0 \\  & =y(x+1){e}^{x} \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}) \\  & =x{e}^{x}+0 \\  & =x{e}^{x} \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{e}^{x}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z}) \\  & =0+2z{e}^{z}+{z}^{2}{e}^{z} \\  & =z(2+z){e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=y(x+1){e}^{x}\,i+x{e}^{x}\,j+z(2+z){e}^{z}\,k.$

Now, we solve $∇h(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x+1){e}^{x}\,i+x{e}^{x}\,j+z(2+z){e}^{z}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{cases}y(x+1){e}^{x}=0 \\ x{e}^{x}=0 \\ z(2+z){e}^{z}=0\end{cases}
$$

The second equation gives $x=0.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0+1){e}^{0} & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the third equation, we get  $z=0$ or $z=-2.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(0,0,0)$ and $(0,0,-2).$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $$
\displaystyle T(\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix})=\begin{bmatrix}u\operatorname{ln}⁡v \\ {u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x=u\operatorname{ln}⁡v$ and $y={u}^{2}{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{u}{v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \frac{u}{v} \\ 2u{v}^{2} & 2{u}^{2}v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot 2{u}^{2}v-\frac{u}{v}\cdot 2u{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y)$ find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-y))\,j \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-y)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-y)\,j \\ ∇f(0,\pi ) & =2(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}-\pi )\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}-\pi )\,j \\  & =0\,i+j \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(0,\pi )\cdot ⟨x-0,\,y-\pi ⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨0,1⟩\cdot ⟨x,\,y-\pi ⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: At which point on the curve ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=xy$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{i}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,j \\  & =(-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ -2y-x & =0 \\ x & =-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-2y$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ (-2y)^{2}-{y}^{2} & =(-2y)y \\ 4{y}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =-2{y}^{2} \\ 5{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $y=0,$ we get $x=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $(x-y)^{2}=2x-y.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2} & =2x-y \\ (x-y)^{2}-2x+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=(x-y)^{2}-2x+y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,0)={f}_{y}(2,0)i-{f}_{x}(2,0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)^{2}-2x+y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)^{2}-2x+y)j \\  & =(-2(x-y)+1)i-(2(x-y)-2)j \\ t(2,0) & =(-2((2)-(0))+1)\,i-((2((2)-(0))-2)\,j \\  & =-3\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-3\,i-2\,j.$

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=3xy+4x+6y-5{y}^{2}$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy+4x+6y-5{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3xy+4x+6y-5{y}^{2})j \\  & =(3y+4)\,i+(3x+6-10y)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,2) & =(3(2)+4)\,i+(3(1)+6-10(2))\,j \\  & =10\,i-11\,j \\  & =⟨10,-11⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨10,-11⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: At which point on the curve $x{y}^{2}=3-2y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{i}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{y}^{2}+2y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,j \\  & =(2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2xy+2 & =0 \\ xy+1 & =0 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{1}{x}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{\left(-\frac{1}{x}\right)}^{2} & =3-2\left(-\frac{1}{x}\right) \\ \frac{1}{x} & =3+\frac{2}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $x=-\frac{1}{3},$ we get $y=3,$ and the corresponding point is $(-\frac{1}{3},3).$

question.:question/problem: At which points on the curve $2xy=2x-y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy & =2x-y \\ 2xy-2x+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy-2x+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2x+y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2x+y)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i-(2y-2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $2\,i-j,$ we must have $t\cdot (2\,i-j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (2\,i-j) & =0 \\ ((2x+1)\,i-(2y-2)\,j)\cdot (2\,i-j) & =0 \\ (4x+2)+(2y-2) & =0 \\ 4x+2y & =0 \\ y & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-2x$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy & =2x-y \\ 2x(-2x) & =2x-(-2x) \\ -4{x}^{2} & =4x \\ 4{x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ 4x(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-1\,\text{or}\,x=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- For $x=-1,$ we get $y=2,$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,2).$

- For $x=0,$ we get $y=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y+5xy-5x{y}^{2}$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(3,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(3,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+5xy-5x{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+5xy-5x{y}^{2})j \\  & =(2xy+5y-5{y}^{2})i+({x}^{2}+5x-10xy)j \\ ∇\,f(3,2) & =(2(3)(2)+5(2)-5(2)^{2})i+((3)^{2}+5(3)-10(3)(2))j \\  & =2\,i-36\,j \\  & =⟨2,-36⟩\end{aligned}
