Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=-3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

Now, since the vector field $F=-3\,j$ is parallel to ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through ${C}_{2}$ will cancel with the net outflow through ${C}_{4}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s\,⟹\,{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x=- 2 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)}\, y=- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)}\, z=3 u \cos{\left(v \right)}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =- 2 \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & =- 2 u \cos{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} & =2 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =- 4 \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & =- 4 u \sin{\left(w \right)} \cos{\left(v \right)} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} & =- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =3 \cos{\left(v \right)} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & =- 3 u \sin{\left(v \right)} & \frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}- 2 \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} & - 2 u \cos{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} & 2 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)} \\ - 4 \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)} & - 4 u \sin{\left(w \right)} \cos{\left(v \right)} & - 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} \\ 3 \cos{\left(v \right)} & - 3 u \sin{\left(v \right)} & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(3 \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)(-1)^{3+1}\begin{vmatrix}- 2 u \cos{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} & 2 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)} \\ - 4 u \sin{\left(w \right)} \cos{\left(v \right)} & - 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)}\end{vmatrix}+\left(- 3 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\right)(-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix}- 2 \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)} & 2 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)} \\ - 4 \sin{\left(v \right)} \sin{\left(w \right)} & - 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos{\left(w \right)}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(24 u^{2} \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(v \right)}\right)\left(\cos^2 w+\sin^2 w\right)+\left(24 u^{2} \sin^{3}{\left(v \right)}\right)\left(\cos^2 w+\sin^2 w\right) \\  & =\left(24 u^{2} \sin{\left(v \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(v \right)}\right)+\left(24 u^{2} \sin^{3}{\left(v \right)}\right) \\  & =24 u^{2} \sin{\left(v \right)}\left(\cos^2 v+\sin^2 v\right) \\  & =24 u^{2} \sin{\left(v \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T$ that maps the $uvw$-space into the $xyz$-space by means of the equations

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation

question.:question/problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)=2 x y^{2} + 2 y z.$ Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $r(t)=⟨e^{t},t + 3,e^{- t}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2],$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

In our case, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨1,3,1⟩ \\ r(2) & =⟨e^{2},5,e^{-2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,3,1)$ and $(e^{2},5,e^{-2}).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(e^{2},5,e^{-2})-f(1,3,1) \\  & =\left(2 \left(e^{2}\right) \left(5\right)^{2} + 2 \left(5\right) \left(e^{-2}\right)\right)-\left(2 \left(1\right) \left(3\right)^{2} + 2 \left(3\right) \left(1\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{10}{e^{2}} + 50 e^{2}\right)-\left(24\right) \\  & =-24 + \frac{10}{e^{2}} + 50 e^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where $D=\{(x,y):1\le x\le 5,\quad 2\le x^{2} + 4 y\le 3\}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le x\le 5,\quad 2\le x^{2} + 4 y\le 3,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x^{2} + 4 y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):1\le u\le 5,\,2\le v\le 3\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\2 x & 4\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving the transformation equations gives $x=u,\ y=- \frac{u^{2}}{4} + \frac{v}{4}$, so the transformation is one-to-one on this domain.

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D e^{x^{2} + x + 4 y}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y & =\iint_D e^{x+(x^{2} + 4 y)}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & =\iint_\Delta e^{u + v}\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\iint_\Delta \left(e^{u + v}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{5} [\int_{2}^{3} e^{u} e^{v}\,\mathrm{d}v]\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{5} \left(e^{u}\right)[\int_{2}^{3} e^{v}\,\mathrm{d}v]\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{5} \left(e^{u}\right)\left[e^{v}\right]_{2}^{3}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{1}^{5} \left(e^{u}\right)\left(\left(e^{3}\right)-(\left(e^{2}\right))\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(- e^{2} + e^{3}\right)\int_{1}^{5} e^{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(- e^{2} + e^{3}\right)\left[e^{u}\right]_{1}^{5} \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(- e^{2} + e^{3}\right)\left(\left(e^{5}\right)-(\left(e\right))\right) \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(e^{5} - e\right)\cdot \left(- e^{2} + e^{3}\right) \\ & =\frac{e^{3}}{4} - \frac{e^{4}}{4} - \frac{e^{7}}{4} + \frac{e^{8}}{4}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,4\le v\le 5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{4}^{5}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{{v}^{2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{4}^{5}{v}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{4}^{5}{v}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{4}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{4}^{5}{v}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}{\int }_{4}^{5}{v}^{2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\,{|}_{4}^{5} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{9}\cdot (125-64) \\  & =\frac{122\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 9,\,2\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{{v}^{2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}{v}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}{v}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{9}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}{v}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡9-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}{v}^{2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\,{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{9}\cdot (64-8) \\  & =\frac{112\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$\iint_S(x-y)\,\text{d}S,$$

where $r(u,v)=⟨2u+2v,\,2u-2v,\,3v⟩$ for $0\le u\le 3$ and $0\le v\le 3.$

*Hint: $‖r_u′\times r_v′‖=2\sqrt{34}.$*

{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{34}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$f(r(u,v))=(2u+2v)-(2u-2v)=4v.$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as

$$\begin{aligned}\iint_S(x-y)\,\text{d}S&=\iint_D f(r(u,v))‖r_u′\times r_v′‖\,\text{d}A\\&=2\sqrt{34}\iint_D 4v\,\text{d}A\\&=2\sqrt{34}\int_0^{3}4v\,\text{d}v\cdot\int_0^{3}1\,\text{d}u\\&=2\sqrt{34}[2v^{2}]_0^{3}[u]_0^{3}\\&=2\sqrt{34}(18-0)(3-0)\\&=108\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x^{2} - x y - 3 y=5.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-2,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=x^{2} - x y - 3 y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=5.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-2,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-2,-1)=f_y(-2,-1)i-f_x(-2,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^{2} - x y - 3 y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^{2} - x y - 3 y)\,j \\ &=(- x - 3)\,i-(2 x - y)\,j \\ t(-2,-1)&=(- \left(-2\right) - 3)\,i-(2 \left(-2\right) - \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(-1)\,i-(-3)\,j \\ &=-i+3\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-i+3\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)}=-4 - e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-4 - e.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)=f_y(1,e)i-f_x(1,e)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(- x - \frac{3 x}{y})\,i-(- 2 x - y - 3 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(1,e)&=(- \left(1\right) - \frac{3 \left(1\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(- 2 \left(1\right) - \left(e\right) - 3 \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(- \frac{3}{e} - 1)\,i-(-5 - e)\,j \\ &=-\left(1 + \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(e + 5\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-\left(1 + \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(e + 5\right)\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y=0.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,1)=f_y(2,1)i-f_x(2,1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + 4 y)\,j \\ &=(4 x + 4)\,i-(- 6 x + 4 y)\,j \\ t(2,1)&=(4 \left(2\right) + 4)\,i-(- 6 \left(2\right) + 4 \left(1\right))\,j \\ &=(12)\,i-(-8)\,j \\ &=12\, i+8\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $12\, i+8\, j.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=4 x^{2} + x y - y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=17.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,1)=f_y(2,1)i-f_x(2,1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(4 x^{2} + x y - y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(4 x^{2} + x y - y)\,j \\ &=(x - 1)\,i-(8 x + y)\,j \\ t(2,1)&=(\left(2\right) - 1)\,i-(8 \left(2\right) + \left(1\right))\,j \\ &=(1)\,i-(17)\,j \\ &=i-17\, j\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} - x y + x \ln{\left(y \right)}=-14 + 2 e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-2,e).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} - x y + x \ln{\left(y \right)},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-14 + 2 e.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-2,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-2,e)=f_y(-2,e)i-f_x(-2,e)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-2,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} - x y + x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} - x y + x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(- x + \frac{x}{y})\,i-(- 6 x - y + \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(-2,e)&=(- \left(-2\right) + \frac{\left(-2\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(- 6 \left(-2\right) - \left(e\right) + \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(2 - \frac{2}{e})\,i-(13 - e)\,j \\ &=\left(2 - \frac{2}{e}\right)\, i-\left(13 - e\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $\left(2 - \frac{2}{e}\right)\, i-\left(13 - e\right)\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)}=12 + 2 e^{2}.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(2,e^{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=12 + 2 e^{2}.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,e^{2})$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,e^{2})=f_y(2,e^{2})i-f_x(2,e^{2})j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,e^{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x^{2} + x y + 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(x + \frac{4 x}{y})\,i-(- 2 x + y + 4 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(2,e^{2})&=(\left(2\right) + \frac{4 \left(2\right)}{\left(e^{2}\right)})\,i-(- 2 \left(2\right) + \left(e^{2}\right) + 4 \ln{\left(\left(e^{2}\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(\frac{8}{e^{2}} + 2)\,i-(4 + e^{2})\,j \\ &=\left(\frac{8}{e^{2}} + 2\right)\, i-\left(4 + e^{2}\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $\left(\frac{8}{e^{2}} + 2\right)\, i-\left(4 + e^{2}\right)\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $4 x^{2} + x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)}=7 - e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,e).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=4 x^{2} + x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=7 - e.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,e)=f_y(-1,e)i-f_x(-1,e)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(4 x^{2} + x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(4 x^{2} + x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(x - \frac{3 x}{y})\,i-(8 x + y - 3 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(-1,e)&=(\left(-1\right) - \frac{3 \left(-1\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(8 \left(-1\right) + \left(e\right) - 3 \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(-1 + \frac{3}{e})\,i-(-11 + e)\,j \\ &=-\left(1 - \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(11 - e\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-\left(1 - \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(11 - e\right)\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y=-6.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(-1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-6.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(-1,-1)=f_y(-1,-1)i-f_x(-1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} + x y + 4 y)\,j \\ &=(x + 4)\,i-(- 6 x + y)\,j \\ t(-1,-1)&=(\left(-1\right) + 4)\,i-(- 6 \left(-1\right) + \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(3)\,i-(5)\,j \\ &=3\, i-5\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $3\, i-5\, j.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- 3 x^{2} - x y - y=-1.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, if we set $f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} - x y - y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,-1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,-1)=f_y(1,-1)i-f_x(1,-1)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- 3 x^{2} - x y - y)\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- 3 x^{2} - x y - y)\,j \\ &=(- x - 1)\,i-(- 6 x - y)\,j \\ t(1,-1)&=(- \left(1\right) - 1)\,i-(- 6 \left(1\right) - \left(-1\right))\,j \\ &=(-2)\,i-(-5)\,j \\ &=-2\, i+5\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-2\, i+5\, j.$

Consider the vector field $F=3\,i$ and a square $C$ with side length $10$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/a2/a2964076c4126d6277625260c45479d1a4fb2028f7e75223a0f5942b15f5a2d2.png)

Now, since the vector field $F=3\,i$ is parallel to ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{4},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net outflow through ${C}_{1}$ will cancel with the net inflow through ${C}_{3}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s\,⟹\,{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

question.:question/problem:
The Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4,\,y=3\sqrt{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$

is given by

{{field-1}}
$=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4 \\ \frac{x+4}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2 \\ \frac{y-2}{3\sqrt{3}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-2)^{2}}{(3\sqrt{3})^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-2)^{2}}{27} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{27} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{27}=1.
$$

question.:question/problem:
The Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=5\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$

is given by

{{field-1}}
$=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{5\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(5\sqrt{2})^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{50} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{3\sqrt{7}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(3\sqrt{7})^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{63} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{50}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{63}={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.
$$

So, the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{50}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{63}=1.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the ellipse

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{x}{4} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{y}{7} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{7}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{49} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

 
Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{49} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{49}=1.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the change of variables 

$$
u=2 x + y,\quad v=y + 2 z,\quad w=3 z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R \left(\left(2 x + y\right) \left(y + 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z):0\le 2 x + y\le 2,\quad 0\le y + 2 z\le 2,\quad 0\le z\le 2\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the change of variables 

$$
u=3 x - 2 y,\quad v=y + 2 z,\quad w=2 z
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R \left(\left(3 x - 2 y\right) \left(y + 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z):0\le 3 x - 2 y\le 1,\quad 0\le y + 2 z\le 3,\quad 0\le z\le 2\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=3 x - 2 y,\quad v=y + 2 z,\quad w=2 z
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v,w):0\le u\le 1,\quad 0\le v\le 3,\quad 0\le w\le 4\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(2\right)(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(2\right)\left(\left(3\right)\cdot \left(1\right)-\left(-2\right)\cdot \left(0\right)\right) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R \left(\left(3 x - 2 y\right) \left(y + 2 z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta \left(u v\right)\cdot \left|\frac{1}{6}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\iiint_\Delta \left(\frac{u v}{6}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{4}\left(\frac{u v}{6}\right)\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left[\frac{u v w}{6}\right]_{w=0}^{w=4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{u v \left(4\right)}{6}\right)-\left(\frac{u v \left(0\right)}{6}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\left(\frac{2 u v}{3}\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{3}\left(\frac{2 u v}{3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(\left[\frac{u v^{2}}{3}\right]_{v=0}^{v=3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(\left(\frac{u \left(3\right)^{2}}{3}\right)-\left(\frac{u \left(0\right)^{2}}{3}\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(\left(3 u\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(3 u\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{3 u^{2}}{2}\right]_{u=0}^{u=1} \\  & =\left(\frac{3 \left(1\right)^{2}}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{3 \left(0\right)^{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x - \frac{y}{4},\quad v=\frac{y}{4},\quad w=\frac{z}{2}
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v,w):1\le u\le 3,\quad 1\le v\le 3,\quad \frac{1}{2}\le w\le 1\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & - \frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & - \frac{1}{4} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{4}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\left(1\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot \left(0\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=8.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R \left(x - \frac{y}{4} + \frac{z}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta \left(u + w\right)\cdot \left|8\right|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\iiint_\Delta \left(8 u + 8 w\right)\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}\left(8 u + 8 w\right)\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left[8 u w + 4 w^{2}\right]_{w=\frac{1}{2}}^{w=1}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(4 \left(1\right)^{2}\right)-\left(4 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right)+\left(8 u \left(1\right)\right)-\left(8 u \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(4\right)-\left(1\right)+\left(8 u\right)-\left(4 u\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\int_{1}^{3}\left(4 u + 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left[v \left(4 u + 3\right)\right]_{v=1}^{v=3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(3 \left(3\right)\right)-\left(3 \left(1\right)\right)+\left(4 u \left(3\right)\right)-\left(4 u \left(1\right)\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(\left(9\right)-\left(3\right)+\left(12 u\right)-\left(4 u\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\int_{1}^{3}\left(8 u + 6\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\left[4 u^{2} + 6 u\right]_{u=1}^{u=3} \\  & =\left(4 \left(3\right)^{2}\right)-\left(4 \left(1\right)^{2}\right)+\left(6 \left(3\right)\right)-\left(6 \left(1\right)\right) \\  & =\left(36\right)-\left(4\right)+\left(18\right)-\left(6\right) \\  & =44\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,4)$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,4)$ to $(- \frac{5}{2},2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+4\,j$ and $b=-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+4\,j)+t[(-\frac{5}{2}\,i+2\,j)-(-i+4\,j)] \\  & =(-i+4\,j)+t(-\frac{3}{2}\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)\,i+(4-2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-\frac{3}{2}t-1$ and $y=4-2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-2t)j \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\left(- \frac{3}{2}\right)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(-\frac{3}{2}t-1)+(4-2t) \\  & =-5t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-5t+2)\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-5t+2)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,2)$ to $(\frac{3}{2},0)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,2)$ to $(\frac{3}{2},0).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+2\,j$ and $b=\frac{3}{2}\,i.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+2\,j)+t[\frac{3}{2}\,i-(-i+2\,j)] \\  & =(-i+2\,j)+t(\frac{5}{2}\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(\frac{5}{2}t-1)\,i+(-2t+2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=\frac{5}{2}t-1$ and $y=-2t+2$ along the segment.

question.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$$
\displaystyle \frac{{x}^{2}}{\frac{5}{4}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{\frac{2}{9}}=1?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=\frac{5}{4}$ and ${b}^{2}=\frac{2}{9}.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=\frac{5}{4},$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $$
\displaystyle a=\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.
$$

- Since ${b}^{2}=\frac{2}{9},$ the length of the vertical radius must be $$
\displaystyle b=\sqrt{\frac{2}{9}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}=\sqrt{5},$ and the minor axis has length $$
\displaystyle 2b=2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\langle - t^{2} + t, t^{3} - t^{2}, - 2 t^{2} + 2 t\rangle$ for $t\in [0,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=\langle - 2 z, 0, - 3 y\rangle,$ evaluate the integral

$$
\iint_S\operatorname{curl}F\cdot\mathrm{d}S.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- t^{2} + t,\quad y=t^{3} - t^{2},\quad z=- 2 t^{2} + 2 t
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\langle - 2 z, 0, - 3 y\rangle \\ & =\langle - 2 \left(- 2 t^{2} + 2 t\right), 0, - 3 \left(t^{3} - t^{2}\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle 4 t^{2} - 4 t, 0, - 3 t^{3} + 3 t^{2}\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r\prime(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\langle \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- t^{2} + t\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(t^{3} - t^{2}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- 2 t^{2} + 2 t\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle 1 - 2 t, 3 t^{2} - 2 t, 2 - 4 t\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t) & =\langle 4 t^{2} - 4 t, 0, - 3 t^{3} + 3 t^{2}\rangle\cdot \langle 1 - 2 t, 3 t^{2} - 2 t, 2 - 4 t\rangle \\ & =\left(4 t^{2} - 4 t\right)\cdot \left(1 - 2 t\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(3 t^{2} - 2 t\right)+\left(- 3 t^{3} + 3 t^{2}\right)\cdot \left(2 - 4 t\right) \\ & =\left(- 8 t^{3} + 12 t^{2} - 4 t\right)+\left(0\right)+\left(12 t^{4} - 18 t^{3} + 6 t^{2}\right) \\ & =12 t^{4} - 26 t^{3} + 18 t^{2} - 4 t \\ & =12 t^{4} - 26 t^{3} + 18 t^{2} - 4 t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\operatorname{curl}F\cdot\mathrm dS & =\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr \\ & =\int_{0}^{1} F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(12 t^{4} - 26 t^{3} + 18 t^{2} - 4 t\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[\left(- \frac{13 t^{4}}{2}\right) + \left(- 2 t^{2}\right) + \left(\frac{12 t^{5}}{5}\right) + \left(6 t^{3}\right)\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(\left(- \frac{13}{2}\right) + \left(-2\right) + \left(\frac{12}{5}\right) + \left(6\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right) + \left(0\right) + \left(0\right) + \left(0\right)\right) \\ & =- \frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\langle 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}, - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 1\rangle$ for $t\in [0,2 \pi).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=\langle - 3 y, 3 x, 0\rangle,$ evaluate the integral

$$
\iint_S\operatorname{curl}F\cdot\mathrm{d}S.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3 \cos{\left(t \right)},\quad y=- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)},\quad z=1
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\langle - 3 y, 3 x, 0\rangle \\ & =\langle - 3 \left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right), 3 \left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right), 0\rangle \\ & =\langle 9 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 9 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r\prime(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\langle \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(1\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}, - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t) & =\langle 9 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 9 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle\cdot \langle - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}, - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 0\rangle \\ & =\left(9 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)\cdot \left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(9 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\cdot \left(- 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(0\right) \\ & =\left(- 27 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(- 27 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =- 27 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} - 27 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} \\ & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\operatorname{curl}F\cdot\mathrm dS & =\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr \\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi} F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left(-27\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[\left(- 27 t\right)\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ & =\left(\left(- 54 \pi\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right) \\ & =- 54 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})j \\  & =(2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2x)i+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)+2y)j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(2(1)(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))-2(1))i+((1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))+2(0))j \\  & =-2\,i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-2,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-2} & =\frac{y-0}{1} \\ x-1 & =-2y \\ x+2y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y={x}^{3}+1$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to point $B(1,2),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}+1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot 1+({t}^{3}+1-1)\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\big\{(x,y,z)\, :\, 0\le 2 x\le 5,\quad 0\le - 3 x + y\le 2,\quad 0\le 3 z\le 3\big\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
0\le 2 x\le 5,\quad 0\le - 3 x + y\le 2,\quad 0\le 3 z\le 3,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=2 x,\quad v=- 3 x + y,\quad w=3 z.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto(u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\Delta=\big\{(u,v,w):0\le u\le 5,\quad 0\le v\le 2,\quad 0\le w\le 3\big\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left(2\right)(-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}+\left(0\right)(-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

The map to $R$ is

$$
T(u,v,w)=\left(\frac{u}{2},\frac{3 u}{2} + v,\frac{w}{3}\right).
$$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R\mathrm{d}V & =\iiint_\Delta 1\cdot |\frac{1}{6}|\,\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}v\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\int_{0}^{5}\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6}\,\mathrm{d}w\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \int_{0}^{5}1\,\mathrm{d}u\cdot \int_{0}^{2}1\,\mathrm{d}v\cdot \int_{0}^{3}1\,\mathrm{d}w \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot [u]_{0}^{5}\cdot [v]_{0}^{2}\cdot [w]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \left(\left(\left(5\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(2\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(\left(3\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right)\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \left(\left(5\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(2\right)-\left(0\right)\right)\cdot \left(\left(3\right)-\left(0\right)\right) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=9$ and the plane $z=3$. The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above. Given that $\text{curl}\,F=\langle - x z,\,- y z,\,x + z^{2}\rangle$, use Stokes' theorem to evaluate $$
\displaystyle \oint_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C.$ One such surface is our graph $S$ with the equation

$$z=g(x,y)=3.$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(3\right)=0\\
\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(3\right)=0.\end{aligned}$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F|_{z=g(x,y)}&=\langle - x z,\,- y z,\,x + z^{2}\rangle|_{z=3}\\
&=\langle - 3 x,\,- 3 y,\,x + 9\rangle\\
&=\langle - 3 x,\,- 3 y,\,x + 9\rangle.\end{aligned}$$

So, we have

$$\begin{aligned}\iint_S\text{curl}\,F\cdot\mathrm{d}S&=\iint_D(-P g_x-Q g_y+R)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(-\left(- 3 x\right)\left(0\right)-\left(- 3 y\right)\left(0\right)+\left(x + 9\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left((0)+(0)+(x + 9)\right)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D\left(x + 9\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.
Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=9.$ Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta,\quad \mathrm{d}A=r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta,$$

we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}\iint_D\left(x + 9\right)\,\mathrm{d}A
&=\int_0^{3}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(r \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 9\right)r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 9 r\right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left[r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 9 r \theta\right]_0^{2\pi}\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left[\left(18 \pi r\right)-\left(0\right)\right]\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\int_0^{3}\left(18 \pi r\right)\,\mathrm{d}r\\
&=\left[9 \pi r^{2}\right]_0^{3}\\
&=\left[\left(81 \pi\right)\right]-\left[\left(0\right)\right]\\
&=81 \pi.\end{aligned}$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))$, given that

$$
u=- 8 x\qquad v=y\qquad w=z.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation

$$
T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T$ is $\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}$.

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}$, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$.

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=-8 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=1 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}-8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-8\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-8\left(1\cdot 1-0\right) \\ &=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=- \frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}2\left(xy\right) \\ yz \\ xz\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=2\left(xy\right),\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2\left(y\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2\left(x\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $2, 1, 1$ multiplies the determinant by $2$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2\left(y\right) & 2\left(x\right) & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\left(y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =2\left(y(xz-0)-x(0-yz)\right)\\  & =2\left(xyz+xyz\right)\\  & =4 x y z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\left(2xyz\right) & =2\left(2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}}\right) \\  & =2\left(2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\right) \\  & =2\left(2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)}\right) \\  & =2\left(2\sqrt{\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)vw}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4 \sqrt{u v w}}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-2\left(1\cdot 1-0\right) \\ &=-2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=- \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}3\left({e}^{x}\right) \\ 3\left({e}^{x+y}\right) \\ 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=3\left({e}^{x}\right),\,v(x,y,z)=3\left({e}^{x+y}\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =3\left({e}^{x}\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =3\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $3, 3, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $18$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3\left({e}^{x}\right) & 0 & 0 \\ 3\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & 3\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & 0 \\ 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =18\left({e}^{x}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =18\left({e}^{x}({e}^{2x+2y+z}-0)\right)\\  & =18 e^{x} e^{x + y} e^{x + y + z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}18\left({e}^{3x+2y+z}\right) & =18\left({e}^{x+(x+y)+(x+y+z)}\right) \\  & =18\left({e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x+y+z}\right) \\  & =18\left(\left(\frac{u}{3}\right)\left(\frac{v}{3}\right)\left(\frac{w}{2}\right)\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{u v w}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}y,\hspace{0.222em}xz⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}uv⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}a{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+bu{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y,\,xz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-2{v}^{2})+{v}^{2}\cdot (-u)+{u}^{2}v\cdot 2v \\  & =-2u{v}^{2}-u{v}^{2}+2{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}-3u{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\cdot {u}^{2}{v}^{2}+(-3)\cdot u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2-3=-1.
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the ellipse centered at $(4,0)$ with horizontal radius $3$ and vertical radius $7.$ Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate the ellipse?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of an ellipse centered at the point $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ are

$$
x=a\cos\theta+h,\,y=b\sin\theta+k,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the ellipse is centered at the point $(4,0),$ $a=3$ and $b=7.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the ellipse are

$$
x=3\cos\theta+4,\,y=7\sin\theta,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{2}{x y},\qquad v=4 x^{3} y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
y=\frac{1}{x},\qquad y=\frac{2}{5 x},\qquad y=\frac{1}{4 x^{3}},\qquad y=\frac{7}{4 x^{3}}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{2}{x y},\,v=4 x^{3} y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{2}{x y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{2}{5 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=5 & ⟹\, & u=5\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=4 x^{3} y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{7}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=7 & ⟹\, & v=7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 7\}
$$

![](images/d3/d3dd7067bbcb0a6e3c901d12a2795500e192594a14e7f1373dd325e4fd270363.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{2}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{2}{x y^{2}} \\ 12 x^{2} y & 4 x^{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{16 x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{y}{16 x}=\frac{x^{2} y^{2}}{16 x^{3} y}=\frac{1}{u^{2} v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{u^{2} v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{u^{2} v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{u^{2}}\,\mathrm d u\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{v}\,\mathrm d v \\  & =(- \frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2})\cdot (\ln 7-\ln 1) \\  & =\frac{3 \ln{\left(7 \right)}}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{1}{x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$

$$

![](images/f5/f506bb81b18dce423e50eedc19841b7a5896230413f7f1a876aa93d27e68edf9.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

$$

$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{y}{16 x}=\frac{x^{2} y^{2}}{16 x^{3} y}=\frac{1}{u^{2} v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{u^{2} v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\int_{3}^{8}\int_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u^{2} v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\  & =\int_{3}^{8}\frac{1}{u^{2}}\,\mathrm d u\int_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{v}\,\mathrm d v \\  & =(- \frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{3})\cdot (\ln 4-\ln 1) \\  & =\frac{5 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{12}.\end{aligned}

Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ shown above. Let $C$ be the path where the semiellipse is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

$$

\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0
$$

III. $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true while statement II is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/1d/1d91a85ccbb948e070db738373ffc5032f4e91a0ba8e04cd14e79276b0e798f8.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- Statement III is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves from $B$ to $A.$

![](images/a8/a8e0bffd04fb7b765d3c654f62b1958ab55a42f0d26cbc9f2b2e31f7d8e6f775.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

question.:question/problem:
![](images/51/512905447203d1d3a96781d20d586f9c4cf5cc9392fab50607b6fc77e9b00121.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y={x}^{2}$ from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,4),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,4)$ to the point $B(0,4).$

Given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=16,
$$ evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $F(x,y)=(- 8 x)\,i+(- 8 y)\,j$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the fact that

$$\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_{C_1}F\cdot\mathrm{d}r+\int_{C_2}F\cdot\mathrm{d}r.$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path $C_1$ can be parametrized as

$$r_1(t)=(t)\,i+(t^{2})\,j,$$

with $t$ running from $0$ to $2$. Along this path, $x=t$ and $y=t^{2}$. Therefore,

$$F(r_1(t))=(- 8 t)\,i+(- 8 t^{2})\,j.$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$r_1'(t)=(1)\,i+(2 t)\,j.$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$F(r_1(t))\cdot r_1'(t)=(- 8 t)(1)+(- 8 t^{2})(2 t)=- 16 t^{3} - 8 t.$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$\int_{C_1}F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=\int_{0}^{2}(- 16 t^{3} - 8 t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\left[- 4 t^{4} - 4 t^{2}\right]_{0}^{2}=-80.$$

$$\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r=(-80)+(16)=-64.$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=3xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and the circle $C$ given by ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\boxed{}\,\text{d}s,
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ is $\mathbf{n}=x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

![](images/38/386f010932b5846e7f47a605a94a5b5d580bd35dbe37512b1583d15d29f3dc70.png)

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(3xy\,i-{x}^{2}\,j)\cdot (xi+y\,j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{C}2{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is $2{x}^{2}y.$

In our case, we need to find an expression for the flux across only the part ${C}_{4}$ of the closed curve $C.$ Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $n=-j.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_C 2 x^{2} y\,\mathrm{d}s
$$

where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 - 3 y^{3}$ traversed between the points $(2,0)$ and $(-79,3)$.

*Hint: Use the parameter $y=t.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y).$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have 

$$
x=x(t)=2 - 3 t^{3}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=\langle 2 - 3 t^{3},\,t\rangle,\quad 0\le t\le 3
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le 3$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 - 3 t^{3})i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)j \\ &=(- 9 t^{2})i+j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(- 9 t^{2})^2+1^2} \\ &=\sqrt{81 t^{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} y,$ then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=2\left(2 - 3 t^{3}\right)^{2}t^{1} \\ &=2 t \left(2 - 3 t^{3}\right)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse defined by

$$
\frac{x}{8}=\cos\theta,\quad \frac{y}{2}=\sin\theta,\quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{8} & =\cos\theta \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(8)^{2}} & =\cos^2\theta \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{64} & =\cos^2\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{2} & =\sin\theta \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(2)^{2}} & =\sin^2\theta \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =\sin^2\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1,$ we get

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{64}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{64}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1.
$$

$$
\frac{x}{11}=\cos\theta,\quad \frac{y}{4}=\sin\theta,\quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{11} & =\cos\theta \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(11)^{2}} & =\cos^2\theta \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{121} & =\cos^2\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{4} & =\sin\theta \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(4)^{2}} & =\sin^2\theta \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =\sin^2\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1,$ we get

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{121}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{121}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}=1.
$$

question.:question/problem:

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}9\left({y}^{2}-2x\right)\,\text{d}y,
$$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,1)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(1+t(3-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1+2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9\left({y}^{2}-2x\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9\left((1+2t)^{2}-2(2t)\right)\\  & =9\left(1+4t+4{t}^{2}-4t\right)\\  & =9\left(4{t}^{2}+1\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =9\left({\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =9\left(2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t\right)\\  & =9\left(2{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =9\left(2(\frac{4}{3}+1)-2(0)\right)\\  & =9\left(\frac{14}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
