Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}3\left(\sqrt{x-1}+y\right)\,\text{d}x,
$$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,2)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3\left(\sqrt{x-1}+y\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\left(\sqrt{(1+t)-1}+2-t\right)\\  & =3\left(\sqrt{t}-t+2\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3\left({\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{t}-t+2)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =3\left({\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{1/2}-t+2)\,\text{d}t\right)\\  & =3\left({[\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =3\left((\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+2)-(0)\right)\\  & =3\left(\frac{13}{6}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}7\left(x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\right)\,\text{d}x,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the three-quarters of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(3,0),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}t,\,\operatorname{sin}t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}t)=-3\operatorname{sin}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=7\left(x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =7\left((3\operatorname{cos}t){e}^{1-\operatorname{sin}^{2}t}\right)\\  & =7\left(3\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7\left({\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}t)\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =7\left(-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\,\text{d}t\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}^{2}t,$ $\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7\left(-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\,\text{d}t\right)& =7\left(-9{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u)\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}[{e}^{1}-{e}^{0}]\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}\cdot (e-1)\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}(e-1)\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}7\left({x}^{2}y\right)\,\text{d}y,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the below-left quarter of the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(-1,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}t,\,2\operatorname{sin}t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}t)=2\operatorname{cos}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=7\left({x}^{2}y\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =7\left((\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}(2\operatorname{sin}t)\right)\\  & =7\left(2\operatorname{sin}t{cos}^{2}t\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7\left({\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}t{cos}^{2}t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}t)\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =7\left(4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}t{cos}^{3}t\,\text{d}t\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7\left(4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}t{cos}^{3}t\,\text{d}t\right)& =7\left(4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{u}^{3}\,(-\text{d}u)\right)\\  & =7\left(-4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u\right)\\  & =7\left(-{u}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{0}\right)\\  & =7\left(-[(0)^{4}-(-1)^{4}]\right)\\  & =7\left(-(-1)\right)\\  & =7\left(1\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}7\left(x+\sqrt{3y}\right)\,\text{d}y,
$$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(2,0)$ and $(0,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(2+t(0-2)),\,(0+t(3-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2-2t,\,3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=7\left(x+\sqrt{3y}\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =7\left((2-2t)+\sqrt{3(3t)}\right)\\  & =7\left(2-2t+3\sqrt{t}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7\left({\int }_{0}^{1}(2-2t+3\sqrt{t})\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =7\left(3{\int }_{0}^{1}(2-2t+3{t}^{1/2})\,\text{d}t\right)\\  & =7\left(3{[2t-{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =7\left(3[(2(1)-(1)^{2}+2(1)^{3/2})-(0)]\right)\\  & =7\left(3(3)\right)\\  & =7\left(9\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the scalar projection formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(\sqrt{6})(4)+(2)(-2)+(-1)(-3)}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{6}-4+3}{\sqrt{29}} \\  & =\frac{-1+4\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{29}}.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{b\cdot a}{|\,a\,|} \\  & =\frac{{b}_{x}{a}_{x}+{b}_{y}{a}_{y}+{b}_{z}{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-1+4\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{(\sqrt{6})^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-1+4\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{11}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{-1+4\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{29}}-\frac{-1+4\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{11}\left(-1+4\sqrt{6}\right)-\sqrt{29}\left(-1+4\sqrt{6}\right)}{\sqrt{319}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $a=⟨-\sqrt{3},-\sqrt{6},1⟩$ and $b=⟨-1,1,\sqrt{6}⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the scalar projection formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-\sqrt{3})(-1)+(-\sqrt{6})(1)+(1)(\sqrt{6})}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{6})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{8}}.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{b\cdot a}{|\,a\,|} \\  & =\frac{{b}_{x}{a}_{x}+{b}_{y}{a}_{y}+{b}_{z}{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+(-\sqrt{6})^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{8}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{30}-2\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{80}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $a=⟨-1,-\sqrt{3},4⟩$ and $b=⟨-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{6},\sqrt{2}⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{b}\,a+{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the scalar projection formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(-1)(-\sqrt{2})+(-\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{6})+(4)(\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{(-\sqrt{2})^{2}+(\sqrt{6})^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2}+4\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{b\cdot a}{|\,a\,|} \\  & =\frac{{b}_{x}{a}_{x}+{b}_{y}{a}_{y}+{b}_{z}{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{20}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a+{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{10}}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{20}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}+4\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{200}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $a=⟨3,\sqrt{5},1⟩$ and $b=⟨-1,-\sqrt{3},2⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the scalar projection formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(3)(-1)+(\sqrt{5})(-\sqrt{3})+(1)(2)}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-3-\sqrt{15}+2}{\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\frac{-\sqrt{15}-1}{\sqrt{8}}.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{b\cdot a}{|\,a\,|} \\  & =\frac{{b}_{x}{a}_{x}+{b}_{y}{a}_{y}+{b}_{z}{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-\sqrt{15}-1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-\sqrt{15}-1}{\sqrt{15}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =-\frac{1+\sqrt{15}}{\sqrt{8}}-\left(-\frac{1+\sqrt{15}}{\sqrt{15}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}\left(-\sqrt{15}-1\right)-(2\sqrt{2}\left(-\sqrt{15}-1\right))}{\sqrt{120}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $a=⟨\sqrt{3},3,-\sqrt{6}⟩$ and $b=⟨-3,-4,-\sqrt{6}⟩.$ Find ${\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the scalar projection formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(\sqrt{3})(-3)+(3)(-4)+(-\sqrt{6})(-\sqrt{6})}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(-\sqrt{6})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-3\sqrt{3}-12+6}{\sqrt{31}} \\  & =\frac{-6-3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{31}}.\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{b\cdot a}{|\,a\,|} \\  & =\frac{{b}_{x}{a}_{x}+{b}_{y}{a}_{y}+{b}_{z}{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-6-3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-\sqrt{6})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-6-3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{18}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =-\frac{3\sqrt{3}+6}{\sqrt{31}}-\left(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}+6}{\sqrt{18}}\right) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}\left(-6-3\sqrt{3}\right)-(\sqrt{31}\left(-6-3\sqrt{3}\right))}{\sqrt{558}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=\left(x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- z\right)\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\left(4 - 4 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(4 t^{2}\right)\,j+\left(\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4 - 4 t^{2},\quad y=4 t^{2},\quad z=\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- z\right)\,k \\ & =\left(4\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 - 4 t^{2}\right)\,i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 t^{2}\right)\,j+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 8 t\right)\,i+\left(8 t\right)\,j+\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(\left(4\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\right)\cdot\left(\left(- 8 t\right)\,i+\left(8 t\right)\,j+\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\right) \\ & =\left(4\right)\cdot\left(- 8 t\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot\left(8 t\right)+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\cdot\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right) \\ & =\left(- 32 t\right)+\left(0\right)+\left(- \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)} \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right) \\ & =- 32 t - \frac{\pi \sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr & =\int_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{-1}^{1}\left(- 32 t - \frac{\pi \sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[- 16 t^{2} + \frac{\cos{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{4}\right]_{-1}^{1} \\ & =[\left(-16\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)]-[\left(-16\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)] \\ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=\left(- 6 x + 5 y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\left(5 t^{2} - 5 t\right)\,i+\left(6 t^{3} - 6 t\right)\,j+\left(\sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5 t^{2} - 5 t,\quad y=6 t^{3} - 6 t,\quad z=\sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(- 6 x + 5 y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k \\ & =\left(30 t^{3} - 30 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=\left\langle 4 x - \frac{1}{z},\,4 y + \frac{2}{z},\,3 z\right\rangle,\quad r(u,v)=\left\langle u e^{v},\,u e^{- v},\,u\right\rangle,\quad (u,v)\in D\subset\mathbb R^2.
$$

Assume $D\subset\{(u,v):u>0\}$, so the vector field is defined on $S$.

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
\iint_S F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf S=\iint_D \boxed{}\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint_S F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf S=\iint_S F\cdot n\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D F(r(u,v))\cdot (r'_u\times r'_v)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'_u & =\left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\right\rangle \\  & =\left\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u e^{v}),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u e^{- v}),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u)\right\rangle \\  & =\left\langle e^{v},\,e^{- v},\,1\right\rangle \\ r'_v & =\left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\right\rangle \\  & =\left\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u e^{v}),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u e^{- v}),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u)\right\rangle \\  & =\left\langle u e^{v},\,- u e^{- v},\,0\right\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}r'_u\times r'_v & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\e^{v}&e^{- v}&1\\u e^{v}&- u e^{- v}&0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}e^{- v}&1\\- u e^{- v}&0\end{vmatrix},-\begin{vmatrix}e^{v}&1\\u e^{v}&0\end{vmatrix},\begin{vmatrix}e^{v}&e^{- v}\\u e^{v}&- u e^{- v}\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle \\  & =\left\langle u e^{- v},\,u e^{v},\,- 2 u\right\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves and lines.
$$
\displaystyle y = \frac{3}{x}, y = \frac{7}{x}, y = 4x, y = 5x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
xy=3,\,xy=7,\,\frac{y}{x}=4,\,\frac{y}{x}=5
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u=xy,\,v=\frac{y}{x}
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=xy$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & xy=3\,⟹\,u=3 \\  & xy=7\,⟹\,u=7\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=\frac{y}{x}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{y}{x}=4\,⟹\,v=4 \\  & \frac{y}{x}=5\,⟹\,v=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 7,\,4\le v\le 5\}
$$

![](images/3d/3dc524083463c8c370ff1f79d68093f0d3f2c2fe1ceb5cd47824782e35a0bac9.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x \\ -\frac{y}{x^2} & \frac{1}{x}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{y}{x}+\frac{y}{x} \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{2v}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3}^{7}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{4}^{5}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (7-3)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x \\ -\frac{y}{x^2} & \frac{1}{x}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{y}{x}+\frac{y}{x} \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{2v}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3}^{7}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (7-3)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z): 1\le x + y\le 4,\quad 1\le x - y\le 4,\quad 1\le z\le \left(x - y\right) \left(x + y\right)\}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=x + y,\quad v=x - y,\quad w=\sqrt{z},
$$

Write the triple integral

$$
\iiint_R 4 \sqrt{z}\,dV
$$

as a repeated integral in terms of $u$, $v$, and $w$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:(u,v,w)\longmapsto (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint_R f(x,y,z)\,dV=\iiint_Δ f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\left|\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x + y,\quad v=x - y,\quad w=\sqrt{z}
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1}$.

$$
T^{-1}:(x,y,z)\longmapsto (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z)).
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
Δ=\{(u,v,w): 1\le u\le 4,\quad 1\le v\le 4,\quad 1\le w\le \sqrt{u v}\}.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} &=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\\\frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix}\\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 0\\1 & -1 & 0\\0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}\\ &=(1)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0\\0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}-(1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z}}\end{vmatrix}+(0)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1\\0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\\ &=- \frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\\ &=- \frac{1}{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}=- w.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$ Since $z\ge1$ and $w=\sqrt z$, the branch is $w>0$.

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R 4 \sqrt{z}\,dV &=\iiint_Δ \left(4 w\right)\left|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\iiint_Δ \left(4 w\right)\left|- w\right|\,du\,dv\,dw\\ &=\int_{1}^{4}\int_{1}^{4}\int_{1}^{\sqrt{u v}}\left(4 w^{2}\right)\,dw\,dv\,du.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x - 6 y,\,v=y,
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 6 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 6 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 6 y)^{2}-(y)=0\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v=u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=16.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} \\ v &=16\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 4,16).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-4\le u\le 4,\,u^{2}\le v\le 16\}.
$$

![](images/38/387e22e062c4ff7f24d26561fe369041f11f59a2b0305f8dc7b3ce49d411031a.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&-6\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}[\int_{u^{2}}^{16}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}[v]_{u^{2}}^{16}du \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}(16)-(u^{2})du \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}(16 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 16 u]_{-4}^{4} \\ &=1(((64)+\left(- \frac{64}{3}\right))-((-64)+\left(\frac{64}{3}\right))) \\ &=1\left(\frac{256}{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{256}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y + 1)\ln (x + 4),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y + 1)\ln (x + 4)) \\  & =\frac{y + 1}{x + 4} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y + 1)\ln (x + 4)) \\  & =\ln(x + 4)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y + 1}{x + 4} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x + 4) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y + 1}{x + 4} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x + 4) \, \mathbf j = 0 \mathbf i + 0\mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y + 1}{x + 4}=0 \\ \ln(x + 4)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y + 1=0,$ which means $y=-1.$ From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x + 4)=0,$ which means that $x=-3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf 0$ at the point $(-3,-1).$

question.:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=x^{2} y^{2} z^{2}$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2 u^{2},\,v,\,v⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ Assume $u\geq0.$ What is the missing expression? Choose an integrand equal to the required expression as a function on $D$.

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=4 \sqrt{2} u.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=4 \sqrt{2} u.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(x^{2} y^{2} z^{2})\,{|}_{x=2 u^{2}\,y=v\,z=v} \\  & =(2 u^{2}\cdot 2 u^{2})\cdot v^{2}\cdot v^{2} \\  & =4 u^{4} v^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4 \sqrt{2} u 4 u^{4} v^{4}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(- 3 u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2 u - 2 v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 v,\,-3,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2 u v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(- 3 u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2 u - 2 v^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 u,\,0,\,- 4 v⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(2 t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(4 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(2 x\right)\,dx+\left(2 y\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(2 \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(2 \left(2 t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(4 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}2 t+16 t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}16 t^{3} + 2 t\,dt \\  &=\left[t^{2}+4 t^{4}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\left(1\right)^{2}+4 \left(1\right)^{4}]-[\left(0\right)^{2}+4 \left(0\right)^{4}] \\  &=[1+4]-[0+0] \\  &=5\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(x\right)\,dx+\left(3 y\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(3 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(3 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(3 \left(3 t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(6 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}t+54 t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}54 t^{3} + t\,dt \\  &=\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}+\frac{27 t^{4}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\frac{\left(1\right)^{2}}{2}+\frac{27 \left(1\right)^{4}}{2}]-[\frac{\left(0\right)^{2}}{2}+\frac{27 \left(0\right)^{4}}{2}] \\  &=[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{27}{2}]-[0+0] \\  &=14\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,1),$ then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_C\left(3 x\right)\,dx+\left(2 y\right)\,dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(2 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(3 x\right)\,dx+\left(2 y\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(3 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(3 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(3 \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(2 \left(t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(2 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}3 t+4 t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}4 t^{3} + 3 t\,dt \\  &=\left[\frac{3 t^{2}}{2}+t^{4}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\frac{3 \left(1\right)^{2}}{2}+\left(1\right)^{4}]-[\frac{3 \left(0\right)^{2}}{2}+\left(0\right)^{4}] \\  &=[\frac{3}{2}+1]-[0+0] \\  &=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

\displaystyle {\int }_C\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x\right)\,dy=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=3 \pi x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(3 \pi t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [1,3]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(6 \pi t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x\right)\,dy &={\int }_{1}^{3}\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}\left(\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}\left(\sin{\left(\frac{\left(3 \pi t^{2}\right)}{2 \left(t\right)^{2}} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(\left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(6 \pi t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}-1+6 \pi t^{2}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}6 \pi t^{2} - 1\,dt \\  &=\left[- t+2 \pi t^{3}\right]_{1}^{3} \\  &=[- \left(3\right)+2 \pi \left(3\right)^{3}]-[- \left(1\right)+2 \pi \left(1\right)^{3}] \\  &=[-3+54 \pi]-[-1+2 \pi] \\  &=-2 + 52 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/a6/a688cf79790cde240a1fabeb768a9500c98e7affc1006c39e35b89582627fb0c.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y)$ shown above. Let $C$ be the path where the elliptic arc is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.
$$

- If the force works *against* the motion  of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.
$$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0
$$ is false, while statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ is true. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion.

![](images/dc/dcc2f364085ccca85e6e6ddd8a5affac51c84f774281b817d4852bd2322bcb1b.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0
$$ is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ the force is still perpendicular to the motion.

![](images/50/508e0ac5f67d7b119ad689ccaede8894268eefe31d9b00f148ddd6bf851de6b4.png)

So, $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0
$$ only.

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [0,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,j+y\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =0\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =2\cdot 0+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\pi \,\text{d}t \\  & =\pi [t]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (2-0) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1,2)}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{y-x+z}{\sqrt{x-z}-\sqrt{y}}=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}\,\frac{y-x+z}{\sqrt{x-z}-\sqrt{y}}=\frac{1-3+2}{\sqrt{3-2}-\sqrt{1}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}\,\frac{y-x+z}{\sqrt{x-z}-\sqrt{y}} & =\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}\,\frac{(y-x+z)(\sqrt{x-z}+\sqrt{y})}{(\sqrt{x-z}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x-z}+\sqrt{y})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}\,\frac{(y-x+z)(\sqrt{x-z}+y)}{{(\sqrt{x-z})}^{2}-{(\sqrt{y})}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}\,\frac{(y-x+z)(\sqrt{x-z}+y)}{x-z-y} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}\,\frac{-(x-z-y)(\sqrt{x-z}+y)}{x-z-y} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}-(\sqrt{x-z}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (3,1,2)}-(\sqrt{x-z}+y) & =-(\sqrt{3-2}+1) \\  & =-(1+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2\cdot {0}^{2}-{0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=0$ (the $x$-axis),  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=0}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{0}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}}=\frac{0\cdot 0}{2\cdot {0}^{2}+3\cdot {0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{5{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=-x$,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-x}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{-{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\frac{-{x}^{2}}{5{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\,\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\lim_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{xy}{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

question.:question/problem: Determine $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-2,0)}(2x-y+3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

$$
f(x,y)=2x-y+3.
$$

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous for all values of $x$ and $y.$ So, we can calculate the limit by substituting $(-2,0)$ into the function:

$$

question.:question/problem: Determine $\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (9,1,3)}\frac{x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{x}-yz}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (9,1,3)}\frac{x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{x}-yz} & =\frac{9-({1}^{2})({3}^{2})}{\sqrt{9}-1(3)} \\  & =\frac{9-9}{3-3} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (9,1,3)}\frac{x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{x}-yz} & =\lim_{x\to (9,1,3)}\frac{(x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+yz)}{(\sqrt{x}-yz)(\sqrt{x}+yz)} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (9,1,3)}\frac{(x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+yz)}{x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (9,1,3)}\frac{\cancel{(x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2})}(\sqrt{x}+yz)}{\cancel{x-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to (9,1,3)}(\sqrt{x}+yz)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to (9,1,3)}(\sqrt{x}+yz) & =\sqrt{9}+1(3) \\  & =3+3 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $6.$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3xy+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+xy+{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot (-1)^{2}+3\cdot (-1)\cdot 1+{1}^{2}}{(-1)^{3}+(-1)\cdot 1+(-1)^{2}\cdot 1+{1}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by factoring the numerator and denominator and then canceling common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3xy+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+xy+{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}} & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+2xy+xy+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}(x+y)+y(x+y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}\frac{2x(x+y)+y(x+y)}{({x}^{2}+y)(x+y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}\frac{(2x+y)(x+y)}{({x}^{2}+y)(x+y)} \\  & =\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}\frac{2x+y}{{x}^{2}+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}\frac{2x+y}{{x}^{2}+y} & =\frac{2(-1)+(1)}{(-1)^{2}+1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{2}.$

In $\bigtriangleup AHB$ we have $\angle AHB=90^\circ$, $AH=5$ and $BH=2$. So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB &= \sqrt{AH^2+BH^2} \\
&= \sqrt{(5)^2+(2)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{25+4} \\
&= \sqrt{29}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $a$ is $\sqrt{29}$. Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{1}{|a|}\cdot a \\
&= \frac{\sqrt{29}}{29}a
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $c=⟨-6,\sqrt{3},-3⟩$ and $d=⟨x,0,4⟩.$ Given that the scalar projection of $c$ onto $d$ is zero, find the value of $x.$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{3y-2x}{7y-6x}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{(7y-6x)^{2}}.
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{3y-2x}{7y-6x}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(3y-2x)\cdot (7y-6x)-(3y-2x)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(7y-6x)}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (7y-6x)-(3y-2x)\cdot (-6)}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-14y+12x+18y-12x}{(7y-6x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4y}{(7y-6x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y))\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot 1}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)){e}^{x+y}}{{({e}^{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y)}{{e}^{x+y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-y).
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=xy\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))) \\  & =x((1)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy\cdot \operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡({y}^{2})\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+xy{sec}^{2}⁡({y}^{2})\cdot (2y) \\  & =x\operatorname{tan}⁡({y}^{2})+2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sec}^{2}⁡({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x+y}+{x}^{2}\sqrt{y},$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(3,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y}+{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y))+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (0+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(3,1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3+1}}+\frac{{3}^{2}}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{19}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ for $f(x,y,z)={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}) \\  & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(4y-x{z}^{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(4y-x{z}^{4}) & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂z}(4y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{4})) \\  & ={e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot (0-x\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{4})) \\  & =-{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\cdot x\cdot 4{z}^{3} \\  & =-4x{z}^{3}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-4x{z}^{3}{e}^{4y-x{z}^{4}}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differenciation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (2x+{y}^{2}\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,\sqrt{3}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(3,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point  where $(x,y)=(3,1)$, can be found by computing $∇g(3,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(3,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{g}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,i \\ &\quad +\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\,i+\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x\,j \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,i+\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)\,j \\ ∇g(3,1) & =\left(\frac{1}{(3)}\right)\,i+\left(\frac{1}{(1)}\right)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇g(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇g(3,1)}{‖∇g(3,1)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{3}\,i+j}{\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}(i+3\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(9,16).$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}4 u \cos{\left(v \right)} \\ 2 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\to\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}$, is given by

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=4 u \cos{\left(v \right)}$ and $y(u,v)=2 u \sin{\left(v \right)}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&=4 \cos{\left(v \right)}&\quad \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&=- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&=2 \sin{\left(v \right)}&\quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&=2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\begin{vmatrix}4 \cos{\left(v \right)}&- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\\2 \sin{\left(v \right)}&2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left(4 \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\cdot\left(2 u \cos{\left(v \right)}\right)\\&\quad{}-\left(- 4 u \sin{\left(v \right)}\right)\cdot\left(2 \sin{\left(v \right)}\right)\\&=8 u\left(\cos^2 v+\sin^2 v\right)\\&=8 u.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2 u^{2} - 2 v^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=2 u^{2} + 2 v^{2}.$

$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}\cos{\left(v \right)} \tan{\left(\frac{u}{2} \right)} \\ \sin{\left(v \right)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\to\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}$, is given by

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\cos{\left(v \right)} \tan{\left(\frac{u}{2} \right)}$ and $y(u,v)=\sin{\left(v \right)}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&=\frac{\cos{\left(v \right)}}{2 \cos^{2}{\left(\frac{u}{2} \right)}}\\\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&=- \sin{\left(v \right)} \tan{\left(\frac{u}{2} \right)}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&=0\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&=\cos{\left(v \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}3 u - 6 v \\ \ln{\left(u + v \right)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}\to\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}$, is given by

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=3 u - 6 v$ and $y(u,v)=\ln{\left(u + v \right)}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&=3&\quad \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}&=-6\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&=\frac{1}{u + v}&\quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}&=\frac{1}{u + v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\begin{vmatrix}3&-6\\\frac{1}{u + v}&\frac{1}{u + v}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left(3\right)\cdot\left(\frac{1}{u + v}\right)-\left(-6\right)\cdot\left(\frac{1}{u + v}\right)\\&=\frac{9}{u + v}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/ad/ad06bc93ffe1e70bf9ca543588c14a1185f306ea19646559d11cc5adadb005bd.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F=4x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where $\mathbf n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds\\
&\quad+\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/83/83bf612af65f14848f10293bea459e926cd8246c2c48ea223709becd7acc1b1b.png)

We compute this integral in two stages.

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}(4x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf i\,\mathrm ds\\
&=4\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=2\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf j,\quad t\in[-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
4\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds
&=4\int_{-2}^{2}2\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(8)\int_{-2}^{2}\mathrm dt\\
&=(8)\cdot 4\\
&=32.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds=32.
$$

- Next, consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2=\mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_2}(4x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf j\,\mathrm ds\\
&=\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+2\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i,\quad t\in[-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{-2}^{2}2\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(2)\int_{-2}^{2}\mathrm dt\\
&=(2)\cdot 4\\
&=8.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds=8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=2\cdot(32)+2\cdot(8)=80.
$$

\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}(-5x\,\mathbf i-4y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf i\,\mathrm ds\\
&=-5\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=1\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf j,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds
&=-5\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(-5)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(-5)\cdot 2\\
&=-10.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds=-10.
$$

- Next, consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2=\mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_2}(-5x\,\mathbf i-4y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf j\,\mathrm ds\\
&=-4\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+1\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
-4\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds
&=-4\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(-4)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(-4)\cdot 2\\
&=-8.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds=-8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=2\cdot(-10)+2\cdot(-8)=-36.
$$

question.:question/problem: The vector $\mathbf{a}$ is directed due north-west and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\hspace{0.167em}|=5$, while the vector $\mathbf{b}$ is directed due south-west and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=12.$ Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{+}\mathbf{b}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we have to find $a+b.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $a+b$ goes from the tail of $a$ to the head of $b:$   

![](images/15/153aff405a3ae0859ff74fcb98deb09e038db7b033cbe54223866c9fe1724fb1.png)

To find the unit vector corresponding to $a+b,$ we have to divide by the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the magnitude, first notice that we obtain a right triangle. So, we can use the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}{|a+b|}^{2} & ={|a|}^{2}+{|b|}^{2} \\  & ={5}^{2}+{12}^{2} \\  & =169\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude is

$$
|a+b|=\sqrt{169}=13,
$$

and the corresponding unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{a+b}{|a+b|} \\  & =\frac{1}{13}(a+b).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}{e}^{x/y},$ find $∇f(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x}{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{y}){e}^{x/y} \\  & =\frac{x-y}{{x}^{2}}{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x}{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}){e}^{x/y} \\  & =\frac{y-x}{xy}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{x-y}{{x}^{2}}{e}^{x/y}\text{ }i+\frac{y-x}{xy}{e}^{x/y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the gradient of $g(x,y)$ at the point $({e}^{2},1)$ if $g(x,y)=(x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =1\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})+(x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}+1+\frac{y}{x} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =1\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})+(x+y)\cdot (-2y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}-2xy-2{y}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-3{y}^{2}-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),\,{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}+1+\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x-3{y}^{2}-2xy⟩ \\ ∇g({e}^{2},1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-{1}^{2}+1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-3\cdot {1}^{2}-2\cdot {e}^{2}\cdot 1⟩ \\  & =⟨2+{e}^{-2},-1-2{e}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$ and $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=f\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,f
$$

First, we calculate the first order partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\text{ }j=2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =({e}^{x+y})(2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})({e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =2x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+2y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2y+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{arctan}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right),\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\hspace{2em} &  & \mathrm{∇}h(x,y)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j)+\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j) \\  & =\frac{y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\frac{x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j+\frac{x\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j+\frac{x\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{y+x\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}((y+x\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right))i+(y\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-x)j).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y)=({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $\mathrm{∇}h(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =2x{e}^{x}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}) \\  & =-2y{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y)=({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇h(x,y)=0:$

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x}\,i-2y{e}^{x}\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{y}^{2}){e}^{x} &=0, \\ -2y{e}^{x} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+2x-{0}^{2}){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x(x+2){e}^{x} & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0$ at two points: $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0).$

question.:question/problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =x+y,\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\text{ }\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}(x+y),\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)(\text{ }i+\text{ }j)+(x+y)(\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\text{ }i)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+1\text{ }j) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-y)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(\frac{1}{2+(-1)}-(-1))\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{2+(-1)}-2)\text{ }j \\  & =2i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,-1)}{‖∇f(2,-1)‖} & =\frac{2i-j}{\sqrt{{(2)}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2i-j}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(2i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =(2x+y+2)\text{ }i+(-2y+x+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =(2(1)+(-1)+2)\text{ }i+(-2(-1)+1+1)\text{ }j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,-1)}{‖∇f(1,-1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy+8y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2)$, can be found by computing $∇f(2,-2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy+8y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy+8y)\text{ }j \\  & =(2x-2y)\text{ }i+(2y-2x+8)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =(2(2)-2(-2))\text{ }i+(2(-2)-2(2)+8)\text{ }j \\  & =8\,i\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-2):$

$$

question.:question/problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2(-1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\text{ }j \\  & =i-j\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,k \\  & =(2x+{x}^{2}yz){e}^{xyz}\,i+({x}^{3}z{e}^{xyz}+2y)\,j+{x}^{3}y{e}^{xyz}\,k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =(2(1)+({1}^{2})(-2)(0)){e}^{1(-2)(0)}\,i+(({1}^{3})(0){e}^{1(-2)(0)}+2(-2))\,j+({1}^{3})(-2){e}^{1(-2)(0)}\,k \\  & =2\,i-4\,j-2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $2\,i-4\,j-2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/3a/3af9e0f9483bf968ebf0db637e74c0536f19d4da6f15895d03ab04f39d1d98b0.png)

Consider the picture above. Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we have to find $a+b.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $a+b$ goes from the tail of $a$ to the head of $b:$

![](images/f9/f95b72a0b508e0cdacef7de386888f3b473aeba01574ce5fb345b9fec74bb900.png)

In $△AHB$, we have $∠AHB={90}^{∘}$, $AH=2$ and $BH=2.$ So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|a+b| & =AB \\  & =\sqrt{A{H}^{2}+B{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $a+b$ is $2\sqrt{2}.$ Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{1}{|a+b|}\cdot (a+b) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}(a+b).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The vector $\mathbf{a}$ is directed horizontally to the right and has magnitude 
 $20$, while the vector $\mathbf{b}$ is directed vertically down and has magnitude  $30.$ Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{+}\mathbf{b}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we have to find $a+b.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $a+b$ goes from the tail of $a$ to the head of $b:$  

![](images/31/3164bddbade652f3268832c5c3551f5e30263ceca95a3696d0da1ef5362853cb.png)

To find the unit vector corresponding to $a+b,$ we have to divide by the magnitude: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{a+b}{|a+b|}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the magnitude, first notice that we obtain a right triangle. So, we can use the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}{|a+b|}^{2} & ={|a|}^{2}+{|b|}^{2} \\  & ={20}^{2}+{30}^{2} \\  & =400+900 \\  & =1300\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude is

$$
|a+b|=\sqrt{1300}=10\sqrt{13},
$$

and the corresponding unit vector is 

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{a+b}{|a+b|} \\  & =\frac{1}{10\sqrt{13}}(a+b).\end{aligned}
$$
