question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{a}=\langle 1,1,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 0,1,2\rangle$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First compute the cross product using a determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}
&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\1&1&0\\0&1&2\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(1\cdot2-0\cdot1)\mathbf{i}\\
&\quad-(1\cdot2-0\cdot0)\mathbf{j}\\
&\quad+(1\cdot1-1\cdot0)\mathbf{k}\\
&=2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}=\langle 2,-2,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude of this cross product is the parallelogram's area:

$$
A=\|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\|=\sqrt{2^2+(-2)^2+1^2}=\sqrt{9}=3.
$$

The lesson diagram illustrates this relationship; its arrows show general vectors.

![The cross-product magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by two vectors.](images/27/2717ed1209f60dac12c3fcb07aea25f99c49b053fe0ce440b7ce996002a067c7.png)

We do not halve the magnitude here because the requested shape is a parallelogram.

question.:question/problem:
The triangle spanned by $\mathbf{a}=\langle x,1,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 0,1,2\rangle$ has area $\sqrt{6}$. Given that $x>0$, find $x$.

$x=${{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Compute the cross product in terms of the unknown component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}
&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\x&1&0\\0&1&2\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(1\cdot2-0\cdot1)\mathbf{i}\\
&\quad-(x\cdot2-0\cdot0)\mathbf{j}\\
&\quad+(x\cdot1-1\cdot0)\mathbf{k}\\
&=2\mathbf{i}-2x\mathbf{j}+x\mathbf{k}=\langle 2,-2x,x\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude is the area of the parallelogram, which is twice the given triangle area. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac12\|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\|&=\sqrt{6}\\
\frac12\sqrt{2^2+(-2x)^2+x^2}&=\sqrt{6}\\
\sqrt{4+5x^2}&=2\sqrt{6}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both sides are nonnegative. Squaring and solving gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
4+5x^2&=24\\
5x^2&=20\\
x^2&=4\\
x&=\pm2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x>0$, the required value is $x=2$. Checking this in the original area formula gives

$$
\frac12\sqrt{4+5(2)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{24}}2=\sqrt{6},
$$

which agrees with the given triangle area.

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the area $A_{\triangle}$ of the triangle spanned by $\mathbf{a}=\langle 1,-1,2\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle 2,1,0\rangle$. Give an exact answer.

$A_{\triangle}=${{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Compute the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}
&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\1&-1&2\\2&1&0\end{vmatrix}\\
&=((-1)\cdot0-2\cdot1)\mathbf{i}\\
&\quad-(1\cdot0-2\cdot2)\mathbf{j}\\
&\quad+(1\cdot1-(-1)\cdot2)\mathbf{k}\\
&=-2\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}=\langle -2,4,3\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding parallelogram has area

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{\mathrm{parallelogram}}&=\|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\|\\
&=\sqrt{(-2)^2+4^2+3^2}\\
&=\sqrt{29}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle is half of that parallelogram, so

$$
A_{\triangle}=\frac12\|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\|=\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the area of triangle $PQR$ with vertices $P(1,-1,0)$, $Q(2,1,-1)$, and $R(0,0,2)$. Give the area in square units.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Form two side vectors with the same starting point:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{PQ}&=\langle2-1,1-(-1),-1-0\rangle=\langle1,2,-1\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{PR}&=\langle0-1,0-(-1),2-0\rangle=\langle-1,1,2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$
Take their cross product:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}
&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\1&2&-1\\-1&1&2\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(2\cdot2-(-1)\cdot1)\mathbf{i}\\
&\quad -(1\cdot2-(-1)\cdot(-1))\mathbf{j}\\
&\quad +(1\cdot1-2\cdot(-1))\mathbf{k}\\
&=5\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}=\langle5,-1,3\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$
The parallelogram's area is the magnitude of this vector:
$$
\lVert\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}\rVert=\sqrt{5^2+(-1)^2+3^2}=\sqrt{35}.
$$
The triangle occupies half the parallelogram, so
$$
T=\frac{\sqrt{35}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1,1,1)$, $B(2,-1,3)$, and $C(3,2,0)$. Let $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}$ be their position vectors from the origin.

Calculate the triangle's exact area in square units.

$T=$ {{area}}

Also choose the expression below that gives this triangle's area.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Position vectors start at the origin. To get sides of this triangle, subtract the same vertex from the other two:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}&=\langle2-1,-1-1,3-1\rangle=\langle1,-2,2\rangle,\\
\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a}&=\langle3-1,2-1,0-1\rangle=\langle2,1,-1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus the correct expression is
$$
T=\frac12\lVert(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})\times(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\rVert.
$$
Using $\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}$ would give an area based at the origin, not at $A$. A dot product does not give parallelogram area. The sum $\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}$ is not the side $\overrightarrow{AC}$, and omitting the factor $\frac12$ gives the parallelogram's area.

Now compute:
$$
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})\times(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})
&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\1&-2&2\\2&1&-1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=((-2)(-1)-2\cdot1)\mathbf{i}\\
&\quad -(1\cdot(-1)-2\cdot2)\mathbf{j}\\
&\quad +(1\cdot1-(-2)\cdot2)\mathbf{k}\\
&=0\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+5\mathbf{k}=\langle0,5,5\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$
Its magnitude is $\sqrt{0^2+5^2+5^2}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2$. Therefore,
$$
T=\frac{5\sqrt2}{2}.
$$
Reversing the cross-product order reverses its direction but leaves this area unchanged.

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the area of triangle $ABC$ with vertices $A(1,0,1)$, $B(3,0,1)$, and $C(1,1,2)$.

Use the two sides starting at $A$:
$$
\mathbf{u}=B-A,\qquad \mathbf{v}=C-A,\qquad T=\frac12\lVert\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\rVert.
$$
The diagram shows the parallelogram spanned by these sides, with $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{v}$. The triangle has half its area.

![](images/27/2717ed1209f60dac12c3fcb07aea25f99c49b053fe0ce440b7ce996002a067c7.png)

Choose the triangle's area in square units.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First subtract the coordinates of the common vertex:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{AB}&=\langle3-1,0-0,1-1\rangle=\langle2,0,0\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{AC}&=\langle1-1,1-0,2-1\rangle=\langle0,1,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$
Compute the cross product component by component:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}
&=\langle0\cdot1-0\cdot1,\;0\cdot0-2\cdot1,\;2\cdot1-0\cdot0\rangle\\
&=\langle0,-2,2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$
Its magnitude is the parallelogram's area:
$$
\lVert\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\rVert=\sqrt{0^2+(-2)^2+2^2}=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2.
$$
The triangle's area is half this value:
$$
T=\frac12(2\sqrt2)=\sqrt2.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of decreasing $t$, where

$$
r(t)=\langle t,e^{t}\rangle,\,t\in [1,2].
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(9 x^{2} y^{3} - 4 x\right)\,i+\left(9 x^{3} y^{2} - 6 y\right)\,j.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=9 x^{2} y^{3} - 4 x$ and $Q=9 x^{3} y^{2} - 6 y.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=3 x^{3} y^{3} - 2 x^{2}+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}9 x^{3} y^{2}+g'(y)&=9 x^{3} y^{2} - 6 y \\ g'(y)&=- 6 y \\ g(y)&=- 3 y^{2}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=3 x^{3} y^{3} - 2 x^{2} - 3 y^{2}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(2,e^{2}) \\ B&=(1,e)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=3 \left(1\right)^{3} \left(e\right)^{3}- 2 \left(1\right)^{2}- 3 \left(e\right)^{2} \\ &=- 3 e^{2} - 2 + 3 e^{3} \\ f(A)&=3 \left(2\right)^{3} \left(\left(e^{2}\right)\right)^{3}- 2 \left(2\right)^{2}- 3 \left(\left(e^{2}\right)\right)^{2} \\ &=- 3 e^{4} - 8 + 24 e^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(- 3 e^{2} - 2 + 3 e^{3}\right)-\left(- 3 e^{4} - 8 + 24 e^{6}\right) \\  & =- 24 e^{6} - 3 e^{2} + 6 + 3 e^{3} + 3 e^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of increasing $t$, where

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} - 3 y\right)\,i+\left(- x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)} - 3 x\right)\,j.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=2 x \cos{\left(y \right)} - 3 y$ and $Q=- x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)} - 3 x.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)} - 3 x y+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)} - 3 x+g'(y)&=- x^{2} \sin{\left(y \right)} - 3 x \\ g'(y)&=0 \\ g(y)&=0+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=x^{2} \cos{\left(y \right)} - 3 x y
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(0,0) \\ B&=(0,\frac{\pi}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=\left(0\right)^{2} \cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}- 3 \left(0\right) \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ &=0 \\ f(A)&=\left(0\right)^{2} \cos{\left(\left(0\right) \right)}- 3 \left(0\right) \left(0\right) \\ &=0\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(0\right)-\left(0\right) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=- 3 e^{x} \cos{\left(y \right)}$ and $Q=3 e^{x} \sin{\left(y \right)}.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- 3 e^{x} \cos{\left(y \right)}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(1 + 4 \pi^{2},2 \pi) \\ B&=(1 + \pi^{2},\pi)\end{aligned}

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- 3 e^{\left(1 + \pi^{2}\right)} \cos{\left(\left(\pi\right) \right)} \\ &=3 e^{1 + \pi^{2}} \\ f(A)&=- 3 e^{\left(1 + 4 \pi^{2}\right)} \cos{\left(\left(2 \pi\right) \right)} \\ &=- 3 e^{1 + 4 \pi^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(3 e^{1 + \pi^{2}}\right)-\left(- 3 e^{1 + 4 \pi^{2}}\right) \\  & =3 e^{1 + \pi^{2}} + 3 e^{1 + 4 \pi^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We used $e^{u+v}=e^u e^v$ to factor the common exponential.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of decreasing $t$, where

$$
r(t)=\langle 3 t,t^{2} - 2\rangle,\,t\in [1,2].
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(- 6 x y + 2 y\right)\,i+\left(- 3 x^{2} + 2 x\right)\,j.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=- 6 x y + 2 y$ and $Q=- 3 x^{2} + 2 x.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} y + 2 x y+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 3 x^{2} + 2 x+g'(y)&=- 3 x^{2} + 2 x \\ g'(y)&=0 \\ g(y)&=0+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- 3 x^{2} y + 2 x y
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(6,2) \\ B&=(3,-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- 3 \left(3\right)^{2} \left(-1\right)+2 \left(3\right) \left(-1\right) \\ &=21 \\ f(A)&=- 3 \left(6\right)^{2} \left(2\right)+2 \left(6\right) \left(2\right) \\ &=-192\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(21\right)-\left(-192\right) \\  & =213.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve $C$, traversed in the direction of increasing $t$, where

$$
r(t)=\langle \ln{\left(t \right)},t^{2}\rangle,\,t\in [2,3].
$$

Evaluate $\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r$ for $F(x,y)=\left(- 3 x^{2} - 3 y\right)\,i+\left(- 3 x - 2 y^{2}\right)\,j.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the fact that $F$ is conservative.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $P=- 3 x^{2} - 3 y$ and $Q=- 3 x - 2 y^{2}.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=- x^{3} - 3 x y+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 3 x+g'(y)&=- 3 x - 2 y^{2} \\ g'(y)&=- 2 y^{2} \\ g(y)&=- \frac{2 y^{3}}{3}+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- x^{3} - 3 x y - \frac{2 y^{3}}{3}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(\ln{\left(2 \right)},4) \\ B&=(\ln{\left(3 \right)},9)\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the potential at each endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- \left(\ln{\left(3 \right)}\right)^{3}- \frac{2 \left(9\right)^{3}}{3}- 3 \left(\ln{\left(3 \right)}\right) \left(9\right) \\ &=-486 - 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)} - \ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3} \\ f(A)&=- \left(\ln{\left(2 \right)}\right)^{3}- \frac{2 \left(4\right)^{3}}{3}- 3 \left(\ln{\left(2 \right)}\right) \left(4\right) \\ &=- \frac{128}{3} - 12 \ln{\left(2 \right)} - \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(-486 - 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)} - \ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3}\right)-\left(- \frac{128}{3} - 12 \ln{\left(2 \right)} - \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{3}\right) \\  & =- \frac{1330}{3} - 27 \ln{\left(3 \right)} - \ln{\left(3 \right)}^{3} + \ln{\left(2 \right)}^{3} + 12 \ln{\left(2 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The vertices of $\triangle ABC$ are $A(1,0,1)$, $B(3,2,1)$, and $C(2,1,3)$. Let $H$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the line $AB$.

The following values have been calculated from the vertices:

$$
AB=2\sqrt{2},\qquad \left|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|=4\sqrt{2}.
$$

Use the area relationship

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle ABC}=\frac12\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|=\frac12 AB\cdot CH
$$

to calculate the length of the altitude $CH$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The cross-product magnitude is the area of the parallelogram, so the triangle has area

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle ABC}=\frac12(4\sqrt{2})=2\sqrt{2}.
$$

The altitude $CH$ corresponds to the base $AB$. Substituting into the triangle area formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\sqrt{2}&=\frac12(2\sqrt{2})CH\\
2\sqrt{2}&=\sqrt{2}\,CH\\
CH&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The altitude is $2$ units.

question.:question/problem: Calculate the length of the altitude $MH$ of $\triangle LMN$, where $L(1,1,1)$, $M(3,0,2)$, and $N(2,3,3)$. Here $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $M$ to the line $LN$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The altitude $MH$ corresponds to the base $LN$, so

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle LMN}=\frac12 LN\cdot MH.
$$

First form two edge vectors with the same starting point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{LN}&=\langle 2-1,3-1,3-1\rangle=\langle 1,2,2\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{LM}&=\langle 3-1,0-1,2-1\rangle=\langle 2,-1,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate their cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{LN}\times\overrightarrow{LM}
&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&2&2\\2&-1&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(2\cdot1-2\cdot(-1))\mathbf i\\
&\quad -(1\cdot1-2\cdot2)\mathbf j\\
&\quad +(1\cdot(-1)-2\cdot2)\mathbf k\\
&=4\mathbf i+3\mathbf j-5\mathbf k\\
&=\langle 4,3,-5\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Its magnitude gives the parallelogram area:

$$
\left|\overrightarrow{LN}\times\overrightarrow{LM}\right|=\sqrt{4^2+3^2+(-5)^2}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore the triangle area and the length of the corresponding base are

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle LMN}=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}2,\qquad LN=\sqrt{1^2+2^2+2^2}=3.
$$

Substitute into the area formula and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{5\sqrt{2}}2&=\frac12(3)MH,\\
5\sqrt{2}&=3MH,\\
MH&=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The altitude is $\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}3$ units.

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the length of the altitude $RH$ of $\triangle PQR$, where $P(1,-1,2)$, $Q(3,0,4)$, and $R(2,1,2)$. Here $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to the line $PQ$.

To help you, the cross product has been calculated:

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}=\langle -4,2,3\rangle.
$$

Its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two edge vectors.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the altitude is drawn from $R$ to the line $PQ$, its corresponding base is $PQ$. From the vertices,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{PQ}&=\langle 3-1,0-(-1),4-2\rangle=\langle 2,1,2\rangle,\\
PQ&=\sqrt{2^2+1^2+2^2}=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The supplied cross product has magnitude

$$
\left|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}\right|=\sqrt{(-4)^2+2^2+3^2}=\sqrt{29}.
$$

The triangle has half the area of that parallelogram:

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}.
$$

Using the matching base and altitude,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}&=\frac12 PQ\cdot RH,\\
\frac{\sqrt{29}}2&=\frac12(3)RH,\\
RH&=\frac{\sqrt{29}}3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The altitude is $\dfrac{\sqrt{29}}3$ units.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The altitude $QH$ corresponds to the base $PR$, so

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac12 PR\cdot QH.
$$

Form the required edge vectors from the vertices:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PR}&=\langle 0-(-2),0-(-2),-3-0\rangle,\\
&=\langle 2,2,-3\rangle.\\
\overrightarrow{PQ}&=\langle 0-(-2),-2-(-2),1-0\rangle,\\
&=\langle 2,0,1\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{PR}\times \overrightarrow{PQ}&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2&2&-3\\2&0&1\end{vmatrix}\\
w_1&=2\cdot 1-(-3)\cdot 0=2,\\
w_2&=(-3)\cdot 2-2\cdot 1=-8,\\
w_3&=2\cdot 0-2\cdot 2=-4,\\
\overrightarrow{PR}\times \overrightarrow{PQ}&=\langle 2,-8,-4\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude of the cross product gives the parallelogram area:

$$
\left|\overrightarrow{PR}\times \overrightarrow{PQ}\right|=\sqrt{2^2+(-8)^2+(-4)^2}=2 \sqrt{21}.
$$

The matching base length is

$$
PR=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+(-3)^2}=\sqrt{17}.
$$

The triangle has half the parallelogram area:

$$
\mathcal A_{\triangle PQR}=\frac12\left(2 \sqrt{21}\right)=\sqrt{21}.
$$

Substitute the area and matching base, then solve for the altitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{21}&=\frac12\left(\sqrt{17}\right)QH,\\
2 \sqrt{21}&=\left(\sqrt{17}\right)QH,\\
QH&=\frac{2 \sqrt{21}}{\sqrt{17}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{357}}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

The altitude is $\frac{2 \sqrt{357}}{17}$ units.

question.:question/problem: Calculate the length of the altitude $MH$ of $\triangle LMN$, where $L(-2,0,1)$, $M(-4,3,2)$, $N(-5,-2,1)$. Here $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $M$ to the line $LN$.

w_3&=(-3)\cdot 3-(-2)\cdot (-2)=-13,\\
\overrightarrow{LN}\times \overrightarrow{LM}&=\langle -2,3,-13\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude of the cross product gives the parallelogram area:

$$
\left|\overrightarrow{LN}\times \overrightarrow{LM}\right|=\sqrt{(-2)^2+3^2+(-13)^2}=\sqrt{182}.

The matching base length is

question.:question/problem: Calculate the exact area of triangle $DEF$ with vertices $D(0,-3,4)$, $E(-2,1,2)$, $F(-3,0,3)$, in square units.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Form two sides with the same starting vertex:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{FD}&=\langle 0-(-3),-3-0,4-3\rangle \\
&=\langle 3,-3,1\rangle \\
\overrightarrow{FE}&=\langle -2-(-3),1-0,2-3\rangle \\
&=\langle 1,1,-1\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Compute the cross product:
$$
\overrightarrow{FD}\times \overrightarrow{FE}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\3 & -3 & 1\\1 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
w_1&=(-3)\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1=2 \\
w_2&=1\cdot 1-3\cdot (-1)=4 \\
w_3&=3\cdot 1-(-3)\cdot 1=6 \\
\overrightarrow{FD}\times \overrightarrow{FE}&=\langle 2,4,6\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude is the parallelogram's area:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\lVert \overrightarrow{FD}\times \overrightarrow{FE}\rVert&=\sqrt{2^2+4^2+6^2} \\
&=\sqrt{56}=2 \sqrt{14}
\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle has half that area:
$$
T=\frac12\lVert \overrightarrow{FD}\times \overrightarrow{FE}\rVert=\frac{2 \sqrt{14}}{2}=\sqrt{14}.
$$

\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle has half that area:
$$
T=\frac12\lVert \overrightarrow{FD}\times \overrightarrow{FE}\rVert=\frac{\sqrt{146}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{146}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the exact area of triangle $LMN$ with vertices $L(-3,-5,-2)$, $M(-3,-4,0)$, $N(-1,-2,1)$, in square units.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Form two sides with the same starting vertex:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{NL}&=\langle -3-(-1),-5-(-2),-2-1\rangle \\
&=\langle -2,-3,-3\rangle \\
\overrightarrow{NM}&=\langle -3-(-1),-4-(-2),0-1\rangle \\
&=\langle -2,-2,-1\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Compute the cross product:
$$
\overrightarrow{NL}\times \overrightarrow{NM}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\-2 & -3 & -3\\-2 & -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
w_1&=(-3)\cdot (-1)-(-3)\cdot (-2)=-3 \\
w_2&=(-3)\cdot (-2)-(-2)\cdot (-1)=4 \\
w_3&=(-2)\cdot (-2)-(-3)\cdot (-2)=-2 \\
\overrightarrow{NL}\times \overrightarrow{NM}&=\langle -3,4,-2\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitude is the parallelogram's area:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\lVert \overrightarrow{NL}\times \overrightarrow{NM}\rVert&=\sqrt{(-3)^2+4^2+(-2)^2} \\
&=\sqrt{29}=\sqrt{29}
\end{aligned}
$$

The triangle has half that area:
$$
T=\frac12\lVert \overrightarrow{NL}\times \overrightarrow{NM}\rVert=\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ follows the Cartesian curve $y^3=x+1$ from $A(-1,0)$ to $B(0,1)$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x+(x+y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Rearrange the curve equation as $x=y^3-1$. Choosing $y$ as the parameter gives

$$
x(t)=t^3-1,\qquad y(t)=t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

At $t=0$ the point is $(-1,0)$, and at $t=1$ it is $(0,1)$, so this parametrization has the required direction. Its derivatives are

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=3t^2,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=1.
$$

Write the given integral as $I$. Substituting both coordinates into both coefficients and retaining the derivative factors gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
I
&=\int_0^1\bigl((t^3-1)t\cdot 3t^2+(t^3-1+t)\cdot 1\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^1(3t^6-2t^3+t-1)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[\frac{3t^7}{7}-\frac{t^4}{2}+\frac{t^2}{2}-t\right]_0^1\\
&=\frac{3}{7}-\frac12+\frac12-1\\
&=-\frac47.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ follows the parabola $y=x^2-x$ from $A(0,0)$ to $B(2,2)$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $y$ is given as a function of $x$, choose

$$
x(t)=t,\qquad y(t)=t^2-t,\qquad 0\le t\le 2.
$$

The endpoints are reached in the stated order. Also,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=1,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=2t-1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y
&=\int_0^2\bigl(t(t^2-t)\cdot 1+t(2t-1)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^2(t^3+t^2-t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[\frac{t^4}{4}+\frac{t^3}{3}-\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^2\\
&=4+\frac{8}{3}-2\\
&=\frac{14}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ follows $y=x^2-x$ from $A(0,0)$ to $B(2,2)$. Consider

$$
\int_C y\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$

*Hint: Use $x(t)=t$ and $y(t)=t^2-t$.*

Using this parametrization, which definite integral is equivalent to the line integral?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The endpoint $x$-coordinates give $0\le t\le 2$. Differentiating the supplied parametrization gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}=1,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}=2t-1.
$$

Substitute into each coefficient and multiply by its corresponding derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C y\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y
&=\int_0^2\bigl((t^2-t)\cdot 1+t(2t-1)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^2(3t^2-2t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the requested definite integral; no evaluation is required.

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(2,1)$ to $B(0,5)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Use the parametrization

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\langle1+t,3-2t\rangle,
$$

with parameter bounds chosen to match this traversal, to evaluate

$$
\int_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First match the parameter to the ordered endpoints:

$$
\mathbf{r}(1)=\langle2,1\rangle=A,\qquad
\mathbf{r}(-1)=\langle0,5\rangle=B.
$$

The traversal from $A$ to $B$ therefore takes $t$ from $1$ to $-1$. Increasing $t$ from $-1$ to $1$ would traverse the segment in the opposite direction.

Here $x(t)=1+t$, $y(t)=3-2t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle1,-2\rangle$, giving $\mathrm{d}x=\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$. Use these derivatives with the bounds just found:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y
&=\int_1^{-1}\bigl(x(t)y(t)x'(t)+x(t)y'(t)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_1^{-1}\bigl((1+t)(3-2t)-2(1+t)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_1^{-1}(1-t-2t^2)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[t-\frac12t^2-\frac23t^3\right]_1^{-1}\\
&=\left(-1-\frac12+\frac23\right)-\left(1-\frac12-\frac23\right)\\
&=-\frac56-\left(-\frac16\right)\\
&=-\frac23.
\end{aligned}
$$

The decreasing parameter bounds already enforce the stated direction; no additional sign change is needed.

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(1,2)$ to $B(3,1)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The endpoint parametrization is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})\\
&=\langle1,2\rangle+t\langle2,-1\rangle\\
&=\langle1+2t,2-t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $x(t)=1+2t$, $y(t)=2-t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle2,-1\rangle$. In particular, $\mathrm{d}x=2\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=-\mathrm{d}t$; the negative sign records the decreasing $y$-coordinate.

Now substitute both coordinates in the product $xy$, retaining the signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x+x\,\mathrm{d}y
&=\int_0^1\bigl(x(t)y(t)x'(t)+x(t)y'(t)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^1\bigl(2(1+2t)(2-t)-(1+2t)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^1(3+4t-4t^2)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[3t+2t^2-\frac43t^3\right]_0^1\\
&=3+2-\frac43\\
&=\frac{11}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(0,0)$ to $B(2,1)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C x\,\mathrm{d}x+y\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})$, with $0\le t\le1$. Here,

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\langle 2t,t\rangle.
$$

Thus $x(t)=2t$, $y(t)=t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle2,1\rangle$, so $\mathrm{d}x=2\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=\mathrm{d}t$.

Substitute each coordinate and its corresponding differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C x\,\mathrm{d}x+y\,\mathrm{d}y
&=\int_0^1\bigl(x(t)x'(t)+y(t)y'(t)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^1\bigl((2t)(2)+t(1)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^1 5t\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[\frac52t^2\right]_0^1\\
&=\frac52.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$
\int_C(x+2y)\,\mathrm{d}x,
$$

where $C$ is the arc of $x^2+y^2=4$ traversed counterclockwise from $(0,2)$ to $(-2,0)$ in the second quadrant, as shown above? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the change of variables formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))x'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

The circle has radius $2$. Choose

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle2\cos t,2\sin t\rangle.
$$

Increasing $t$ moves counterclockwise. The starting point $(0,2)$ corresponds to $t=\pi/2$, and the ending point $(-2,0)$ corresponds to $t=\pi$. This interval traces exactly the indicated arc.

Now compute the two factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))&=2\cos t+4\sin t=2(\cos t+2\sin t),\\
x'(t)&=-2\sin t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C(x+2y)\,\mathrm{d}x
&=\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}2(\cos t+2\sin t)(-2\sin t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=-4\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(\cos t+2\sin t)\sin t\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x$ decreases along the arc, so the negative sign in $x'(t)$ is essential. Using $y'(t)=2\cos t$ would construct a different differential.

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$

$$

where $C$ is the line segment traversed from $(-1,1)$ to $(2,2)$, as shown above? Do not evaluate the integral.

*Hint: Use $\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3t-1,t+1\rangle$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the change of variables formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))x'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

The supplied parametrization starts at $(-1,1)$ when $t=0$ and ends at $(2,2)$ when $t=1$. Thus the limits are $0$ and $1$.

Differentiate the $x$-coordinate:

$$
x'(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3t-1)=3.
$$

Substitute both coordinates into the function:

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=(3t-1)+2(t+1)=5t+1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C(x+2y)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_0^1(5t+1)\cdot3\,\mathrm{d}t=3\int_0^1(5t+1)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

The factor $3$ comes from $\mathrm{d}x=3\,\mathrm{d}t$; substituting into the function alone omits it.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the change of variables formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))x'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

First put the ellipse in standard form:

$$
x^2+\frac{y^2}{3}=1.
$$

Its horizontal semiaxis is $1$ and its vertical semiaxis is $\sqrt{3}$. Choose

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sqrt{3}\sin t\rangle.
$$

The start, leftmost point, and finish occur at $t=\pi/2$, $t=\pi$, and $t=3\pi/2$, respectively. Thus $\pi/2\le t\le3\pi/2$ traces the specified left half in the required direction.

Substitute and differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(\cos t)^2(\sqrt{3}\sin t)=\sqrt{3}\cos^2t\sin t,\\
x'(t)&=-\sin t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C x^2y\,\mathrm{d}x
&=\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2}\sqrt{3}\cos^2t\sin t(-\sin t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=-\sqrt{3}\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2}\cos^2t\sin^2t\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Although $x$ returns to $0$, the integral need not vanish: $x$ decreases on the upper half and increases on the lower half, while $y$ changes sign. The product $x^2y\,x'(t)$ is nonpositive on both halves. Retain the signed derivative rather than replacing it with speed or $|x'(t)|$.

This uses $x\prime(t)=-2\sin t$, which belongs to $\mathrm{d}x$.

Therefore,

=\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(4\cos^2 t+\sin t)\cos t\,\mathrm{d}t.

The factor $\cos t$ retains its sign: $y$ decreases along this arc.

where $C$ is the complete ellipse $x^2/4+y^2/9=1$, traversed once clockwise starting at $A=(0,3)$, as shown above? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a parametrization $\mathbf r(t)=\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle$ that follows the directed path,

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\int_a^b f(x(t),y(t))\,y'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Choose a parametrization that begins at the top of the ellipse and initially moves to the right:

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle2\sin t,3\cos t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi.
$$

It lies on the ellipse because $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$. At $t=0$ the point is $(0,3)$; at $t=\pi/2$ it is $(2,0)$. The path therefore runs clockwise, and the interval $[0,2\pi]$ covers it exactly once.

The differential contributes

$$
y'(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3\cos t)=-3\sin t.
$$

Substituting into $f(x,y)=x+y+1$ gives

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=2\sin t+3\cos t+1.
$$

Substituting these expressions, the requested line integral becomes

$$
\int_0^{2\pi}(2\sin t+3\cos t+1)(-3\sin t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Factoring out $-3$ gives the equivalent definite integral

$$
-3\int_0^{2\pi}(2\sin t+3\cos t+1)\sin t\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Although $C$ is closed, the integrand is not unity. The initial and terminal points alone do not determine this integral.

Evaluate

\int_C x^2y^3\,\mathrm{d}y,
$$
where $C$ is the lower-left quarter of the ellipse $4x^2+y^2=4$, traversed from $(-1,0)$ to $(0,-2)$, as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write the ellipse as $x^2+y^2/4=1$. A parameterization that follows the indicated quarter-ellipse is
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle\cos t,2\sin t\rangle,\qquad \pi\le t\le\frac{3\pi}{2}.
$$
At these bounds the points are $(-1,0)$ and $(0,-2)$, respectively. Use the signed derivative $y'(t)=2\cos t$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C x^2y^3\,\mathrm{d}y
&=\int_\pi^{3\pi/2}(\cos^2 t)(2\sin t)^3(2\cos t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=16\int_\pi^{3\pi/2}\sin^3 t\cos^3 t\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$
To integrate, keep one factor of $\cos t$ for the differential and use $\cos^2 t=1-\sin^2 t$. With $u=\sin t$ and $\mathrm{d}u=\cos t\,\mathrm{d}t$, the bounds become $0$ and $-1$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
16\int_\pi^{3\pi/2}\sin^3 t\cos^2 t\cos t\,\mathrm{d}t
&=16\int_0^{-1}u^3(1-u^2)\,\mathrm{d}u\\
&=16\left[\frac{u^4}{4}-\frac{u^6}{6}\right]_0^{-1}\\
&=16\left(\frac14-\frac16\right)\\
&=\frac43.
\end{aligned}
$$
The positive result is consistent with the direction: $x^2y^3$ is negative inside this arc and $y$ decreases, so the signed contributions are positive.

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ follows $y=x^{2} + 1$ from $A(1,2)$ to $B(2,5)$. Evaluate

The path $C$ follows $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ from $A(0,0)$ to $B(1,1)$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(4 y e^{x y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(-1\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Choose a coordinate parameter that keeps the curve smooth.

$$
x(t)=t^{3},\qquad y(t)=t.
$$

The stated endpoints give $t=0$ at $A$ and $t=1$ at $B$; retain that order in the integral. Differentiation gives

$$
x'(t)=3 t^{2},\qquad y'(t)=1.
$$

Write the coefficients of $\mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}y$ as $P$ and $Q$. Substitute both coordinates and multiply by the corresponding derivative. Denote the two contributions by $A(t)$ and $B(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(t)&=\left(4 \left(t\right) e^{\left(t^{3}\right) \left(t\right)}\right)\cdot \left(3 t^{2}\right) \\ &=\left(4 t e^{t^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(3 t^{2}\right) \\ &=12 t^{3} e^{t^{4}}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\ &=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

The differential form uses the sum of these contributions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(A(t)+B(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{1}\left(12 t^{3} e^{t^{4}} - 1\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[- t + 3 e^{t^{4}}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ &=\left(-1 + 3 e\right)-\left(3\right) \\ &=-4 + 3 e
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the parametrization $x=\cos{\left(t \right)}$, $y=2 \sin{\left(t \right)}$. The endpoints and clockwise traversal give $t$ from $2 \pi$ to $\pi$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{d}x &=- \sin{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ \mathrm{d}y &=2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the coordinates and their signed differentials. Let $U$ be the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}x$ term and $V$ the contribution from the $\mathrm{d}y$ term:

$$
\begin{aligned}U(t) &=\left(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(- \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ V(t) &=\left(- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\left(2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
I=\int_{2 \pi}^{\pi}[U(t)+V(t)]\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Using $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$, combine the terms to obtain

$$
I=\int_{2 \pi}^{\pi}\left(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} + 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

An antiderivative of the displayed integrand is $F(t)=4 t - \frac{3 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{2}$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}I &= \left[4 t - \frac{3 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{2}\right]_{2 \pi}^{\pi} \\ &= \left(4 \pi\right)-\left(8 \pi\right) \\ &= - 4 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(2,2)$ to $B(0,4)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(- x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(2 y^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 2,2\rangle+t\langle -2,2\rangle \\
&=\langle 2 - 2 t,2 t + 2\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=2 - 2 t$, $y(t)=2 t + 2$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -2,2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=- x^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2 y^{2}$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(2 - 2 t\right)^{2}\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=8 t^{2} - 16 t + 8, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(2\right)\cdot \left(2 t + 2\right)^{2}\cdot \left(2\right) \\
&=16 t^{2} + 32 t + 16.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(24 t^{2} + 16 t + 24\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[8 t^{3} + 8 t^{2} + 24 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=8 t^{3} + 8 t^{2} + 24 t, \\
F(1)&=8 \left(1\right)^{3} + 8 \left(1\right)^{2} + 24 \left(1\right) \\
&=40, \\
F(0)&=8 \left(0\right)^{3} + 8 \left(0\right)^{2} + 24 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(40\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=40.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(0,-2)$ to $B(1,0)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(- x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 0,-2\rangle+t\langle 1,2\rangle \\
&=\langle t,2 t - 2\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=t$, $y(t)=2 t - 2$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle 1,2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=- x$ and $Q(x,y)=y$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(t\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=- t, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2 t - 2\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\
&=4 t - 4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(3 t - 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[\frac{3 t^{2}}{2} - 4 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=\frac{3 t^{2}}{2} - 4 t, \\
F(1)&=\frac{3 \left(1\right)^{2}}{2} - 4 \left(1\right) \\
&=- \frac{5}{2}, \\
F(0)&=\frac{3 \left(0\right)^{2}}{2} - 4 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(- \frac{5}{2}\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=- \frac{5}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(1,2)$ to $B(0,1)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(- y^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 1,2\rangle+t\langle -1,-1\rangle \\
&=\langle 1 - t,2 - t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=1 - t$, $y(t)=2 - t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,-1\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=x^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=- y^{2}$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1 - t\right)^{2}\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=- t^{2} + 2 t - 1, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)^{2}\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=t^{2} - 4 t + 4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(3 - 2 t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- t^{2} + 3 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- t^{2} + 3 t, \\
F(1)&=- \left(1\right)^{2} + 3 \left(1\right) \\
&=2, \\
F(0)&=- \left(0\right)^{2} + 3 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(2\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}

&=\langle -1,-1\rangle+t\langle -1,1\rangle \\
&=\langle - t - 1,t - 1\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=- t - 1$, $y(t)=t - 1$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,1\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=1\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=2 x$ and $Q(x,y)=- y$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(2\right)\cdot \left(- t - 1\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=2 t + 2, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(t - 1\right)\cdot \left(1\right) \\
&=1 - t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(t + 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=\frac{t^{2}}{2} + 3 t, \\
F(1)&=\frac{\left(1\right)^{2}}{2} + 3 \left(1\right) \\

F(0)&=\frac{\left(0\right)^{2}}{2} + 3 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=\frac{7}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(-3,1)$ to $B(-4,3)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Use the parametrization

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\langle - t - 2,2 t - 1\rangle,
$$

with parameter bounds chosen to match this traversal, to evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(- x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(1\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Match the parameter to the ordered endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(1)&=\langle -3,1\rangle=A, \\
\mathbf{r}(2)&=\langle -4,3\rangle=B.
\end{aligned}
$$

The traversal therefore takes $t$ from $1$ to $2$. The order of these bounds records the direction.

Here $x(t)=- t - 2$, $y(t)=2 t - 1$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=- x y$ and $Q(x,y)=1$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(- t - 2\right)\cdot \left(2 t - 1\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=- 2 t^{2} - 3 t + 2, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\
&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{1}^{2}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{1}^{2}\left(- 2 t^{2} - 3 t + 4\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} - \frac{3 t^{2}}{2} + 4 t\right]_{1}^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} - \frac{3 t^{2}}{2} + 4 t, \\
F(2)&=- \frac{2 \left(2\right)^{3}}{3} - \frac{3 \left(2\right)^{2}}{2} + 4 \left(2\right) \\
&=- \frac{10}{3}, \\
F(1)&=- \frac{2 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3} - \frac{3 \left(1\right)^{2}}{2} + 4 \left(1\right) \\
&=\frac{11}{6}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\int_C\left(x + 2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
$$
where $C$ is the line segment directed from $A=\left(1,-1\right)$ to $B=\left(3,1\right)$, as shown.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $I$ denote the requested integral. The path can be parameterized by
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2 t + 1,2 t - 1\rangle.
$$
The parameter runs from $t=0$ at $A$ to $t=1$ at $B$. Use the signed coordinate derivative $y'(t)=2$.
$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=6 t - 1
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(6 t - 1\right)\left(2\right)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_{0}^{1}12 t - 2\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}12 t - 2\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[6 t^{2} - 2 t\right]_{0}^{1}\\
&=\left(4\right)-\left(0\right)\\
&=4.
\end{aligned}
$$
 The differential is $\mathrm{d}y$, so an arc-length speed factor is not used.

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent line at $P=(1,0)$ to the curve $xe^{xy}+y^2=x^2+y$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First express the curve as a level curve by moving all terms to the left:

$$
F(x,y)=xe^{xy}+y^2-x^2-y=0.
$$

The point is on the curve because $F(1,0)=1+0-1-0=0$. For the first term, use the product rule for the $x$ derivative and the chain rule for both partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}F_x(x,y)&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}-2x,\\ F_y(x,y)&=x^2e^{xy}+2y-1,\\ \nabla F(1,0)&=\langle 1+0-2,1+0-1\rangle\\ &=\langle -1,0\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero even though its second component is zero. It is normal to the tangent line, so

$$
\begin{aligned}\langle -1,0\rangle\cdot\langle x-1,y\rangle&=0,\\ -(x-1)&=0,\\ x&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent is vertical. The zero value of $F_y(1,0)$ does not mean that the tangent is horizontal; the gradient points horizontally, and the tangent is perpendicular to it.

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=x^2+xy+2y^2$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through $P=(1,-1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a nonzero gradient, the tangent line to a level curve at $P=(x_0,y_0)$ satisfies

$$
\nabla f(P)\cdot\langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle=0.
$$

Find the partial derivatives and evaluate them at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=2x+y,\\ f_y(x,y)&=x+4y,\\ \nabla f(1,-1)&=\langle 2(1)-1,1+4(-1)\rangle\\ &=\langle 1,-3\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is normal to the level curve and to its tangent line. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\langle 1,-3\rangle\cdot\langle x-1,y+1\rangle&=0,\\ (x-1)-3(y+1)&=0,\\ x-3y-4&=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Here $f(1,-1)=2$. The figure shows this level curve, its tangent, and a normal arrow in the gradient direction.

![Level curve through P with its tangent and normal gradient arrow](images/e0/e0d4ac4ba1ada8c2611d8c6a2ea112f008a3891acb81a4312b851589453b131e.png)

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=e^{xy}+x^2-2y$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through $P=(1,0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
When taking a partial derivative, hold the other variable constant. The chain rule gives $\partial(e^{xy})/\partial x=ye^{xy}$ and $\partial(e^{xy})/\partial y=xe^{xy}$. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=ye^{xy}+2x,\\ f_y(x,y)&=xe^{xy}-2,\\ \nabla f(1,0)&=\langle 0\cdot e^0+2,1\cdot e^0-2\rangle\\ &=\langle 2,-1\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

This gradient is nonzero, so it is a normal vector to the tangent line. Using the displacement from $P$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(1,0)\cdot\langle x-1,y\rangle&=0,\\ \langle 2,-1\rangle\cdot\langle x-1,y\rangle&=0,\\ 2(x-1)-y&=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, the tangent is $2x-y-2=0$.

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x^2+2y^2=3.$ Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2.$ The point lies on the level curve $f(x,y)=3$ because $1^2+2(1)^2=3.$

The gradient is normal to the level curve. A nonzero vector perpendicular to it is

$$
\mathbf t=f_y\mathbf i-f_x\mathbf j.
$$

Compute the partial derivatives, then evaluate at $(1,1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x, & f_y(x,y)&=4y,\\
f_x(1,1)&=2, & f_y(1,1)&=4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus a tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf t(1,1)=4\mathbf i-2\mathbf j.
$$

Indeed, $\nabla f(1,1)=2\mathbf i+4\mathbf j$ is nonzero, and $(2)(4)+(4)(-2)=0.$ Any nonzero scalar multiple of $4\mathbf i-2\mathbf j$ is also tangent; only one of the listed vectors has this direction.

The diagram shows the curve and the perpendicular normal and tangent directions at the point.

![Ellipse with perpendicular normal and tangent directions at P](images/cc/cce5568a87e18aa17da2c3a8d86bcb81f735882a23cb8765df17cfa4e113c264.png)

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $x^2y=xy+y^2.$ Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(2,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring all variable terms to one side:

$$
x^2y-xy-y^2=0.
$$

Set $f(x,y)=x^2y-xy-y^2.$ Then the curve is $f(x,y)=0,$ and $f(2,2)=8-4-4=0.$

A tangent vector is $\mathbf t=f_y\mathbf i-f_x\mathbf j.$ Differentiating while holding the other variable constant gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2xy-y,\\
f_y(x,y)&=x^2-x-2y.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the given point,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(2,2)&=2(2)(2)-2=6,\\
f_y(2,2)&=2^2-2-2(2)=-2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf t(2,2)=-2\mathbf i-6\mathbf j.
$$

The gradient $6\mathbf i-2\mathbf j$ is nonzero, and $(6)(-2)+(-2)(-6)=0,$ so the vector is tangent. Any nonzero scalar multiple is also tangent; the other listed vectors are not perpendicular to this gradient.

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $xe^{xy}=e^2+2e-ye^x.$ Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring all variable terms to the left and set

$$
f(x,y)=xe^{xy}+ye^x.
$$

The curve is the level curve $f(x,y)=e^2+2e.$ The point is on it because $f(1,2)=e^2+2e.$

We need $\mathbf t=f_y\mathbf i-f_x\mathbf j.$ Apply the product and chain rules before substituting the coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+ye^x,\\
f_y(x,y)&=x^2e^{xy}+e^x.
\end{aligned}
$$

In $f_x,$ differentiating $xe^{xy}$ contributes both $e^{xy}$ and $xy e^{xy};$ in $f_y,$ the chain rule contributes the second factor of $x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(1,2)&=e^2+2e^2+2e=3e^2+2e,\\
f_y(1,2)&=e^2+e.
\end{aligned}
$$

A tangent vector is consequently

$$
\mathbf t(1,2)=(e^2+e)\mathbf i-(3e^2+2e)\mathbf j.
$$

The gradient is nonzero since both components are positive. The dot product is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f(1,2)\cdot\mathbf t(1,2)
&=(3e^2+2e)(e^2+e)\\
&\quad -(e^2+e)(3e^2+2e)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the vector is tangent. Any nonzero scalar multiple is also tangent; none of the other listed vectors has this direction.

question.:question/problem:
At which point on the curve $x^2+y=4$ is a tangent vector perpendicular to $\mathbf j=\langle 0,1\rangle$?

Use $F(x,y)=x^2+y$ and the tangent-vector formula $\mathbf t=\langle F_y,-F_x\rangle$. Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve is the level curve $F(x,y)=4$. Its partial derivatives are $F_x=2x$ and $F_y=1$, so a tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf t(x,y)=\langle 1,-2x\rangle.
$$

For this vector to be perpendicular to $\mathbf j$, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf j&=0\\
-2x&=0\\
x&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=0$ into the original curve: $0^2+y=4$, so $y=4$. Thus the point is $(0,4)$. Here $\mathbf t=\langle 1,0\rangle$ is nonzero and has zero dot product with $\mathbf j$. Every other listed point lies on the curve, but has $x\ne0$ and hence a nonzero dot product.

question.:question/problem:
At which points on the curve $x^2y-xy^2=2$ is a tangent vector perpendicular to $\mathbf i-\mathbf j$?

Choose the option giving all such points.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $F(x,y)=x^2y-xy^2$, so the curve is $F(x,y)=2$. Compute the partial derivatives and a tangent vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_x&=2xy-y^2, &F_y&=x^2-2xy,\\
\mathbf t(x,y)&=\langle x^2-2xy,\,y^2-2xy\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The given vector is $\mathbf i-\mathbf j=\langle 1,-1\rangle$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t\cdot(\mathbf i-\mathbf j)&=0\\
(x^2-2xy)-(y^2-2xy)&=0\\
x^2-y^2&=0\\
(x-y)(x+y)&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both branches must be checked against the original curve.

If $y=x$, then $x^2x-xx^2=0$, which cannot equal $2$. This branch supplies no points.

If $y=-x$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^2(-x)-x(-x)^2&=2\\
-2x^3&=2\\
x^3&=-1\\
x&=-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $y=1$. At $(-1,1)$ the original expression equals $1-(-1)=2$, and $\mathbf t=\langle 3,3\rangle$ is nonzero with $\langle 3,3\rangle\cdot\langle 1,-1\rangle=0$. The answer is $(-1,1)$ only. The other points in the answer choices also lie on the curve. At $(2,1)$, the tangent vector is $\langle 0,-3\rangle$, whose dot product with $\langle 1,-1\rangle$ is $3$. At $(-1,-2)$, it is $\langle -3,0\rangle$, whose dot product is $-3$. Neither point qualifies.

$$

\mathbf t(x,y)&=\langle 2y+2x,\,2x-2y\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Perpendicularity to $\mathbf j$ requires

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf j&=0\\
2x-2y&=0\\
y&=x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $y=x$ into the original curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}

2x^2&=18\\
x^2&=9\\
x&=3\quad\text{or}\quad x=-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y=x$, the points are $(3,3)$ and $(-3,-3)$. The tangent vectors there are $\langle 12,0\rangle$ and $\langle -12,0\rangle$, both nonzero and perpendicular to $\mathbf j$. The other listed points also lie on the curve, but fail $y=x$. Select exactly $(3,3)$ and $(-3,-3)$.

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=- x + y + \sin{\left(x^{2} - y \right)}$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through $P=(-1,1 - \pi)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Hold the other coordinate constant when taking each partial derivative. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=2 x \cos{\left(x^{2} - y \right)} - 1 \\ f_y(x,y)&=1 - \cos{\left(x^{2} - y \right)} \\ \nabla f(-1,1 - \pi)&=\langle 1,2\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it is **normal** to the tangent line. Its dot product with the displacement along the line is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-1,1 - \pi)\cdot\langle x + 1,y - 1 + \pi\rangle&=0 \\ x + 2 y - 1 + 2 \pi&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying or dividing the whole equation by a nonzero constant preserves the line. Thus the tangent equation is

$$
\langle 1,2\rangle\cdot\langle x + 1,y - 1 + \pi\rangle=0
$$

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=- 2 x^{2} - 2 x y^{2} - 3 y$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through $P=(-2,0)$.

$$

$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it is **normal** to the tangent line. Its dot product with the displacement along the line is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-2,0)\cdot\langle x + 2,y\rangle&=0 \\ 8 x - 3 y + 16&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying or dividing the whole equation by a nonzero constant preserves the line. Thus the tangent equation is

$$
\langle 8,-3\rangle\cdot\langle x + 2,y\rangle=0
$$

question.:question/problem: Given the function $f(x,y)=\ln{\left(3 x^{2} + 2 y^{2} + 3 \right)}$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through $P=(1,1)$.

Multiplying or dividing the whole equation by a nonzero constant preserves the line. Thus the tangent equation is

\langle 3,2\rangle\cdot\langle x - 1,y - 1\rangle=0

question.:question/problem:
At which points on the curve $2 x^{2} - 2 x y + 4 x + y^{2} - 2 y + 2=25$ is a tangent vector perpendicular to $\mathbf v=\langle 7,-3\rangle$?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $F(x,y)=2 x^{2} - 2 x y + 4 x + y^{2} - 2 y + 2$, so the curve is $F(x,y)=25$. A tangent vector is $\mathbf t=\langle F_y,-F_x\rangle$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_x&=4 x - 2 y + 4\\
F_y&=- 2 x + 2 y - 2\\
\mathbf t(x,y)&=\langle - 2 x + 2 y - 2,- 4 x + 2 y - 4\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Perpendicularity requires

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t\cdot \langle 7,-3\rangle&=0\\
- 2 x + 8 y - 2&=0\\
- 2 (x - 4 y + 1)&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

The condition gives $y=\frac{x}{4} + \frac{1}{4}$. Substitution into the original curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{25 x^{2}}{16} + \frac{25 x}{8} + \frac{25}{16}&=25\\
\frac{25 (x - 3) (x + 5)}{16}&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $x=-5$ or $x=3$. Recovering the other coordinate gives $(-5,-1)$ and $(3,1)$.

Thus the qualifying points are $(3,1)$ and $(-5,-1)$. All listed points lie on the curve. The following nonzero tangent vectors check every choice:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf t(4,5)&=\langle 0,-10\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle 7,-3\rangle=30\\
\mathbf t(-6,-5)&=\langle 0,10\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle 7,-3\rangle=-30\\
\mathbf t(2,7)&=\langle 8,2\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle 7,-3\rangle=50\\
\mathbf t(-4,-7)&=\langle -8,-2\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle 7,-3\rangle=-50\\
\mathbf t(3,1)&=\langle -6,-14\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle 7,-3\rangle=0\\
\mathbf t(-5,-1)&=\langle 6,14\rangle,\qquad \mathbf t\cdot \langle 7,-3\rangle=0
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $2 e^{x y}=3 x - 3 y + \frac{2}{e^{2}} + 9$. Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(-1,2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Bring the variable terms to one side and set $f(x,y)=- 3 x + 3 y + 2 e^{x y}$. The curve is the level curve $f(x,y)=\frac{2}{e^{2}} + 9$, and $f(-1,2)=\frac{2}{e^{2}} + 9$ confirms that the point lies on it.

A tangent vector is perpendicular to the nonzero gradient. Use $\mathbf t=f_y\mathbf i-f_x\mathbf j$. Differentiate while holding the other variable constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=2 y e^{x y} - 3\\ f_y(x,y)&=2 x e^{x y} + 3\end{aligned}
$$

At the supplied point,

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(-1,2)&=2 \left(2\right) e^{\left(-1\right) \left(2\right)} - 3\\ &=-3 + \frac{4}{e^{2}}\\ f_y(-1,2)&=2 \left(-1\right) e^{\left(-1\right) \left(2\right)} + 3\\ &=3 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus one tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf t(-1,2)=\left(3 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf i+\left(3 - \frac{4}{e^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Multiplying by $-1$ gives the listed tangent vector $-\left(3 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf i-\left(3 - \frac{4}{e^{2}}\right)\,\mathbf j$. The gradient is nonzero. The dot product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(-1,2)\cdot\mathbf t(-1,2)&=\left(-3 + \frac{4}{e^{2}}\right)\left(3 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}\right)\\ &\quad-\left(3 - \frac{2}{e^{2}}\right)\left(-3 + \frac{4}{e^{2}}\right)\\ &=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Any nonzero scalar multiple has the same tangent direction; none of the other listed vectors is perpendicular to this gradient.

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $3 \cos{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(y \right)}=x - 3 \sin{\left(x y \right)} - \frac{\pi}{2}$. Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(\frac{\pi}{2},0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:

A tangent vector is perpendicular to the nonzero gradient. Use $\mathbf t=f_y\mathbf i-f_x\mathbf j$. Differentiate while holding the other variable constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=3 y \cos{\left(x y \right)} - 3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(y \right)} - 1\\ f_y(x,y)&=3 x \cos{\left(x y \right)} - 3 \sin{\left(y \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

At the supplied point,

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(\frac{\pi}{2},0)&=-1\\ &\quad - 3 \sin{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)} \cos{\left(\left(0\right) \right)}\\ &\quad +3 \left(0\right) \cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \left(0\right) \right)}\\ &=-4\\ f_y(\frac{\pi}{2},0)&=- 3 \sin{\left(\left(0\right) \right)} \cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)}\\ &\quad +3 \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \left(0\right) \right)}\\ &=\frac{3 \pi}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus one tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf t(\frac{\pi}{2},0)=\frac{3 \pi}{2}\,\mathbf i+4\,\mathbf j.
$$

The gradient is nonzero. The dot product is

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(\frac{\pi}{2},0)\cdot\mathbf t(\frac{\pi}{2},0)&=\left(-4\right)\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\right)\\ &\quad-\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\right)\left(-4\right)\\ &=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Any nonzero scalar multiple has the same tangent direction; none of the other listed vectors is perpendicular to this gradient.

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $2 x \ln{\left(y \right)}=- x^{2} + x y + 2 e$. Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(-2,e)$.

$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the plane curve $- x e^{y^{2} + 1}=x y - 3 y - 4 + e^{2}$. Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point $(-1,-1)$.
